- - - - MY WORLD. I have no need of a stately ship, No fear of a rolling sea; In chosen books I.take my trip

With the goodliest conipany ; And whether I read of southern skies Or the wealth of an eastern port. I may see the world thro' an author's eyes, May dwell in a camp or court. Thro' wonderful eketcla-books that belong To an artist friend of mine, I visit the places of legend and Bong So famous along the Rhine; I breathe the spirit of old romance As I sail the northern main; I tread the vine-clad vales of France, And look for my castles in Spain. The song of Venetian gondoliers, As they guide their moonlit boats. I seem to hear, or the mountaineer's Tyrolean echo-notes. I may see the heather's purple plumes Among the banks and braes, Or wander where the primrose blooms Along the English ways. I seek the land of the midnight Bun, Or trace the source of the Nile; I find the cedars of Lebanon,
Or study Crete awhile. Whenever I tire of time and tide,

No matter how far I roam, I have only to lay my book aside To find myself at home. The world is wide and the world is fair, The heroes good to see, But a hearth and home, and friends to share, Are all the world to me; And to sigh in vain for foreign sight There surely is no need, As long as people live to write, And I may live to read.

Fox TER7aISItS AS PETS.—There are few breeds of dogs more popular than the fox terrier, and at this we don't wonder, as they are cheerf al companions, nice to look at, clean in their habits, eager and persevering as workers, and, throughout, are what they look to be, perfect gentlemen amongst dogs when well broken and trained. Nothing can be more annoying and disgusting than a yelping, barking, and jumping cur, fighting with other dogs, chasing cats, and continually returning home with marks of the conflict upon him; but when a fox terrier has been well trained he is above all this kind of thing, and is ever ready to obey the word of command. This breed of dogs can do good work, as they have a very keen sense of smell, and their activity en- ables them to kill their game whilst some other dogs would only be thinking about it. They were first used by hunts men for bolting foxes from their earths, but since the intro- duction of shows they have become most fashionable, and few young men who can afford such a luxury think their equipment complete without a fox terrier. That they are worthy of this favour goes without saying, and there is no probability of their losing their hold on public opinion. CANana IN Doos' RMS.—Dogs are often troubled with alcanker or running at the ear, caused no doubt by high feeding, want of vegetables and exercise. The first named can easily be remedied by reducing both the quantity and quality of the food, and the two latter are not difficult to provide for. The cause is heat of the stomach, and it is much better to have the trouble come out at the ear than the dog break out in sores all over the body. It is not dif- ficult to cure if taken in time, and the following is one of the best ways of treating it :—Give the dog some ground yellow sulphur mixed with a little grease over night, and a dose (size of dog to decide the quantity to be given) of castor oil next morning. The morning the oil is given, wash the dog's ear well out with common soft soap dissolved in warm water, using a small piece of *Tong when applying it. Knead the ear gently from the outside, rinse it well out, and then apply a stopping of Fuller's earth dissolved in warm water, so as to make it into a stiff mud. As is well known, the Fuller's earth is very healing, and as the water evaporates from the heat of the ear the earth dries up the little sores. This should be repeated two or three times, when it will be found that the cure is effected. Then it is necessary to see that the same thing is not brought on again by a neglect of proper care and attention. Titanium CATS—There are few households without a cat, but very often, we fear, is it regarded simply as a means of getting rid of mice, or as a plaything for the children. It can, however, be a constant source of pleasure to young and old if properly trained, and a cat over which the-neces- sary trouble is taken will be regarded with an amount of affection which will secure it proper and considerate treat- ment. Cats are capable of great affection, and perhaps of all pets except dogs are the most sensible. The first re- quisite for training is to regard the cats kindly, and to gain its full confidence and love. Till this is done it will look with suspicion upon all that is done, and the training will be very difficult, if not impossible. One of the commonest tricks is jumping throngh the arms or a hoop, over a chair back, and we have heard of a cat able to leap over an open door quite easily. To secure this, the training should begin when they are very young, or they will never excel in it. A piece of meat should be put at different elevations, gradually increasing the height ,and if the cat receives the meet as a reward each time it performs the feat then it will

She is 26 feet in length and about - 5 feet in beam, drawing about 2 feet of water, and is fitted with a 22-inch propeller screw. On board are stowed away under the flooring and seats, fore and aft, forty-five accumu- lators, each a cube 10 inches in dimensions, of the latest type as devised by Messrs. Sellon and Volckmar, being a modifi- cation of the Plante accumulator. Fully charged with electricity, they are calculated to supply power for six hours at the rate of 4 horse-power. These storage cells are placed in electrical connection with two Siemens dynamos of the size known as D 3, furnished with reversing gear and regula- tors, to servo as engines to drive the screw propellor. Either or both of these motors can be "switched" into circuit at will. At the day of the trial trip the vessel started from the wharf of the works of the above company. After a run of a few minutes down the river, and a trial of the powers of the boat to go forward, slacken or go astern at will, her head was turty'd Citywards, and she sped silently along the. southern shore, running about eight knots an hour against the tide. At 37 minutes past 4 o'clock London Bridge was reached, where the head of the launch was put about. Slip- ping down the ebb, the wharf at Millwall was gained at one minute past 5, thus in 24 minutes terminating the trial trip of the Electricity. The total electro-motive force of the accumulators at the trial was 96 volts, and during the whole of the long run the current through each machine was steadily maintained at 24 amperes. This corresponds to an expenditure of electric energy at the rate of 3 141 horse power. As this boat is the first electric launch that has been constructed in this country, and the very first in which the electric propulsion of a vessel has been undertaken on a commercial scale, no small amount of interest attaches to this first practical success. -Iron.

IN Pacatons.—One of the most troublesome die. eases at the present time of year is roup, which is simply a developed cold. If it is not properly attended to the bird begins to loose flesh, and soon dies. The first symptoms are a sneezing or shaking of the head, as if the bird was trying to get rid of some obstruction in its nostrils, or it may sim- ply be a discharge at the nostrils and a swelling up of the eyes. These all represent one disease, and as soon as no- ticed should command attention. The bird so affected must be separated at once from the others, and put into another room in a cage by itself. some only fasten the affected bird up in a cage in the ordinary loft, but as the disease is very contagions this is not enough. The room should be warm and free from draughts, or the pigeon will not have an opportunity of recovering. The remedy consists of roup pills, which are sold in nearly every market town by chemists, and of these Walton's or Guest's are the best, but if they cannot be got copaiba capsules are the next best. Some effort must be made to get rid of the obstruction in the nostrils, and for this purpose nothing is better than so- lution of chlorinated soda, which can be obtained at the chemist's, or Condy's fluid may be used. The eyes, nostrils, and month must be well washed out with whatever is used in this way, and the internal and external remedies re- peated until the bird has recovered. MAKING A PIGEON LOFT.—Some persons are able to gratiff their taste for pigeon-keeping to the very fullest extent, and whatever they think necessary to the comfort of the birds, or that will add to pleasure of the owner, they get, whether it ,cost shillings or pounds. We have heard of pigeon houses that have cost hundreds of pounds, and the inmates equally as much, but this is the exception, for the rule is that those who keep pigeons must be content to make the most of the opportunities which are at their dis- posal without going to any great expense. And we do not know bat that as mach pleasure is got out of the pets in this way, for it is the birds themselves and not the fittings of their houses which constitute the owner's hobby. Where it is possible the best plan is to devote a room at the top of the house, an unused stable, a loft above a stable, or any other suitable place to the birds, for a strong building as a basis is always a great preventive of disease, as in cold weather the birds are kept comfortable and healthy. Raving se lected the place, it must be properly ventilated, and for this purpose, nothing is better than the iron ventilators, which can be purchased so cheaply now-a-days. If inserted near the ceiling of the room these can be opened and closed at will, and the foul air thus escape. The floor is better made of cement if on the ground, or of wood if not; and, as to the fittings, we must leave the description of them to next week. CAGES FOR CANARY BREEDING.—It may seem a strange time of year to speak about canary breeding, but it will be much better for the new beginner who intends to breed a few canaries next season—and this certainly adds to the zest with which the hobby is followed, for merely keeping a single canary in a cage is not sufficient to sustain it—to prepare his cages now, and then they will be ready when wanted. The most business-like cage is a combination of two compartments, about eighteen inches square in front- age, and about ten inches in depth, made of wood, and wired only in front, with or without a drawboard at the bottom. The wood should be three-eighths of an inch in thickness, for the lighter it is, consistent with strength, the better. The front may be movable, and entirely of wire, with wire door, or wired into the wooden framework of the box. In either case the door should be sufficiently large to admit the hand, as many little things require to be done in the inside of the cage, and the door is not merely to be regarded as a means of inlet and outlet for the birds. Two such cages or compartments made In one box, and separated by a fixed partition with a small door in the centre, is the form in which °reeding cages are generally made, and are known as the "two-pair" arrangement. Some breeders have their baxes made in sets of various numbers to suit the walls of their rooms, and their fronts in sets to correspond. When operations are conducted upon a large scale the arrange- ments of the breeding-room require to be arranged so as to economise time, and hence the necessity of making every- thing as simple, yet as effective, as possible. When, how- ever, the breeder has advanced to that stage he does not need our assistance, and it is not necessary for us to pro- vide for his requirements. But as everyone must make a commencement, and it is a foolish thing to begin on a large scale, as the learning of small things give the knowledge necessary to the conducting of greater ones, our remarks will be of advantage to the • beginner, who can be content always to work on in a modest way, or enlarge his opera- tions just as he thinks fit.

MAKING A RABBIT EITTC/L—Supposing that the box of which the hutch is to be made is purchased or put together, one side must be left entirely open at first, and this will form the front, on which a frame will have to be fixed. Before doing this, put a partition in the box, fifteen inches from one end, with an arched hole in it, so that the occupant can pass from one compartment to the other. When this is done, a frame must be made to exactly fit the open side, at each end of which space will be wanted for doors. The space at the larger end should be 2 feet wide and 12 inches deep, and the door will have to be made this size, but in this door, about It inches from the top, a piece 12 inches by 2 inches must be cut out. As soon as this is done, bore holes down through the 1 inch strip of wood, and passing IEIO-ugh the vacancy into cue solid wood below. Into these holes pieces of wire an eighth of an inch in thickness, and four inches long, are to be passed, thus making a safe place for ventilation, and when either metal or leather hinges and fastener are pat on the door is finished. The space at the smaller end in front of the sleeping compartment must be made 12 inches deep and 9 inches wide, but it is to be made solid, with no opening. This being hang, and wire or wooden laths fitted to the rest of the frame, the hutch ie complete, but should the door not fit closely, put a piece of leading on the inner side for the door to shut agalpsr, and this will prevent all draught. In fact, so simple a provision as this is worth the extra troub!e in every case, as it ensures perfect freedom from draught. The hutch can be painted if thought fit, and as soon as a thick layer of sawdust has been placed in the bottom of the hutch, with a good bed of hay, all is ready for the rabbit, and he will find himself in very comfortable quarters.

div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILITY'
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY'
[Published ky 2lfr. E. .7. Kibbletokite, 31, Tavistock-street London, W.C., and reprinted by permission.] THE THYNNES.

The history of the Thynnes is singularly uneventful; except the murder of one member of the house it presents hardly any feature of interest, save in the acquirement of the property which the Thynnes possess. The Marquis of Beth, however, is fully entitled to a place in "Our Old Nobility," though his superior title is not a hundred years old, and his second title a little less than two hundred. He is the owner of Longleat, one of the most magnificent mansions in the country, which is surrounded by a park of 4,500 acres, and his landed possessions amount to 55,425 acres, with a rent-roll of £67,002, situated as follows:

Wilts 19,977 acres. Somerset Salop Hereford Monaghan 23,027 „ Lord John Thynne has also 14,981 acres in Cornwall, Bed- ford, and Devon, with a rent roll of £13,461. The Thynnes were Poitevins, who came over to England in the reign of John, to assist that tyrant in fighting his rebellious barons. For some time they were known by the name of De Boteville. Geoffry de Boteville, one of the Poitevin adventurers who came over to assist John, subse- quently held certain lands at Stretton and Boteville, in Shropshire, under the great Earl of Arundel. Twice they lost a part of these lands, but some portion of them was held by William Thynne, Master of the Household to Henry VII. Either William Thynne or his brother was Chief Clerk of the Kitchen to Henry VIII. Sir John Thynne, the son or nephew of Henry VIII.'s Clerk of the Kitchen, died, in the reign of Elizabeth, one of the richest landowners in the South of England At the time of the Reformation, the Thynnes certainly held no lands at all, save a small estate in Shropshire; in the reign of Elizabeth they-were in posses- sion of most of the great estates in Wilts and Somerset now held by the Marquis of Bath. Their rise as a great terri torial house was prodigiously rapid ; and yet, save as regards Hornsingham, a manor of 2,000 acres, held by Lord Hunger- ford, who was attainted, and whose property in this place was granted to John Thynne, they do not appear to have acquired much by any direct grants from the Crown. How are we to account for their great landed acquisitions in such a short space of time? Sir John Thynne (who was knighted at the Battle of Musselburgh) was the favourite and Secretary of the Pro- tector Somerset. I have already alluded to the frightful rapacity of the statesmen of the days of Edward 'el,, and need not dwell upon it further now. It is stated in the records of the Thynne family that Sir John was twice im- prisoned in the Tower along with his master, and that the second time he only escaped with a fine of £6,000 and the loss of several great offices and good leases. He seems to have played a very safe and clever game. He did not obtain direct grants from the spoil of the monastic houses, but he made extensive and advantageous purchases from those who did. When such vast estates were being fluna away right and left by those whose duty it was to conserve the property of the Crown, there must have been plenty of good bargains in land, and Thynne, as the Secretary of the Protector Somerset, must have had choice opportunities of making them. But whence had he the means? He seems to have had some connection with the .City of London, for in the Thynne records there is an agreement between himself and the Corporation that he should hold the office of Packer of the City of London, on payment of a sum of £66 13s. 4d. annually to the Corporation. But, beyond this, he had the good forture to marry the daughter of Sir Richard, and the sister and eventually co-heir of Sir Thomas Gresham, the great London merchants. With this lady he had as a dowry the manor of Buckland and Laverton, in Wilts, the manor of Foston, in Leicestershire, and lands in half-a-dozen parishes in Yorkshire. In the course of his life he was pur- chaser of lands in about forty different parishes, the vendors being Sonierset himself, the Earl of Oxford, Lord Stourton, Lord Seymour of Sudeley, and a number of others. The site of the mansion of Longleat, where was formerly a small monastic house, was purchased of Sir John Horsey. Most

of the extensive park and surrounding lands were purchased of the Court of Augmentations, and before the Reformation had been parcel of. the extensive possessions of the rich Abbey of Glastonbury, which had been given as a dowry to Queen Katharine Parr. I note that in the time of the Commonwealth another Wiltshire manor was purchased by Sir James Thynne; but, for the most part, the extensive estates of the Marquis of Bath in Wilts and Somerset are the same as were acquired by his prudent ancestor, whose lucky marriage provided the ready cash, and whose Court connections provided the ready opportunity. Sir John Thynne was Comptroller of the Household to the Princess Elizabeth, but he appears to have been too timid to attend upon her in the hour of danger, and to have been deservedly neglected by her in the time of her prosperity. Her acces- sion to the Throne brought him no honours nor rewards, and he appears to have occupied himself with the building of Longleat, which it took him twelve years to erect in its original form. Sir John Thynne, eldest son of Sir John, followed his father's example in going to the City for a wealthy bride. He married the daughter and heir of Sir Rowland Hayward, twice Lord Mayor of London, who brought him on her mar- riage a considerable estate in Shropshire. His great grand- son, Thomas Thynne (popularly known as Tom of Ten Thousand," because of his great wealth) was murdered by some ruffians hired by Count Konigsmark, the disappointed lover of Lady Elizabeth Ogle, a great heiress, of whom Thynne was the accepted suitor. The story, illustrated in stone upon the tomb of Thomas Thynne in Westminster Abbey, is too well known to need detailed recapitulation here. On the death of Thomas Thynne, the estates passed to a younger descendant of Sir John Thynne, who was almost immediately afterwards created Viscount Weymouth, with remainder to his younger brother. He died without male heirs, and was succeeded by his nephew, with whom the title nearly expired; but he left a posthumous son, who subsequently married Lady Louisa Carteret, grand-daughter of Granville, Earl of Bath, and daughter of John Carteret, Earl Granville. The possessions of the Carterets and Gran- villes subsequently passed, through this marriage and the marriage of one of the Leveson-Gowers, to the Thynnes and the Leveson-Gowers. The title of Earl Granville has recently been revived in an offshoot of the latter house. Younger sons of the first Marquis of Bath held the title of Baron Carteret, which is now extinct; but I presume that the estates are those now held by Lord John Thynne, a younger son of the second Marquis.

- The first Marquis of Bath, the title being evidently selected from the connection of the family with the Gran- villes, who had held the Earldom of that place, was created Marquis in 1789. For a period of about thirty years he held various offices, being successively Lord of the Bedchamber, Groom of the Stole, Master of the Horse, and the Secretary of State. Of the succeeding holders of the title there is nothing noteworthy to record. They were consistent Con- servatives in the time of the signing of Magna Charta—they have been consistent Conservatives almost ever since. Before the passing of the first Reform Bill the Thynnes had posses- sion of the rotten borough of Weobly, and of one of the close Corporation seats for Bath itself. As a rule, the Thynnes seem to have been moderate in their demands upon the national purse; but then it must be remembered that their wealth is great, and that they are not so numerous a clan as the Edens or the Beresfords. There is one exception, the Rev. Lord John Thynne, who, as a landowner with a rental of £13,461, might be reasonably expected to leave to less favoured men the rewards of the Church, even if he were anxious to take part in its sacred work. Yet I find that this nobleman has been Canon of Westminster for the last forty-eight years, with £2,500 a year and a residence; and, further, that he had a sinecure rectory in Somerset, given to him by his father or brother, value £l6B and a house, from 1832 to 1872. What with incomes and residences, he must have had from the Church in the course of his life over £130,000. Lord John had a brother, Charles, who was formerly a Prebend of Canterbury and Rector of Longbridge (another family livitig), but he went over to Rome. There is another Thynne in the Church, a son of the Rev. Lord John Thynne, who is Rector of Kilk- hampton (X 712 and a house), one of his father's livings, and also Prebendary of Exeter. The present Marquis of Bath, though nominally- a Con- servative, has manifested an independence which entitles him to considerable respect. Throughout the discussion arising out of the Eastern Question he has been a warm supporter of the enlightened policy which would fain have combined Europe in an endeavour for the peaceful and gradual deliverance of South-Eastern Europe from the Ottoman yoke. The Marquis repeatedly contributed to the funds of the Eastern Question Association; and he has still more recently shown his warm interest in the cause of the Bulgarians by proceeding on a visit to Eastern Roumelia.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. Wm. Brennan Andrews, Q.C., has been appointed a judge of the Court of Exchequer in Ireland, in Succession to Baron Fitzgerald, resigned. Mr. T. P. O'Connor addressed a meeting of Irishmen at Ashton-uesler-Lyne on Saturday, and said the prospects of the Irish people were never brighter than they are at present. The Land Act could not be considered as a final settlement of the land question. Such a settlement was one which would result in the destruction of landlordism, for it was doomed to death, and die it should. Four men have been committed for trial at Galway, charged with attempting, last March, to blow up Weston House, Galway, the residence of Mr. Mahon, a magistrate. The prisoners were arrested on the evidence of one James Jones, who says they induced him to supply dynamite and to accompany themselves and others when the attempt was made by the offer of a share of £seo to be received from "the Republican Brotherhood." The Rev. Dr. Kavanagh writes to the Freeman's Journal, giving examples of court valuers who, before their appoint- ment, were in the employment of landlords notorious as rackrenters. The duty, he continues, of fixing fair rents in the Irish land courts has been confined to men whose tradi- tions, prejudices, and previous history unfit them for this important work. It is an extraordinary fact that, in select- ing court valuers under the Land Act, the Irish Executive told all Catholics to stand aside. This selecting clearly in- dicates what Irish Catholic farmers have to expect in the Land Courts where the rents are fixed by court valuers. A FORTUNATE CONSTABLE.—"Protection " duty in Ire- land is not usually regarded as pleasant either by military or police, but in one case, says a Dublin correspondent, it has proved to be both pleasant and profitable. About two years ago Miss Ellard, a young, handsome, and accomplished lady, owner of a large estate at Oola, in the county of Limerick, was fired at, fortunately without injury. A con- stabulary guard was assigned for her protection' ard one of thern,Sub-constable Sheedy, showed so much devotion to her personal safety that she resolved to retain him as her protector for life. They were married on Saturday, and started for London to spend the honeymoon. The -lucky, constable becomes by his gallant discharge of duty master of an estate worth £lO,OOO a year. Mr, O'Donnell, M.P., in a letter to the Freeman's Journal says that the "Parliamentary party" were never consulted as to the constitution of the new" Council," and deplores the "clandestine course which had been adopted." Mr. Louden, barrister, who claims to be one of the founders of the Land League, vigorously denounces those who dubbed him " coward " and "renegade " at the meeting of the Con- vention, and explains that some of Mr. Parnell•s suite in Parliament cherish a deadly hatred of him because he would not vote for the payment of " bloated salaries" to them out of the League funds. Mr. Louden describes one of his assailants as " a wretched hireling skilled in moral assassination," and another as " the paid nominee of a money-grubbing group of decayed politicians." THE MURDERS IN PIRENIX PARK: WESTGATE'S STORY.— On Saturday, Inspector Swanston, of Scotland Yard, arrived in Dublin with the master, first mate, and steward of the Gladstone, in which ship Westgate sailed from Swansea to South America. To Mr. Jenkinson, director of the Criminal Investigation Department, and Mr. S. L. Anderson, crown solicitor at Dublin Castle, they detailed Westgate's COR. fession of his participation in the assassination of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke. The Home Secretary is determined to probe his story to the bottom, though the authorities in Dublin—having traced his career—believe he had nothing to do with the murders. A member of the Dublin detective force will be sent to Jamaica to bring West- gate home. In his deposition, Westgate alleged he was employed by a publican named O'Connor, not a member of Parliament as published; that of £2O he received he gave his wife £lO • and that his real name was not William Westgate, but 'Michael O'Brien, in which name he signed the deposition. The statements are untrue. He gave no money to his wife. The owner of the Gladstone sent her a month's wages, which she received pursuant to the address Westgate gave when signing the ship's papers. Westgate's information did not lead to the discovery of some knives found by the police. His confession is accounted for by his shipmates as the result of the eccentricity and brooding melancholy which sometimes characterised his conduct.

SUPPOSED REPRIEVE YOH MICHAEL WALSH. It is understood that Michael Walsh, the youthful pri- soner under sentence of death in Galway gaol for the murder of Constable Kavanagh, has been reprieved, and that the death sentence has been commuted to one of penal servitude for life. His brother Patrick was recently execu- ted in Galway for the murder of the herdsman Lydon, which murder Kavanagh was engaged in investigating when he himself was assassinated.

A most extraordinary case of fraud came before the Aldershot magistrates on Thursday. Samuel Rabey Leigh, who was attired in the costume of a Church of England minister, and haying the title of "Rev." on his cards, was charged with having obtained by fraudulent means £2O worth of jewellery from Mrs. Cooper, of Odiham, Hants, on the 29th of September. The prisoner, it appears, turns out really to be a desertet from the Army Service Corps, and has travelled England representing himself to be a mission- ary from Africa, and has promoted religious revival meet- ings in many large towns also delivered lectures on African missionary work, and in the garb of a parson has obtained a quantity of goods from an endless number of people. He was pawning a goli watch in London whets the pawnbroker, suspecting him,sent for the police,at which the prisoner tore up a Quantity of duplicates in the shop, which, when placed together, proved to be tickets of goods belonging to people in all parts of England. He has undergone two years' im- prisonment before for a similar offence. In order to give the police time to make further inquiries he was remanded fora week.

At the Dale-street Police Court, Liverpool, in Thui sday before Mr. Raffles, a middle-aged man of respectable appear. ance, named Peter M'Culloch, who was formerly a merchant in business in Liverpool, and who said he was now a com- mission agent in Dublin, was charged with smuggling 2,8731b5. of tobacco on the 12th May last. From the state ment of Mr. Paxton, who prosecuted, it appeared that the prisoner was charged with being concerned in the illegal importation of a large quantity of tobacco and cigars, which were found concealed in a consignment of flax on board a vessel which arrived in Liverpool in May last. The war rant had been obtained on sworn depositions, and his wor ship had no power to deal with the case at present, as the amount was so large. Mr. Paxton then applied for a remand in order that the Commissioners of Cpstoms might decide how to proceed in the matter.—Mr. Berry (Bartlett and Berry), who appeared for the prisoner, said he did not object to a remand, and asked for bail.—Mr. Baffles refused to allow bail, and remanded the prisoner for a week. div.head: IRISH NATIONAL CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE IRISH NATIONAL CONFERENCE.

The Irish " National Conference" Wa-s-heldlri—D-Üblin on Tuesday. Mr. Parnell was voted to the chair. He read at the outset a letter from Mr. Patrick Egan, who asked that he might be relieved of the treasurership of the Land League, and gave an account of his dealings with the funds of that body. Mr. Egan said there had passed through his hands since the founding of the League a sum of £244,820. Of this sum about £50,000 was spent in the relief of distress in 1379-80, and over £15,000 on the State trials of Decem- ber, 1880, and January, 1881, and nearly £148,000 had been expended on the work of the League, and he had now in hand the balance of £31,000. Mr. Egan closed with a refer- ence to "the stale falsehcod about deficiences and dissensions in out ranks." The Chairman next explained the objects of the proposed new association to be the procuring of national self-goverument, land-law reform (incloding peasant proprietary), local self-government, and extension of the Parliamentary and municipal franchises, and th e development of the industrial interests of the country. The reforms embraced the abolition of the centralisation system of government, and also the abolition of the office of Lord Lieutenant. The new association is to be called the Irish National League. Mr. Parnell denied that the cause of the Land League was dying either in Ireland or in America. Mr, Davitt followed, and declared that until the land of Ire-

At Oldham 'al Thursday, John Wolacott, a man of geri- i naau thhnour istey atog isne se t hhi his cwh ii dt lreemma nillye as apipde at hr ae nye e raepd wetaine p edfclor ll and he could not see Mt, penal said they had 1 no authority to int:rfere, and the applicant must consult a solicitor. The remains of Miss Fanny Parnell were brought to New York on Wednesday from Philadelphia en routs for Boston, where they will be interred. A military and civic pro- cession escorted the body as far as the Boston railway station. At the meeting of the Rishton Local Board on Thursday evening a letter was read from Mr. Christopher Parker, rate ' collector Rishton, resigning the post of clerk to the board, to which he was appointed a month ago at £lOO per annum, because his appointment was not generally approved, only, four members voting for him. His resignation was unani- mously accepted, and Mr. Helm, surveyor, Accrington, was appointed in his place. The Oldham Finance Committee, on Thursday evening, had under consideration a scheme of "enclosed tramways," intended to connect Liverpool with the manufacturing towns for the transit of goods, the estimate being that carriage could in this way be cheapened one-third. The committee expressed a favourable opinion. At Bolton, on Thursday, the Rev. J. S. Birley, committed for trial a collier whom he termed " the biggest brute he had ever seen in the dock." The collier had, in his Satur- day night's drunken fit, beaten his wife in a barbarous man- ner and had destroyed the sight of one of her eyes, and Mr. Birley very truly said that any punishment the magistrates had power to inflict would not be commensurate with his deserts. _ _ _ _

The Wreck Register for the year which has been issued shows that in 1880-1 the number of wrecks and collisions on the coasts of the United Kingdom was 1,056 in excess of those in 1879-80. The number given in the register is 3,575, and 984 lives were lost. During the past 27 years there have been 55,416 wrecks around our coasts, involving a loss of 19,534 lives. The greatest consternation prevails amongst the farmers at Bradfield, near Sheffield, owing to the conduct of a band of incendiaries who are firing the stacks there. No less than four fires have taken place this week, and a large quantity of hay and corn has been destroyed. The Sheffield Fire Brigade are now at another fire at High Bradfield, and not only the stacks but the farm buildings have been greatly damaged. An announcement on Thursday that Mr. Barry Sullivan will come forward as a Parliamentary candidate in the Home Rule interest is commented on by the Irisk Times. It says : —" Of course, his constituency will be one from which an unfaithful member is to be summarily ejected by Mr. Par- nell. Other companions for this budding statesman may be expected in time, including, it is hoped, Mr. Dion Bouci. can't, and, above all, Mr. Toole." Much indignation has been excited amongst Evangelical Protestants in Ireland by the appointment of the Rev. S. Weldon, curate of St. Bartholmew's Church, Dublin, to a canonry in Christ Church Cathedral. Mr. Weldon took a prominent part some years ago in circulating a book called "Portal's Manual," which advocated. confession and other extreme doctrines. The Protestant Defence Association have protested against the appointment, as also against a proposal to present the Archbishop of Dublin with a crosier.

The first batch of troops engaged at Tel-el-Kebir, who have returned to Portsmouth, disembarked on Thursday morning from the City of Lincoln, bringing the D battery, first brigade, Royal Artillery consisting of five officers and 199 men; and from the Tower Hill with A battery, first brigade Royal Artillery, composed of seven officers and 194 men. The troops, who appear in first-rite health, were to be conveyed direct to Shorncliff in the course of the day..

-John Saunders was charged at the Old Bailey, on Thurs- day, with burglary at Stamford-hill, and with shooting at a groom named Howe. He pleaded guilty to the former charge. Mr. Poland prosecuted, and opened the graver charge to the jury. Evidence haying been given bearing out previous statements the jury immediately returned a verdict of guilty of attempting to murder. Mr. Justice W illiams passed sentence of penal servitude for life. On Thursday afternoon a serious accident occurred at the Huttycrew Stone Pit, belonging to Messrs. Lloyd and Mill- ward, Darwin, which resulted in one of the workmen named William Berry, of Sudellside, being seriously crushed and otherwise injwed through the falling of a large portion of the roof. It was some time before he could be extricated from his perilous position. A similar accident occurred about a month ago. On Wednesday evening an inquest was held at Flint en the body of John Bartley, foreman of labourers at Messrs. Muspratt's Chemical Works, Flint, and bandmaster of the local Volunteer band. Deceased was riding out of the works on the footplate of an engine, when, in jumping back- wards, he struck against an iron cylinder, and was thrown under the waggons, which, passing over his neck, nearly de- capitated him. Death was instantaneous. A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned.

A serious accident occurred on Wednesday on the Bolton and Bury Canal, Little Lever. A retaining wall is being built between the canal and the river Irwell, and on Wed- nesday, whilst the men were hoisting a store, weighing 15 cwt., out of a boat by means of a jib-crane, the girder rod snapped, and the stone and crane were precipitated into the foundations, where a number of men were working. Four were seriously injured, one, William Burgess, of Farnworth dangerously. The difficulties under which the poor labour in obtain - ing prompt medical assistance were forcibly illustrated at an inquest held on Thursday before the Bolton coroner. T.he wife of a shoemaker, named Reddy, was taken seriously ill. The first doctor appealed to refused to attend with- out his fee, and a parish doctor who was next seen declined to go without the relieving officer's order. When this was obtained and the doctor went the woman was found dead in her chair. The coroner strongly condemed such red tapeism. THE CHARGE AGAINST A LONDON EDITOR.—AE the Old Bailey, on Thursday, Mr. C. Williams, editor of the Evening Nom, surrendered to his bail on a charge of assaulting Mr. Hyndman, managing director of that paper. Mr. Besley, for Mr. Williams, said Hyndman had written a letter, in which he said his presence at the office at a particular time might-be calculated to excite anger, but he considered un- necessary force was used to expel him. Mr. Williams had no thought of using unnecessary force. The jury acquitted Mr. Williams under the Recorder's direction. EXTRAORDINARY MAGISTERIAL MUDDLE. No little excitement has prevailed at Cambridge at the discovery that all the borough magistrates appointed at Cambridge for the last ten years have been acting without having qualified before the proper authority. They should be sworn in at the quarter sessions, but have only qualified before two borough justices. On Thursday morning, seven of the justices, some of whom were appointed some quarters since, attended before Mr. J. R. Bulwer, Q.C., the Recorder, and took the oaths. It is said that legal proceedings will be instituted to procure the reversal of some decisions given, and the quashing of some convictions by these justices.

A destructive fire resulting in the total demolition of the Church Bridge Spinning Mill at Church, near Accrington, occurred on Thursday morning. The fire broke out through friction at a mule in the second storey a few minutes after six, immediately after the hands had commenced work, and some of them had a difficulty in making their escape, one having to be carried out through being overcome by the smoke. Rain was falling, and there was a strong breeze, which caused the flames to spread with amazing rapidity, and in an hour the entire mill was completely gutted, the roof and walls falling with a succession of alarming crashes. Messrs. Steiners' steam fire-engine and the Accrington Cor- poration engine soon arrived, but the firemen were power- less, and directed their attention to saving an adjoining weaving shed. The mill was a four-storey erection and ten windows long, and contained 28,000 spindles. The damage is estimated at about £25,000, the mill having been recently provided with new machinery. The mill is worked by Cap- tain Barlow, of Blackburn, trading as the Church Bridge Mill Company. One hundred hands were employed. The damage is partially covered by insurance. A Portsmouth correspondendent telegraphs that while the transport City of Lincoln, which on Thursday morning dis- embarked a battery of Artillery, lay at Spithead on Wednes- day night, eight of sixteen prisoners who came home in her, and who had been put in irons for safety, broke loose. After disabling the sentry, they broke into the spirit room, where they drank freely of wines and spirits, and became so drunk that a scene of much confusion ensued, and the greate§t difficulty was experienced in taking them back to the cells, and when there the medical officer had to stay with them for the remainder of the night, most of them being utterly incapable and senseless. The stomach pump had to be ap- plied in the worst cases, and with good effect, but Private John Pearce, 2nd Derbyshire Regiment, was so weakened by the operation that in spite of the most vigilant care he gradually sank, and died on Thursday morning. Pearce was brought home under sentence of five years' penal servitude for being drunk while on sentry duty in Egypt. Great ingenuity must have been exercised by the prisoners in getting out of their irons, as when the lights were out they seemed perfectly secure. The prisoners have since all been removed to Portsmouth military prison to be further dealt with.

MR. CHILDERS ON THE SHORT SERVICE SYSTEM.-Mr. Childers, the secretary for war, in reply to a vote of confi- dence passed by his constituents on the 4th instant, makes ta o or three important and interesting statements in re- ference to the Egyptian campaign and its bearing upon the recent changes in our military organisation. Tha right hon. gentleman states that 41,000 men were equipped for service in Egypt without the embodiment of a single militia battalion, and with the aid of less than one-fifth of our reserves. The result has shown that twice that number of efficient soldiers could be despatched from home within a month of the expedition being sanctioned by Parliament, and this without its being necessary to embody more than half the militia or to obtain any aid from India. Th 3 average length of service of the infantry soldiers who fought at Tel-el-Kebir was about five years, and but for the short time during which the new organisation has been in force, the battalions of the line would have been in so efficient a condition as to render un- necessary any call on the reserves when they embarked. Under the present rules of -discipline—that is to say, without corporal punishment—the conduct of our troops throughout the campaign was excellent, and Mr. Childers thinks we have every reason to congraulate the country on the army reforms of the last twelve years. He still sees no reason for increasing our army, but if we have already done something to improve its organisation, he hopes any lessons we have learned during the recent campaign will enable us to carry that improvement still further.

Conflicting telegrams a;e-Pu-blith—e-a-in regard to the latest Egyptian difficulty. On one band, it is positively stated that Mr. Mark Napier will defend Arabi before the court martial, the Egyptian Government having permitted him to choose his own counsel, whether native or foreign; and, on the other, it is asserted that the Cairo authorities have flatly refused a demand of Lord Granville that Arabi should be permitted to enjoy the assistance of an English lawyer. Possibly an explanation of the matter may be found in the customary procedure of the Egyptian courts. At the preliminary inquiries in Egypt,as in most continental countries and in Scotland, accused persons are not permitted to be represented by counsel, and it is only when these in- vestigations are concluded and the charge definitely formu- lated that legal advice is allowed. It may be that the Egyptians have simply acted on this principle, and that when the public court opens Mr. Napier will be admitted as the representative of the rebels. Meanwhile, it is satisfac- tory to know that strong denial is given to the reports of illtreatment baying been inflicted on Arabi in prison. A correspondent in Cairo sends a summary of the state- ments made by Arabi in his defence. These statements consist mainly of testimony given in coart, but partly of words spoken in interviews with a friend, which Arabi wishes to be made known to the English public. As regards the defence of Alexandria, Arabi declares that he acted under the orders of the Khedive, and afterwards only obeyed the orders of the Government for the time being. He frankly admits that he never expected to be long able to resist the invasion, but thought he could probably do so long enough to convince England that the rebellion was a , true national movement, and win her sympady. He sur- rendered to the English in full confidence that he would have the usual treatment of a military prisoner of war. He ' maintains that he is an English, not an Egyptian prisoner, ' and demands the assistance of an English lawyer. He declares that be will defend himself if denied English nounsel.

The chiefs of the Egyptian Ministry have expressed a strong opinion that peace will not be assured unless Arabi is executed, and they profess to be able to convict him of complicity in the massacre and pillage at Alexandria. Arabi has solemnly denied all.complicity in those crimes. The insurgent chief is further reported to have said that when he reached Cairo, and found the inhabitants unwilling to continue the struggle, he at once bowed to their decision, and surrendered.

According to later accounts, it appears no progress has been made with the proceedings against Arabi, and the dis- inclination of the Egyptian Government to allow English counsel to appear on his behalf clearly increases. Their contention is put as follows You may resume possession of Arabi and try him yourselves if you choose, and we will stand aloof. But what impression will be produced on the country if Arabi is defended by an Englishman at the in- stance of England, the Power which has sent an army to Egypt in order to suppress him? The very arguments which must be employed in the defence would be so many attacks on the Khedive, who is the protege of the English." The Times correspondent at Alexandria is of opinion that the simple deportation of Arabi without trial weuld be less fraught with evils to Egypt than the interference of English counsel in a native court. A telegram from Cairo, dated Thursday night, says "The Egyptian Government has most reluctantly consented this afternoon to the admission of the. English counsel, Mr. Broadley and Mr. Napier, with their solicitor. They ex- pect to see Arabi to-morrow. lhe Ministry threatened to resign in the event of this concession being mader but a split appears inevitable in any case, and Rubar Pasha may very shortly fill the post of Premier. All here desirous of fair play appreciate the firmness of the British Government in insisting on the condition as regards the counsel."

Tamar for England. Sir Garnet Will;tlev leaves to-day (Saturday) in her Majesty's despatch vessel Iris for irieste. Official intimation is made in Cairo that the coupon of the United Debt is now fully assured out of the specially assigned revenue, without having recourse to the general in- come of the State.

A correspondent at Alexandria telegraphs that goods of all kinds, except machinery, are pouring in in great quan- tities. The supplies of cotton are daily becoming larger. On Saturday 800 bales arrived. There are Pays a special correspondent, 113 prisoners now in gaol at are, and Government are still searching for 30 ethers. Sir E. Malet has written to the British consular agents to send lists of political prisoners and to see that they receive humane treatment. Our correspondent further states that a scheme for admitting a certain number of foreign judges to the native courts is being discussed. A general order is issued by the Commander-in-Chief, stating that the Queen has ordered a medal to be granted to all troops engaged in the recent operations in Egypt, with a clasp added for those who took part in the assault of Tel-el- Rebir.

From Constantinople comes the statement that several of the Port Said labourers had been arrested, "but solely with a view to their identification." Lord Dufferin, how- ever, had the men taken to the British Consolate when they were liberated, not troubling to make any official represen- tation on the subject. Rumours of threatening agitation at Alexandria on Sun- day night alarmed the military authorities so much that troops were kept patrolling the streets throughout the night. There was, however, no disturbance. A special correspondent says there is considerable excitement among the lower class natives, and seditious meetings are held nightly in the cafés. The Banffshire Journal says—The honour of being not only the first officer but the first man of the British army who got inside the line of defence at Tel-el-Kebir is claimed by a Banffshire man, Lieutenant G. S. A. Harvey, B Com- pany 42nd Royal Highlanders (Black Watch). Lieutenant Harvey had a narrow escape and a hot time of it, as he broke two swords—his own and another he took from an Egyptian. Prince Bismarck has disposed very conclusively of the interesting story related to the Paris correspondent of the Times "by a politician who had just passed through" the French capital. In this imaginary conversation the Prince was made to say that he had at one time the idea of invest- ing German funds in the Suez Canal, as Lord Beaconsfield did subsequently, and to express certain decided opinions as to the control of the Canal. The conversation, it is now de- clared, nexer took place. A meeting of the Egyptian committee was held on Tues- day evening in London with special reference to the trial of Arabi Pasha. An address in the form of a resolution was read by Karl Blind, declaring that the conduct now being pursued towards Arabi was an infringement of the law of nations, and denouncing the despatch of an armed force by this country without a declaration of war. After some dis- cussion it was resolved to print and circulate the declaration, and also an amendment thereto, and to make strenuous efforts to save Arabi's life.
The Daily News says that the Cape Government have decided to recommend the Cape Parliament to abandon Basutoland.

Telegrams from Rassia and Germany report very severe weather. In Eastern Russia the navigation of rivers is already partially suspended. An International Congress of the friends of peace was opened on Tuesday at Brussels. Letters were read from Mr. Gladstone and Lord Derby regretting their inability to be present. Much damage was caused in a portion of the Island of Cuba on Saturday last by a cyclone. The streams in the districts of Vueltrabajo overflowed, and many persons were drowned. The bodies of 15 have since been recovered, but others are still missing. A Renter's telegram from Paris states that the Gendarmes at Montceau lea Mines discovered a number of dynamite cartridges near a school. The fuse was extinguished without any explosion occurring. Two thousand troops are stationed in the neighbourhood of Montceau lee Mines. Marshal Serrano and Senor Sagest& have been in confer- ence together, and the circumstance has naturally excited great interest at Madrid. The attempt to bring about an agreement on the basis of the constitution of 1869, which still further restrained the power of the Sovereign, is as yet far from being successful. The report that Russia is " massing" troops on her frontier in Asia Minor appears to be confirmed from Con- stantinople. The three powers, Russia, Persia, and Turkey, have each large bodies of troops on their respective frontiers. The Persians are in arms against the Sheikh Obeidullah, who has incited some of the Kurdish tribes to revolt against the Shah. The Turks allege that the Sheikh is supported by the Russians. The death is announced from Wiesbaden, at the age of 78, of Professor Korner, the author of various philosophic works. In his younger days the deceased founded free religious " congregations in various towns in Germany, and he had to flee to America in consequence of his participation in the revolutionary troubles of 1848. In his will he desired that his body should be taken to Gotha for cremation. A MURDERER BURNT ALIVE.-0110 Of the most atrocious criminals in America, a negro named Jerry Cox, when lying under sentence of death for killing his mistress and then placing her corpse on the rails to be cut up by an express train, set fire to the gaol in which he was confined at Nash- ville, and was burnt alive in the building. He had pre- viously perpetrated a double murder in circumstances of appalling atrocity. About midnight on the 2nd instant people were awakened by the roar of flames, and many hastened to the gaol, but on their arrival they found the walls and bars glowing red with heat, while the murderer within was screaming in his death agony. In less than an hour the gaol was a mass of fruins. :Early next morning the body of Cox was found, and a great crowd stood appalled at the murderer's fate. A " promient" politician in St. Louis, bearing the ominous name of Slayback—and of course a colonel—has been despatched by Mr. Cockrell, the editor of the Post Despatch, of that city. The Colonel denounced the news- paper, at a political meeting, and the newspaper, instead of treating its assailant with disdain, retorted in kind. Thereupon the irate Slayback waited upon the editor, in company with a friend, for the purpose of demand- ing retraction. Mr. Cockrell was full of fight, and both sides drew pistols as a matter of course. It happened that the editor was the more expert of the the two in the use of the revolver, and the unhappy Colonel was slain. The affair has created a little excitement in St. Louis, but the verdict of public opinion may be anticipated with great con- fidence by the person chiefly concerned. THE FENNYROU Tnier...—The notorious Fennyrou case was concluded in Paris on Saturday. It will be remembered that Mann and Gabrielle Fennyrou, husband and wife, and Lucien, the brother of the first-named prisoner, were charged with having murdered the apothecary Aubert, the lover of the woman, under circumstances of appalling barbarity. The case was tried before the ordinary Assize Court, and re- sulted in the condemnation of Mann to death, of Gabrielle to penal servitude for life, and of Lucien to imprisonment for a long term. A technical objection was taken to the trial. The judge, out of desire to spare the public more nauseating details than were necessary, omitted to read the depositions of another of Gabrielle's lovers, whose testimony was utterly irrelevant to the issue. On this ground the conviction was quashed and a new trial ordered, which re- sulted on Saturday in the sentencing of Mann and Gabrielle to penal servitude for life and the acquittal of Lucien. AUDACIOUS ATTEMPT AT ABDUCTION.—An extraordinary attempt at abduction has just been made at the convent of the Dames Blanches at Nantes. A young gentleman living in the town got some papers printed bearing an exact resem- blance to those used by the Procureur de le Republique. These he filled up in due form appending thereto the signa- ture of a well-known magistrate. The result was that to all outward appearance a certain commissary of police was ordered to arrest and hand over to the legal authorities a young lady residing at the convent, the motive assigned for such an unusual step being one that was by no means com- plimentary to the morals of the innocent maiden. The forgery was most cleverly contrived, bat, unluckily for the Lothario, the Superior had still to be faced. Having invested in the orthodox tricolour scarf, this romantic citizen of Nantes persuaded one of his friends to play the part of the commissary of police, and proceeded with him to the con- vent, where the forged papers were produced. The Superior, however, proved equal to the occasion. Experience had rendered her acquainted with the features of the local com- missaries, as well as with the rudiments of legal procedure. This commissary was totally unknown to her, nor had she ever heard of an arrest under similar circumstances. The worthy lady, therefore, declined point blank to surrender the girl, or to restore tbe sham document, sending out at the same time for a bondjide commissary of police. The young men immediately decamped; and although an active search has since been instituted, the inventor of the ruse whose initials are given as C. de B.; d has not yet been found.

Lord Colin Campbell, M.P. for Argyllshire, is so unwell that he will be linable to take his seat when the house re-assembles. A report was current on Tuesday that the ironclad Superb, one of the Mediteranean Squadron, had touched a shoal near Corfu, but had been got eff by the aid of the Temeraire. Nothing was known at the Admiralty of the reported accident. Mrs. Mary Forbes, of Great Crosby, was on Wednesday committed for trial at the Liverpool Assizes on a charge of setting fire to her house, which, with the furniture, was in- sured for a considerable amount. The evidence showed that shavings and newspapers had been laid down in continuous lines from room to room, and that the fire had been started in three distinct places, at each of which shavings and other materials had peen heaped together. Fortunately, the fire was discovered soon after it began, and Mrs. Forbes was , promptly taken into custody. div.head: TURKEY AND ENGLAND.
div.p: TURKEY AND ENGLAND.

A Constantinople correspondent telegraphs that, notwith- standing the efforts to conceal the truth, England's reply to the Turkish Note on the Egyptian question has caused great exasperation at the Palace. The fanatical party took advantage of rae Sultan's anger to accuse the Grand Vizier of the loss of Egypt, and even demanded his banishment. A meeting was held at the Palace to consider what attitude should be adopted towards this country. Said Pasha ex- pressed the opinion that the surest way to hasten the ruin of Turkey was to oppose England. Latest news, however, from Constantinople, is of a more satisfactory nature than it has been for some time past, and indicates that the influence of Said Pasha is gaining the ascendancy. The Sultan has approved of the reply by Said to Lord Dufferin's note on the question of the withdrawal of British troops from Egypt. The Turkish reply, which is' couched "in very friendly terms," intimates that the Porte is ready to enter into negotiations with Lord Dufferin for the settlement of the affairs in Egypt. This may not mean much, but it is at least an indication that the Sultan recognises that a policy of abstention will not promote his interests. FRANCE AND ENGLAND. A Berlin correspondent telegraphs that the negotiations between England and France respecting the Egyptian question are proceeding satisfactorily, and there is every hope that a friendly understanding will soon be arrived at. The leading Berlin papers say that France will be obliged to accept moderate proposals from England with regard to Egypt, and that she will have to renounce her share in the financial control; as in the events of disagreements the French navy would be totally unfit to encounter that of England. THE NEW EGYPTIAN ARMY.

It is stated by the Egyptian Gazette that the effective strength af the new Egyptian army is to be 11,000, with English and native officers. The non-commissioned officers will be Albanians, Turks, and Bulgarians, chosen from the late army. It is added that the total force of the Gen- darmerie will be 1,500 men. Baker Pasha has informed a Cairo correspondent that he has modified his opinion respecting the native officers, who will be admitted more largely into the army and Gendarmerie than he at first in- tended. A telegram from Berne states that the Federal Council has prohibited the enrolment of Swiss recruits for the Egyptian Gendarmerie.

div.head: CONTROL.
div.p: THE CONTROL.

Writing on the subject of the Progressist or National Party, a correspondent says every member of it is convinced that the maintenance of the Control in its present form is not necessary as a guarantee for the fulfilment of the coun- try's financial engagements. It is contended that the work might just as well be performed by the Commissioners of the Public Debt, and that its existence, therefore, means an unnecessary burden upon the Treasury. The Progressist leaders do not object to the employment of Europeans under certain conditions. They are only too well aware, they say, that the hope of Egypt lies in English intervention. They do not object to the highest positions being filled by Euro- peans, but urge that in other posts the work could be done as honestly, as efficiently, and more cheaply by natives. According to a Cairo telegram, it is considered likely that the Egyptian Ministry will not summon the French Comp- troller to the Cabinet councils, so that his resumption of office can only be nominal. M. Bredif, the French Comp- troller General, left Paris on Tuesday on his way to Alexan- dria. It must be presumed that his object is to take up the position he formerly occupied, and this Wye would force our Government to state its intentions at once.

REFORMS IN TURKEY. Said Pasha has submitted to the Sultan a new reforming programme, to which, however, his Majesty has not yet given his sanction. The Premier suggests that the relations with all the Powers should be similar, that Ministers should be responsible for their own departments, that army ex- penses should be reduced and the gendarmerie developed, and that reforms be introduced in Armenia. Russia has sug- gested that the payment of the war indemnity shofill begin in January next. The Porte demur'. Said Pasha has dismissed the Governor of Broussa, a former grand vizier, from his post. Thisis regarded as an indication of Said's determination to introduce extensive administrative reforms. According to a Constantinople correspondent, both the Saids in the Cabinet have deter- mined to resign unless Mahmoud Nedim is dismissed ; but the Sultan hesitates between the two.

div.head: VICTOR HUGO'S MANIFESTO.
div.p: VICTOR HUGO'S MANIFESTO.

The following is the text of a manifesto of Victor Hugo on the subject of Arabi's trial : "They are trying Arabi. What is Arabi? Is he a rebel ? Yes, says the Khedive, loudly. No, softly whispers the Sultan. Is he a liberator? A liberator of whom? The Egyptian people shall be, and shall be great till the twentieth century. At this time it has not come into being. Is he a belligerent? That implies war. Now, at this moment war does not exist. There are military facts as to which England will have to give explanations, but as to war there is none. England is not at war with Egypt; England is not at war with Turkey. What, then, is Arabi? He is a prisoner. We, the passers-by, the unknown, the first-comers, we exist, we live, and the Governments labour close to us. What they do they conceal from us; we do not know it • perhaps they do not know it themselves. But we see what they do not see; we see before us in the depth of the horizon what the future is doing; we behold Islamism crumbling away in the east, Catholicism collapsing in the west, Africa awakening to civilisation. All that is before us ; Governments may conceal from us what they do ; we see what civilisation is doing; we are content. The penalty of death has summarised and represented the old crittlinal justice of the past. It has been the angel of oldetl legisla- tions. To-day it is judged and condemned. Within the last 50 years 27 States have removed it from their statute book- The Governments that retain it—France alas ! resort to it as little as they can. They are afraid and ashamed of it. There is not a single enlightened juryman who consents to sign a verdict entailing the penalty of death. It is no longer an angel ; it is a spectre. Hero people stop us and say the penalty of death is more power- ful than ever. The two worlds adopt it. So little is it dead that it kills. Arabi is going to be shot. That language surprises but does not disquiet us. No, civilisation is not barbarism; no, savagery is not modern justice ; no, civilisa- tion does not kill a man, as old societies did, without exactly knowing why; no, civilisation does not commence the great work of which the twentieth century will be full by a deed which is an enigma for those who commit it, and a crime for those that look on.—Vlcroß HUGO." div.head: TRADE NuTES.
div.p: TRADE NuTES.

At a meeting on Monday of delegates representing the miners of North Wales it was decided to apply at the end of this week for an advance of 15 per cent. in wages. A strike of gun-lock filers at Darlaston, commenced on Monday, has been brought to a close, the employers having conceded the advance demanded, namely, 1d per lock. Owing to a dispute with the local authorities, the whole of the Swansea cabmen struck work on Thursday. Business was partially stopped, and immense inconvenience caused. The result of a ballot taken on Saturday on the board of arbitration in the north of England iron trade was officially- declared at Darlington on Monday. There voted for the con- tinuance of the board 5,481, and against 1,320. The total number of subscribers is 10,307. BILLS OF Si AND FAILITRES.—In the week ending Oc- tober 14, 1882, there were 823 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 191 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 193, a I decrease of 25. The totals for portion of year to October I 14, 1882, are—bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 37,117, a decrease of 2,637; the failures gazetted number 8,337, a decrease of 779.—Stubb's Hereantile Gazette.

_ A special delegate meeting of miners was held on Tues- day night, in the Miners' Hall, Wigan. Over 40 delegates, representing 12,000 men, attended. After considering the notices to be delivered to the employers for an advance in wages on the 18th inst., a proposition was passed that each pit set of men appoint a deputation to wait upon their em- ployers for a report on the wages question on or before the 25th inst. It was also resolved to hold another special meeting on the 26th inst. _ _

At mass meetings of the miners engaged in the Stafford- shire and Worcestershire coal trade, held on Thursday, at Rowley, great dissatisfaction was expressed at the sliding- scale which regulated wages, it being contended that good workmen could not earn more than 18s. per week, and it was resolved that steps be taken for the total abolition of the sliding-scale. It was also resolved to hold a conference with the view of increased wages being demanded. A deputation of the representative employers and opera- tives of the South Staffordshire Mill and Forge Wages Board waited upon Alderman Avery, mayor of Birmingham, on Thursday, and asked him to accept the office of president, the vacancy arising through the resignation of Mr. Richard Chamberlain, ex-mayor. His worship promised to give an answer in a day or two. The operatives contend that the improved state of the trade justifies an advance in wages, and have given notice to this effect to the employers. The representatives of the Board will be called together at Birmingham or Wolverhampton on the 30th inst. to settle the question. THE LANCASHIRE IRON' TRADE.—There was a fairly good attendance on the Manchester Iron Exchange on Tuesday, but only a very moderate amount of business appeared to be stirring. The market does not seem as yet to have settled down to the advance in prices which have been announced since the quarterly meetings, and although the uneasy feeling caused by the agitation in the coal trade tends to give strength to the upward movement in values, orders are by no means freely offered at the full advance in rates now being asked. Lancashire makers of pig iron are now quoting 508 to 50s 6d, less 21- for forge and foundry numbers respectively, delivered equal to Manchester and Lincolnshire, and Derbyshire brands range from 50s up to 52s per ton, less 2. Finished iron makers all round report plenty of work in band, and there is a good trade being done, especially in sheets and hoops for shipment, Egyp- tian orders for the latter, which were held back during the war, being now pressed forward. Prices, however, are irregular; in exceptional cases £7 is being asked for local bars, but the average makers' prices are £6 15s to £6 17s 6d, with lower qualities of Lancashire bars to be bought at £6 105 per ton, delivered equal to Manchester. Hoops are quoted at £7 5s to £7 10s, and local sheets at £8 12s fid to £8 15s. Tau COLLIERS' AGITATION.—The Conference of miners' delegates from North Staffordshire, Lancashire, Cheshire, Yorkshire, Derbyshire, and North Wales, resumed its sitting at the Old Town Hall, Manchester, on Saturdiy, Mr. E Cowey, Chairman of the Yorkshire Miners' Association, again presiding. The proceedings were again private, but the following resolutions were, we understand, adopted : W." That the counties of Lancashire, Yorkshire, Derby- shire, and North Wales give in the notice for an advance of wages of 15 per cent. simultaneously, between the 16th and 19th inst." (2) "That the question of how, and to what extent, support shall be given to those districts or portions of districts, which may have to fight for the 15 per cent. advance, be referred back to the various districts, and that this Conference stand adjourned to hear reports from the districts, to determine the amount of support to be given, and to decide any other important question involved in the wages question." (3) "That we recommend all districts concerned in this question to consider the best means of re- striction between now and the next Conference, and to give all the support in their power during the fight for the ad- vance, and that no advance be accepted conditionally pend- the decision of the general wages question." THE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE.—The .31-ark Lane Express says: "During the past week the weather has been very mild, and for 'the most part dull and rainy. The season continues favourable for agricultural operations, and is likely to result in good seedbeds for wheat. There has been no improvement to note with regard to the condi- tion of farmers' wheat. In some of the provincial markets a shilling more money has been made for fine and dry samples. Flour has been a dull trade, but prices remain nominally unchanged. Old oats are in request at harden- ing rates. Beans and peas remain unchanged in value. Trade for foreign wheat off stands in London has been in a condition of extreme tension, and on Friday there were in- dications of weakness on the part of sellers. Prices remain unaltered, except that red winters have gained about six- pence during the week. In Liverpool on Friday wheat was generally purchaseable at a penny per cental decline from Tuesday's rates. Flour shows no quotable alteration in value. Maize has improved in value to the extent of about two shillings during the week. Mediterranean barleys were sixpence dearer on Friday in London. Oats have gained about threepence since Monday. Off coast cargo trade for wheat has been very quiet, and buyers act with great caution."

THE LABOUR MARBET.—The labour market has entered on few important changes, but several large sections of miners remain very unsettled, and extensive strikes are not unlikely in the districts affected. Meanwhile the continu- ance of the Arbitration Board in the northern iron trade has been secured by a large majority vote of the workers con- cerned. In Cleveland a small increase in the wages of the blast furnacemen has been declared. At Birmingham the staple trades continue fairly employed, but in some branches foreign competition is somewhat keenly felt. In Lincoln- shire the leading implement manufacturers are still well engaged. At Middlesborough building is progressing in various directions, and the local trades remain well em- ployed. In the textile trades there is some improvement in the carpet branch at Kidderminster, but several firms are still running short time. At Nottingham the lace trade is inactive. At Huddersfield the manufacturers of better class coatings keep well employed, and at Leeds the same class are well off for contracts. At Dundee the jute trade is active. In the metropolis the miscellaneous industries are fairly employed, but as winter approaches there is a slight increase in the registered vagrancy. At Workington the new steel works are already employing a large number of men, and many more will shortly be engaged. Domestic servants are in active:demand in London and all the leading towns. Latest advices from Castle Garden, New York, show that notwithstanding the advanced season, labour of all kinds is in good deman and splendid harvests both in the United States and Canada are reported. Good men for railroading and lumbering are still required.—Labour News. THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—A generally good de- mand is kept up for all classes of coal throughout this district, the wages agitation no doubt tending to stimulate inquiries beyond present requirements. Supplies are kept low by a restriction on the output, which, although not very seriously felt in the immediate neigbourhood of Man- chester, is pretty general throughout West Lancashire, and the only class of fuel which is at all in excess of require- ments is slack, of which the production has recently been exceptionally large. Any actual pressure of demand is due, however, more to the limited Output of the collieries rather than to the large requirements of consumers, and to some extent no doubt it is intensified by the fact that many of the colliery proprietors, in view of the threatened stoppage of the pits, are reserving their stocks as much as possible. The orders already in hand will, with the present output, keep a considerable proportion of the Lancashire pits going well over a month, and many of the colliery proprietors are not disposed to book further orders at present beyond small quantities to their regular customers. Prices are very firm, with a slight upward tendency here and there in some of the best house coals. At the pit mouth quotations are about as under :—Best coal 10s, seconds 7s 6d to Ss 6d, common house coal (3s 6d to 7s, steam and forge coals Os to 6s 63, burgy 4s 9d to 5s 3d, and good ordinary slack Sc 6d to 4s ' per ton. Shipping has not been quite so good, and the recent advance in prices is being with difficulty main- tained.
