I RUNCORN 2ND V. ANYiET.D WINDERERS.—The second team of the Runcorn Fotb ill Club were down on the card to play the Anfield Wanderers at Run-crn on Saturday afternoost. The opposing team, however, sent wont that they would not be able to play the match, and Runclrn lost the chance of onoe more distinguishing itself on the field. RUNCORN TAM O'SHANTIIRS V. WIDNES match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday last. Widnee won the toss, andresolved to play with the wind. Os time b,ing called the result stood as follows, viz. :—Runcors Tarn O'Shanters, two tonchdowns ; Widnes Recreation, one touch in goal, one dead ball, one touchdown. EARLESTOWN Anocurrox V. BIRICTON WANDERERS (2ND TEams).—This match was played on the ground of the latter, near Northwich, on Saturday afternoon last. The home team won the toss, and Earlestown kicked off. For the first half time the visitors severely pressed their opponents and scored repeatedly. During the second half the play was more era but a good game ended in a victory for Earlestown by four goals to none. VULCAN v. ST. Histarics RANGERS (2ND PRAM)—Plaved on Saturday on the Rangers' ground, and ended in an easy victory for the home team by a goal, four tries, and five minor paints, to two tries and three minor points. The tries for the ho me team were got by Hartley (3), Parr, and Whalley, and thoee for the. visitors by Fairclough and Ferguson. Besides those men- tioned, Finney, Foreman. and IrLaughlan, for the Rangers, and Slater, Williams, and Porteus for the Vulcan, also played well.

GOLBORNE V. EVERTON (2ND TRAMS).—These teams met for the first time on Saturday at Stanley Park, and a pleasant and evenly-contested game resulted in favour of Everton by four goals to three. Golborne scored first, Laban. who played re. markably well, making the first goal. This aroused the Ever. tonians to quicker action, wLen Taylor after along run finishing with a good shot, made the score even. The score was shortly afterwards augmented by Sinnott, from a eentre by Taylor on the left, who made some splendid runs: Golborne now scored again, Eidyard putting the ball through. As the fortunes of the game appeaten to ran in alternate grooves, Everton, not to , be denied, made a rush, and Scott by a kick over his head added another goal to the credit of the hnne team. On the change of ' ends the play was remarkably good, the ball being first at one goal and then at the other. Two more goals were scored this half for Everton by filar-tett, and one for Golborne by Hem. brou2h. The Everton played a good game throughout, as did I also Golborne.

HA.TDOCK TENITERINCE v. OUGHT.RINGTON (la-mal). —The Haydrek Temperance Club journeyed to Ougbtrington, on Saturday afternoon last, to play their second match this season. The game commenced at three o'clock, Oughtrington whining the toss and playing with the wind in their favour. The visitors kicked off, and for a long time the play was even and exciting, each eleven scoring one goal before the change of ends. The visitois afteewards set to work with renewed er orgy, and completely overpowered their opponents. The leather wss kicked through the posts time after time, and the Haydockers ultimately won by seven goals to one. All the Temperance men worked hard and well, but the pick were T Wedgwood, P Twist, and 8 Harrison. The following were the teams :—Haydock T R Maudesley, goal; T Hatton and W Knowles, backs; J Carter and A Barnes, half-backs; J Riackley, S Harrison, J Wedgwood (captain). P Twist. T Twist, and T Plant, forwards. Oughtrington J Smith, goal; A B Biggs and T Thomason, backs; W Kirkpatrick and J Wood, half- backs; G Dodson, J Shaw, H Thomason, E Smith, J G Smith, and E Eustace, forwards. WARRINGTON V. lONGSIGUT.—A match between these clubs was played at Warrington on Saturday last, resulting, after a remarkably even and exciting game, in a draw, the score being —for Warrington one goal, one touchdown, and one touch in goal; Longsight one goal and two touchdown. The play was witnessed by upward of 200 spectators. For Warrington every man played well, Gregory, Pemberton, and Rigby being fre- quently applauded. The smart kicking of Moores, the Long- sight full back, was the chief feature in the play of the Long- sight men. Teams—Warrington T Walsh, full back; W Gregory, W Lomas, Blakey, three-quarter backs; E Warren (captain). T Pemberton, half backs; F Turner, W Leigh, J Leitch, 0 Adamson, H Ashton, J Critchley, W Povey, J Rigby. J Myles, forwards, Longsight W Moores, full back; Dunker- ley, J Baxton and S Hamnett, three-quarter backs; W 31 May. son. J H Turner. half backs: E Oldfield (captain), J Beresford, Andrews, 3 E Biggs, F Clarke, B Wood, W H Ross, F Clarke, F Magher, forwards, The match on Saturday next is between the Warrington second team and St. Elphin's first team, on the Warrington ground. Considerable local interest is attached to this match, and in the event of fine weather a large number of spectators are expected.

1 11INCORN v. ITALTmEN.—This match was played at Walkden on Saturday last, and a very pleasant and exciting game ended in a draw. Broady and Page were the only absentees from the Runcorn side. Walkden had, however, called in the aid of ; three Swinton players. Walkden kicked off, and Clarke re- turned, but the ball was soon back in Runcorn's quarter, Yatee helping it forward. A series of packed scrimmages took place, both sides being evenly matched, and it was some time before the ball got loose. Runcorn at length broke through, and Joule, by an excellent dribble, compelled Walkden to touch down. On the drop out Mason was to the fore with a run, but was tackled by the ankle, and unfitted for the remainder of the game. From another hard scrimmage Hughes had the ball passed to him, and gained cossiderable ground. Being collared, he passed to Johnson, who also ran well. Another hard scrim- mage took place, in which Runcorn held their own, but an the "break up" a rush was made into the Runcorst half. This was well stopped by Clarke. During the second part of the game both teams waxed warm, and good play was seen on both sides. Runcorn now had to play uphill, but a combined rush of the forwards, heeded by Wright and Atherton, compelled Walkden to touch down. After the dron out Yates got hold, and brought the play to neutral ground. Hughes was next to show forward, and an excellent kick sent the ball close to the Walkden goa), where a severe tussle was engaged in. Wallecleta got the ball loose, Allen dribbling in grand style. Andrews, by a " dodgy " run, recovered the lost ground. Walkden, how- ever; played up with a will, and at length compelled Runcorn to touch down. The light now became bad, and the game ter- minated as follows :—Runcorn, three minor points; Walkden, three minor points. The forwards on both sides played splendidly, and the backs were frequentiy cheered for their excellent passing and kicking. Teams—Runcorn: J Sherleek. full back; W Mason, T Johnson, and W Larkin, three-quarter backs; H Hughes (captain) and H Andrews, half-backs; F Joule, W Wright, H Atherton. J Gatley, W CJX, .1 Lewis, T Cleave, J B Clarke, and E Hankineon, forwards. Walkden: Rushton, back; Yates (captain), Grundy, and Jones, three- quarter backs; B Iguley and Smith, half-backs; Allen, Cook. Jones, finally, Jackworth, Mullen, lirrmson, Jackson, and G-araner, forwards. EARLESTOWN ASSoCiATIIIN V. BARNTON WANDERERS.—This match was played on the ground of the former, at Wargrave Moss, on Saturday afternoon last, there being a fair attendance of spectators. ~,The visitors' captain (Evans) won the toss, and chose to play with the wind in his favour during the first half. Degnall kicked off for Earlestown, the leather being passed to the left wing. Sims and Mather took it into the Barnton quar- ters, the fermer player making several good runs: but the visitors' Lacks played splendidly, and the ball was each time returned. After about a quarter of an heur's even play the home team began to assert their superiority, and notwithstand- ing the wind blowing against them they severely pressed their opponents. Twenty minutes from the commencement E. Corey ram the leather up the field and abet it through the posts amidst applause. A few minutes later lie repeated the si me operation, while in quick succession Sims shot the leather outside the goal, and Duxbury kicked it over the top bar. Another splendid run was made up the right wing, which ended in Corey scoring a third , gaol for Earlestown. Jtnt before half time was called the same I player again sent the leather in front of the Barnton uprights, 1 and alter a scrimmage Holdcroft succeeded in putting it through the posts for the fourth time. Half time was then called, and ends were changed. During the second half the game war all in favour of the home team, who from beginning to end made one continual attack on the visitors' stronghold. Frequent corner kicks fell to their side, but the Earlestonians were very unlucky and failed to add to their score. The visitors played on the defensive, and as a consequence some difficulty was experienced in getting the leather throueh the uprights, which were frequently endangered. The match thus resulted in a victory for the home team by four goals to none. The goal keeper and backs for Earlestown played exceedingly well, while that of the half backs were also very good. The following were the teams: Earlestown—James Appleton, goal; R Green (captain) and E. Bradshaw, backs; J. Taylor and R. Bowker, half backs; E. Corey and J. Duxbury, right wing; Jr: Sims and J. Mather, left wine; A. Dagnall and H.' Holeroft, =Are. Umpire—Mr. J. C. Wilson. Barnton War.- derers—J. Ellen, goal; J. Lamb and R. Riley. backs; J. Ast- bury and T. Johnson, half backs; J. Bowyer and W. Banks, right wing; J. Howard and G. Burge s, left wing; W. J. Evans (captain) and W. Woodward, centre. Umpire—Ur. J. Hewitt.— the players afterwards adjourned to the Sunbeam Inn, where a social and enjoyable meeting wis held. .

Walter Robert Garland, who had established a "bogus " emigration agency in Manchester, and used it as a means of defrauding several persons, was on Wednesday tried at the City Sessions and sentenced by the Recorder to 12 months' imprisonment. LETTER BOXES IN MAIL Inams.—On and after the Ist November, letter boxes for the receipt of late letters from the public will be affixed to all mail trains in which sorting duty is performed. The letter box will be suspended out- side the sorting carriage at each station at which the train stops, and the practice of taking in letters at the door of the sorting carrive will be discontinued. The letters must bear an extra fee of -.1.d., prepaid by stamp. THE EXAMINER.
SATUR DAY, OCTOBER 21, 1882.

A Conference, promoted by the chief supporters of I the suppressed Irish Land League, was held in Dublin on Tuesday, and though it can scarcely be pronounced a success, it is instructive as showing what is to be the future course of action he Irish Parliamentary party lad by Mr. Parnell. The Conference was, of course, attended by Mr. Parnell•-who had the honour of presiding—and his followers ; the, cx -suspects and revolutionists were present in large numbers ; but I the moderate Liberal element in Irish politics was conspicuous by its absence. For some time past there have been complaints that no statement has been made public showing how the funds subscribed on behalf of the Land League were expended; and since the stoppage of the supplies from America these complaints have been more frequent. Probably it was owing to this fact that the Conference was on Tuesday favoured with a communication from the tressa-er o tle fwo 1, M. E.;an, who i tifl in w1,1;:a;;:: 11in nri to clulaere'2ut,

and who now seems irons to be relieved of his de: duties and to return to hie; Ansiness in Dublin. From Mr. Egan's letter we lean thtit, hip Ge 0ct.,1879, when he assumed the purse striegs, there has passed through his hands no less a stem than £244,800. Of this Mr. Egan estimates that Sge;000 was disbursed in the relief of distress; over .E 15,000 was spent on the State trials of Ilecember, 18.80, and January, tEBz, while nearly £148,000 was expended theough the General Land League and the Ladies' Land League in support of evicted tenants, in providing wooden houses, in law costs, in sheriffs' sales, in defence against ejectments, and upon the "general expense of organisation." Mr. Egan has, contrary, we believe, to general expectation, a balance in hand of £3l 900 "to turn over to whoever shall be duly authorised to take charge of it ;" but seeing the League was suppressed by the Government as an illegal organisation, it may be a question for consideration how far the Conference could authorise anyone to interfere with Mr. Egan's treasure. At any rate it does not appear to have instructed any- one to do so. We are grateful to Mr. Egan for the information which he has given, but we should have been better pleased had it been more com- plete. lc Would, We think, have been of interest had the expense of the organisation itself been stated more fully instead of being lumped with other items, beceuse there is a suspicion that some of the office-bearers have had the lion's share of the morey. If that is not the case, there is the more reason that the suspicion should be dispelled, so that it may be known the office-bearers have been acting from thoroughly disinterested motives. It has also been generally understood that several of the Land League members of Parliament have been paid, and well paid too, for their services, but of that there is no mention whatever. There is nothing to be ashamed of in the transaction, and the remuneration, if any, of each member might as well be given in detail. If they have not been paid anything, then again let that be publicly known in order that the patriotism of these members may no longer be doubted. Better a statement of some kind than none at all, appears to have been the feeling which animated Mr. Egan, but we question whether one so bald is likely to inspire much confidence in the "Irish National League," which is now to take the place of the defunct organi- sation, and to suceeed, we suppose, to its. funds. In support of the new movement more money will of course be required, though it is doubtful whether after past experience it will be obtained. The objects of the "Irish National League," which were referred to in detail a week or two ago in this column, are briefly summarised by Mr. Parnell, as—first, national self-government; second, land reform ; third, local self-government; fourth, the extension of the fran- chise ; and fifth, the development and encouragemeut of the labour and industrial interests of Ireland. No sound Liberal could offer opposition to any of these objects except the first, which, of course, is the ol() Home Rule cry, pure and simple. This is positively unattainable, and to us it is a matter of surprise that so much tithe and energy should be wasted in discussing it. If Home Rule were conceded to Ireland there would be no reason why it should not also be granted to Scot- land and Wales if demanded, and the Empire thus dismembered would speedily decline. Its prosperity and influence consists mainly in the maintenance of the Union, and they who agitate for its severance can be no friends of England, as it is impossible they can be of Ireland. Perhaps it is thought necessary by some of the Irish agitators to keep the Home Rule ball rolling in order to secure funds for their coffers; but it would at least be more honest when the goal is found to be beyond reach to abandon its pursuit. The Conference itself, by the uproar which characterised its proceedings, provided an excellent reason why Hone Rule should not be granted, for if in a Parliament on College Green such disturbances as those witnessed on Tuesday were to take place often, there would be very little time left for legislation. The second object aimed at by the League is the reform of the Land. Laws, and to this we can have no objection, though much has already been done for Ire- land in this respect. Mr. Parnell tells us that the only settlement, which will be a final one, is that which will ensure occupying farmers the right to become the owners by purchase of the holdings which they occupy and till. Already we have very nearly arrived at that stage, and the mode by which its complete accomplishment is to be obtained is sketched by Mr. Parnell, who advocates the advance by the State of the whole of the purchase money, and the extension of the period of re -payment over 63 years. The scheme is, on the whole, a feasible one, and we are glad to find provision is made in it for the labourers, who are deserving of more consideration than they have hitherto received; but it is impossible that it can be worked out satisfactorily in either one or two sessions of Parliament, and therefore it will be neces- sary for the Irish farmers to wait and hope. Mean- while they enjoy this advantage, that under the Land Act their rents are being reduced to something like a reasonable amount, and with a struggle they can relieve themselves of the arrears which have pressed so heavily upon them. The third object of the League is stated to be the.attainment of local self-government by the formation of county and other Boards. The power now vested in the Lord Lieutenant and in grand juries selected by him, and who are absolutely irresponsible, would be swept from them, and vested in representative boards, the mem- bers of which should be responsible to the ratepayers with whose money they would deal. Mr. Gladstone is already, it may be stated here, committed to a scheme of county government for England, and doubt- less the same will be extended to Ireland. The exten- sion of the franchise is the fourth object which the League aims at, and there seems no valid reason why the franchise in Ireland should not be extended and assimilated to that of England. The Government are already pledged to do this, and their pledge they are anxious to fulfil. But it should be remem- bered that if Ireland, in the matter of the franchise, is less favoured than England, as regards representation the Emerald Isle has a distinct advantage over England, Scotland, and Wales; and we may say that no extension of the franchise in Ireland will be satis- factory on this side of St. George's Channel unless it is accompanied by a redistribution of seats on the same basis as in England, that is to say, if England is to remain as it is in regard to represen- tation. The last object aimed at by the League is the development and encouragement tof the labour and industrial interests of Ireland, which may be passed over with the observation that if the people of Ireland will only follow peaceful pursuits, and em- ploy their energy and capital in the development of the native industries, the country is likely to be much more prosperous, and its people more contented and happy than hitherto. We hope, however, that in this matter therais to be no resort to Protection, which the new programme of the League would seem to imply. After all, the great point in the programme" is that relating to Home Rule, and if that is to be con- ceded it is unnecessary to discuss the others. • To our mind, if there is anything which Ireland wants at the present time more than another, it is rest, and we can but express our regret that this new agitation should have been inaugurated. During the past few years the country has experienced nothing but turmoil and trouble; yet at the present time there are evidences on every hand of greater coutenimout. P.aliament, too, during the past few sessions, has been occupied with little more than Irish btviness, but Parliament is getting tired of this; and we believe the Irish members will be well advised if they do not attempt to push their claims too far. With one exception, the reforms for which they are clamouring come within the range of practical po'i,ios, and if they will welt patieetly, 'he r;•!or.e,-) w;:I be el.:tele:el,

I have r eceived„through the medium of The Examiner office, a communication addressed "Mr. Flaccus," having reference to a "local note" respecting the Runcorn Burial Board finances. The communication draws my attention to Ithe fact that "the Burials Act ot 1857 extended the time for the repayment and made the sinking fund system com- pulsory." If my friend will again read the note to which he inferentially takes exception he will see it simply asked for information on the point, and suggested that it would have been well if it had been included in the original pro- posal which called it forth. My correspondent goes on to say—" As your remarks will have re-opened the subject in the ratepayers' minds, perhaps you will say something in your next to place the Burial Board in a right position before the public." This is only reasonable, and by way of doing so I will ask my friend to inform the public as to the limit of extension allowed by the Act, and also whether or no the Burial Board are strictly adhering to that limit. The communication is written in such a fair and gentlemanly spirit that I regret my inability to send it you for insertion, it being marked "private."

Sir -Stafford Northcste seems to me very unfortunate. He can scarcely open his mouth without the Standard —which is, or once was, the representative of the Tory party—taking him to task. The fact is Sir-Stafford is too honest for the Standard, he has a sincere conviction that in the Egyptian question the Government has only done what he and his party would have done had they been in pewer, and this conviction manifests itself now and again ha his speeches. Sir Stafford's speeches in Scot lid have given mortal offence to the Standard, e.special!y tl:e sreech at Inverness, and the consequence was that on ti,t.i.rday the editor thus doubled-up the leader of the Opposition in the Commons:—" It would be uncandid to pretend that at Inverness the leader of the Opposition in the Lo-wer House contributed either light or illustration to urg,-nt contro- versies. He is avowedly not fertile in ideas, but on has ordinarily shown penetration and a conamand of homely phrases. Last night he wandered from top7c to topic, leav- ing each one pretty much as he found it. Sir Stafford him3elf is one of the leaders of a party, yet it is some- times said he cannot lead them to victory. In any case he must sound a louder and more definite note than any struck at Inverness if he is to have his Tel-el-Kebir." Sir Stafford may be pardoned for exclaiming—save me from my friends!

Some few days ago Lord Carnarvon made the astounding assertion that " Three-fourths of the literary power of the country,and four-fifths of the intellectual ability,"are en the Conservative side. Lord Carnarvon would never have been foolish enough to have said any such thing but for the very sufficient reason that he knew the statement was incapable of proof, and he supposed it would be swallowed without question, as too many other Tory statements are. Lord Northbrook, at Liverpool, however, pulled the statement to pieces, and a writer in the Times has this week been doing the same thing. The writer in question submits, without classification, the following list of men of literary power or intellectual ability, who (allowing for occasional dislike of particular measures or Ministers) are Liberal in the broad, general sense of the term, and who, at all events, are not on the Conservative side :—" Froude, King- lake, Lecky, Freeman Herbert Spencer Trollope, Browning, Matthew Arnold, Olin-Thant, Leslie ' Stephen, Trevelyan, Hayward, Jowett, Reeve, Hughes, Rawlinson, Layard, Fer- guson, Spottiswoode (P.R.S.), Lubbock, Owen, Tyndall, Huxley, Grove, Henry Smith, Goldwin Smith, Gavan "Duffy, Grant Duff, Cartwright, Bain, Tulloch, Torrens, F. Harrison, Harcourt, Brodrick, Lord E. Fitzmanrice, Lowe (Lord Sherbrooke), Lord Dufferin, Lord Houghton, the Duke of Argyll, Gladstone." Methinks the Tories cannot produce such a list of distinguished men. But there is another striking test of the political tendency of educated intellect to which attention has been called in the Times. At the election for the University of Oxford in 1865, in which Mr. Gladstone was beaten by Mr. Gathorne Hardy (Lord Cranbrook), of the electors who had taken honours or gained prizes, two to one voted for Mr. Gladstone; of first-class men, four to one; of double first, eight to one. Comment here is unnecessary.

The anniversary meetings in connection with the United Kingdom Alliance have this week been held all over the country, and the speakers thereat have been more than usually jubilant. When, however, the work which the , Alliance has done is taken into consideration, there is, I think, just cause for rejoicing. Since the accession of the present Government to power especially the progress which the Alliance has made is most marked. Not only has , the principle of local option been again and again affirmed by increasing majorities, but much work of a practical character has been accomplished. A Sunday Closing Bill has been passed for Ireland, a similar measure has jail, come into operation in Wales, and I venture to predict that in a very short time the public- houses throughout the length and breadth of England will very soon be closed the whole of Sunday. Rapid strides are already being made in several of the counties, as for instance in Cornwall a Sunday Closing Bill for which has been read a second time, and would now be working. but for the obstructia e tactics of a Tory nonentity. Another st.tp in advance is that which was gained by the passing of Mr. Ritchie's bill, giving magistrates a veto on the granting of "off licences" for the sale of beer. As the law previously stood there was practically "free trade in beer," as Sir Wilfrid Lawson puts it, and heel there not been a stop put upon this the country would have bee* over-run with licensed houses. That, however, has happily been averted, thanks to a Tory. It is often urged against the Alliance that it is a political organisation, and that it is confined almost exclusively to Liberals; bat a glance at the list of subscribers will at once satisfy any one that such is not the case. The Alliance has the very warm and hearty support of both Liberals and Conservatives, who are united against a common foe, and I earnestly wish it every success.

The news from Egypt this week is comparatively tame, and centres in the forthcoming trial of Arabi. It is now doubted whether the Court Martial, before whom he is to be arraigned, will assemble before a week's time. It is not yet settled, either, whether the rebel is to have the benefit of English counsel, but whether he does or not thcre is likely to be some startling disclosures at the trial. It is question- able whether the Egyptian authorities will be able .to show any complicity on the part of Arabi in the massacres of the 11th June; but Arabi professes to be able to prove that so far as regards the defence of Alexandria he acted under the instructions of the Khedive, who, if that be really so, must have been playing a double part. It is satisfactory to know there is no truth in the rebel being, as was alleged, treated with harshness; justice demands that dark as his crimes may he he should have fair play, and that he should not be tortured in confinement. The strong feeling of antipathy which the Sultan manifested towards England, when she declined to give any information about the remora' of her troops, has passed away, and His Highness now professes the most friendly feeling towards us. He discovers that he cannot afford to throw himself outside the pale of the Egyptian settlement, and, of course, he is likely to gain more by appearing to be our friend. The re-organisation of the Egyptian army, under Baker Pasha, is at present under the consideration of the Ministry at Cairo, with what result remains to be seen. Troops returning from the campaign are now landing on English soil almost daily, and they are everywhere receiving a right royal welcome. Sir Garnet Wolseley, the hero of the cam- paign, embarks to-day. His arrival will be eagerly awaited. FLACCUS.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTTIORITY.—The Ray. Canon Barclay presided at the meeting of this Authority held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. There were present the Revs John Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. C. Rigby, J. Ashta, T. Andrews, J. Alidwood, W. Jackson, James Darbyshire, J. Highfield, J. Smith, C. Moon- field, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk). —Dr. Bride, medical officer of health, reported that during the year ending September 30th, 1832, the registrar's returns recorded 145 births and 72 deaths in the three districts com- prised in the union. Of the births 81 were males, and 64 females (birth rate 7.5 per 1,000). Of the deaths 35 were males and 37 females (death rate 31 per 1,000) ; as against 128 births (birth rate 66 per 1,000) and 67 deaths (death rate 3.4 per 1,000) during the corresponding quarter of 183'. Of the deaths 20 were under 5 years of age, 13 others being under one year ; and 52 were 5 years and upwards.—This was all the business of public interest. PROPOSED RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION FOR RUNCORN.— A meeting of ratepayers is called for Tuesday next, in Bethesda schoolroom, Runeorn, for the purpose of establishing a Ratepayers' Association in the town. Attempts have been previously made to form an association, but on each occa- sion the efforts of the promoters have proved abortive, so little interest have the ratepayers manifested in the matter. It cannot be denied that in Runcorn some organisation competent to criticise the actions of the governing bodies of the town, and on certain matters to advise them, is much needed, but if the criticisms are to have any effect, and the advice any weight, the association must be formed of repre- sentative men well acquainted with the opinions of the com- munity. One thing the association, if formed—and there is every prospect that on this occasion it will be—may be expected to remedy is the disorganised manner in which elections for members of the Board of Commissioners are conducted, consequent upon the want of some proper method of nominating candidates. The aims of the asseciation as published on the prospective programme are—(l) To acquire a power of control over the public expenditure of the town, and to see that all moneys are wisely and judiciously spent. (2) To watch over the appointments to the public offices, and to see that only fit and proper persons are retained in them. (3) To promote the return of representatives (un- biassed by any political motives) to the governing bodies of the town. (4) To protect purity of voting at elections for Commissioners, and to guard the interests of the ratepayers generally. - - -

THE BOATMAN'S "BOOZE" AND ITS REST:MT.—Yesterday at Runcorn Police-court, before Captain C. Hazlehurst and Mr.ll. Reynolds, James Taylor, hand on board the narrow boat "Maria," was charged on remand with having on the 15th inst. feloniously stolen £4 Os 2d., and a bag from the person of Joseph Guy, master ot the canal boat Egypt. On Saturday Guy's, the prisoner's, and another's boat were lying in the Bridgewater canal at Runcorn. During the evening of that day Guy left his boat and went into the town, where in a public-house he met the prisoner and his brother. At closing time they left together and entered the boat "Vesta," where they stayed about an hour and a half. Guy drank some whiskey, and having seen that his money, four sovereigns and four old half-pennies were safe in his pocket, he went to sleep in the cabin. When he awoke neat morning, about half-past seven, he missed his money, and also his watch, and from something he was told he went on board the "Maria" and asked the prisoner and his captain for his money. They both denied any knowledge of it. Guy, however, found in the cabin one of the old half-pennies of which he had been robbed, and which he could identify by certain mrrks, and accused the prisoner of stealing his money. The prisoner persisted in denying his guilt, but after the lapse of about three-quarters of an hour, he took from the claw with which the boat was laden the four missing sovereigns, stating that he could not find the halfpennies or the purse. Afterwards the prisoner was apprehended. Prosecutor found his watch hanging 011 a rail in the cabin where he had slept. —James Moore master of the boat ",Maria," said he saw the prosecutor pufl:out his bag containing money on Saturday night, and he also heard him promise to lend a man 10s. Before going to bed on re- turning to the boat, witness told the prisoner to go =I fetch half-a-sovereign and a shilling or two from "Joe " (the prosecutor)—and have a bit of "game "with him. He then fell asleep, and never remembered anything more about it. Nes, morning, when the prisoner was accused with 'stealing, he told him to return the money if he had it, but it was not until the prosecutor threatened to fetch a policeman that he brought the money.—P.C. Davenport deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who, when charged with tha theft, said "I did net mean to steal the money ; only have a bit of game."—Captain Ilazlehurst said he con- sidn‘ed the ease too suspicions to allow the prisoner to go soot free, and he would hC committed to tate his trial at the , next B,7:Fsions. HARTLIND WESLEYAN CIIAPEL, WIDNES.—This chapel, the memorial stones of which were laid a few months ago, is approaching completion so far as the outward fabric is concerned, and it is expected that it will be opened for public worship early next year. The cost of the building is not fully covered, and with the object of adding to the funds the members of the Sunbeam Juvenile Temple 1.0.G.T., gave an entertainment in Oakland-street Wesleyan Chapel, on Monday evening. The Rev. R. Harper, superix- tendent of the circuit, presided, and delivered a brief address. The programme was of a miscellaneous character. Recitations were given by Bros. James Broderick, T. Perrin, J. Langdon, A. Perrin, T. G. Hatton, G. Wendt, John Broderick, A. Spiby, J. W. Jones, J. Johnson, H. Smith, and Sisters M. Dodd, E. Taylor, S. Wendt, Bradburn, and A. Collings. Sister E. Gough sang "Lo, the sun is o'er the hill tap ;" Bro. T. J. Hatton, "The trundle bed ;" Bro. G. Wendt, "Pass me not ;" Sister M. Gough, " Strong to save ;" Sister A. Collings, " The vacant chair ;" Sister Merryfield, " Swecit and low ;" Sister Bradburn, "Hearts of oak;" Sister E. Lawton, " Don't go in to•night ;" Sister M. Birkhall, "The drunkard's home ;" Sister M. Bold, " Little sister's gone to sleep ;" Sister E. Bold, "Angels guard my little ones ;" Bro. J. Johnson, "Ring the bell, watchman." A duet, "The better land," was given by Bro. and Sister • Wendt; and a trio, "The servant's reward," was sung by the Sisters Bold and Harper. The children sang several hymns and melodies, in which the audience joined. A dialogue, entitled "The children's pleadings," in which 13 juvemilts took part, was also given.

Musica.r.. FRsTivar, AT RIINCORN.—On Monday evening a musical festival, or what would, perhaps, be better termed a concert of sacred music, was held in Runcorn Public Hall. There was a large assemblage of people, and the re- served seats were moderately well filled. The object of the concert was to raise a sum of money to add to the bazaar fund which has been formed for the purpose of providing a residence for the missionary of the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen, and no doubt a good sum was realised. The programme consisted of hymns and choruses by such authors as Hatton Brown, Haydn, Gounod, Handel, Nuvello. They were rendered by a choir composed of the representatives of the various choirs in the town, numbering upwards of one hundred voices, and their performances were very meritorious. The anthem, "I will sing of mercy " (Novello) by five trebles and an alto, although capable of im- provement, was sung with considerable taste; whilst the rendering of the chorus, "0 Father, whose Almighty power," (Handel) was all that could be desired. The soloists were Miss Lambert, of Warrington, and Mr. Eaton Batty, of Birkenhead. Miss Lambert's first piece was Sullivan's charming song, "The lost chord." It was at once evident that Miss Lambert, who is ever welcome with Runcorn audiences, was suffering from some little nervousness; and the piece was not sung with her usual power of expression. The interpretration of the sentiment of the piece was, how- ever, by no means commonplace, and she received an en- thusiastic encore to which she responded with "Creation's , hymn." When she had sung partly through the piece she was compelled to retire from the plat- form. Later on in the evening, however, she had sufficiently recovered from her indisposition to render the solo "I dreamt I was in Heaven" (Costa), which she sang in her happiest manner, and, in response to a hearty encore, she bowed her acknowledgments. The audience were not to be denied, and she repeated part of the solo. Mr. Eaten Batty, who has a voice of great power and compass, gave a pleasing interpretation of the solo " Thou'rt passing hence my brother, by Sullivan, and received an encore, to which, however, he did not respond. In Mr. Batty's second effort, "There is a green bill far away," the fine qualities of his ,voice were heard to great advantage, and he was loudly ap- plauded. The concert, from every point of view, must be regarded as a success, and was highly creditable to Mr. Jno. 11-a-Iford, who wielded the baton. Miss Clough presided at the harmonium and Miss Jukes at the pinaforte. We must not forget to mention the excellent performances of the orchestral band, which is deserving of all praise.

CHARGE AGAINST A MOTHER OF' THREATENING TO DROWN HER CHILD: HORRIBLE STORY.—A respectable looking woman, named Ellen Jones, was placed in the dock at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, to answer a charge of threatening to drown her child N ellv, seven years of age.— Mr. Superintendent Williamson said the prisoner was a semp- stress or machinist, and from what he could glean, travelled about the country with the child Nelly, which she said was her own. On Thursday night, about half-past nine, Mrs. McQuinn, wife of Andrew McQuinn, bootmaker, Top Locks, heard screame proceeding from the direction of Waterloo Bridge. She went there and found the prisoner by the side of the child, who was _prying very much, and stated that her mother had been trying to drown her in the canal. What the child had told him (Mr. Williamson) in reference to her mother, since the latter had been in the cells, was sufficient to cause the magistrates to shudder. The child made a most horrible statement. The girl, who appeared very intelligent, said she and her mother came to Runcorn on Saturday, and had been living in lodgings. On the previous night they were looking for lodgings and when on the bridge her mother asked her to come and look at the boats, and placed her on the parapet of the bridge; then her mother left her on the parapet alone, and she fell off into the road. She screamed because her mother was going to drown her. There were no boats.—Mrs. McQuien said the child was crying terribly and wringing her little hands when she arrived on the bridge. The prisoner was ceiling her a naughty girl, and witnees asked the girl why she cried. She replied "Oh my mother wants to drown me in that water." The prisoner then said her daughter • had a "dirty nasty disposition" same as her father, and used other foul expressione witness did not care to repeat.—The prisoner: I might have said I would put her in the water to frighten her, but I had no intention of harming my own child. lam deeply sorry, please forgive me.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson said he did not wish to be hard upon the woman, but the child told him that her mother had been travelling , about the country for the last two months, and that she had been in gaol in every town she had visited, and the girl had been taken to the Workhouse. The tale told by the child was very bad and he was sorry he could not repeat it to the Bench. The child would be far better away from her.—Prisener : I never beet my own child. Did your enemnia ever beat you Nelly—speak the truth dear. There is no mark upon_ my child. I deeply love her.—Ceptein Reeehurst said the fielsoner had placed her- self in a serious posqien. There must be some truth in what the child said. The Bench would discharge her. but for the future she had better take care what she did. The Priscr'r th.,11 lit the court, by the c c • • 1111-td,

So sudden and enthusiastic was the out- burst of popular acclamation at this point, that it disconcerted the horses certainly more than the music of the military band had done, and probably snore than any volley from the enemy. They soon, however, became accustomed to the loud cheering and the constant waving of hats, handkerchiefs, and flags, for the same scene repeated itself at almost every stage of their long march of about seven miles. When the Horse Guards' band had ceased playing, the red-coated instrumentalists of the Life Guards were prompt to take up the strain. Alter- nately the bands played a succession of lively airs, and a good humoured smile was often excited in the crowd by the more or less appropriate nature of their selections, which included, "Slap bang, here we are again," " When Johnnie comes marching home," "Bonnie Dundee," and "Home sweet home." Unless as a tribute to the defeated enemy, the aptness of the selection was less obvious in the case of " Let me like a soldier fall I" the Horse Guards having enjoyed entire immunity from losses in the course of the short but decisive campaign. From West India Dock-road the troopers marched straight ahead into the apparently interminable length of Com- mercial road, in the first portion of which there was but a sparing display of flags, although here and there might be seen mottoes, inscribed by loyal East-enders, with such words as "Well done, Boys! Welcome home!" At Stepney Police Station the services of the constabulary were for the first time employed in keeping the line of route, which at the earlier stage of the march had been sufficiently well preserved by the populace themselves. Throughout the whole of the long march the crowds were continuous and the cheering and waving of hats, handkerchiefs, and flags incessant, and nothing could have been more enthusiastic than this reception.
LATEST NEWS.

Replying to a correspondent M. Mundella says he is op- posed to the proposition to establish free elementary schools, and to throw the expense of them on the Consolidated Fund. On Thursday night an extraordinary shooting case occurred at Coventry, a boy named Henry Clements being shot in the street by a Lid named Bosworth, only 15 years of age. The latter ran away after discharging the revolver, • and on being arrested said it went off accidentally. The unfortunate ;ad is suffering from a severe gun-shot wound in the chest, and lies at the hospital in a critical condition. . Yesterday morning, the Oak Bank Cotton Mill, Bolling- ton near Macclesfield, was completely destroyed by fire. The four upper rooms were worked by Mr. George Holden, and the lower rooms by Mr. Brier, calico printer. The mill was fourteen windows long, and eight wide, and contained 30,000 spindles. The estimated aamage is £45,000. The owner is Mr. Hall, of Manchester. The premises were insured. THE CRISIS IN THE YORKSHIRE COAL TRADE. TWENTY THOUSAND NOTICES SERVED. I From information received yesterday morning at the offices of the Yorkshire Miners' Association, Barnsley, it appears that close upon 11,000 notices have been served by miners and trammers alone in South Yorkshire. A similar number has also been served in West Yorkshire, so that fully 20,000 notices have been given. In many in- stances the owners have given all day men notice to leave work, thus providing for a stoppage if necessary. MR. TREVELYAN IN SELKIRK. Yesterday afternoon the Right Hon. George Otto Trevel- yan was presented with the freedom of the Burgh of Selkirk. In returning thanks, Mr. Trevelyan referred to the condi- tion of Ireland, and contended that agrarian outrages had greatly diminished. He hoped for peace and prosperity. He strongly condemned the adverse critisism to which the Government had been subjected, and asked for support for the policy which was being pursued at the present time. In order to retain lodia it was necessary to have a settled Government in Egypt, and a naval station at the Cape of Good Hope.

Mr. James Ball, jun., presided. A well-selected pregramme was gone through in good style, and the performances of the various ladies and gentlemen who took part were highly creditable. ALLEGED EXTRAORDINARY FORGERIES AND FRAUDS BY A SOLICITOR'S CLens.--John Winzar, a solicitor's clerk, formerly employed in that capacity at Runcorn, was charged at the Leicester County Sessions, on Thursday, with a series of extraordinary alleged forgeries and frauds. The prisoner had for the last four years been employed by Mr. Councillor T. Wright, solicitor, and he had also been secretary of the Starr-Bowkett Society, living in a handsome villa at Nal, borough. Mr. T. Wright and Mr. T. B. Neale prosecuted, and Mr. Burnaby, barrister, appeared for the defence. Mr. Wright, in opening the case, explained that the prisoner was an experienced conveyancer, having been employed as such at Runcorn. as well as in Leicester. In 1880, a Mr. Haden, of Cliff Hill, applied to him (Mr. Wright) for an investment, and he recommended him several. But the same day pri- soner w,ote to him dissuading him from accepting any, and offering him as security a piece of his own property at Nat, borough. Mr. Haden, never dreaming that he was dealing with an accomplished swindler, lent him £BOO on the lot, and as security received a forged duplicate of a deed which he had already given to the Starr-Bowkett Society. In the second place prisoner was a member of Lord Brougham Lodge, 200, M.U., and he took advantage of his position to obtain a loan of £7OO upon the security of a forged deed of the whole of his property at Narborough. But in this instance the signatures were of such a character that anyone who had seen the pri- soner write once or twice could identify the forger. In the third case prisoner became aware that Mr. Mann, as trustee for a poor cripple girl, was to receive two cheques of £2o.c and £4OO. He accordingly induced him to endorse the cheques to himself, and gave him as a security for the 440( a second duplicate forged deed on the whole of the Na r. borough property. Indeed, the only difference between ta and the one he had palmed off on the Lord Brougham Lo, was in the dates. These were three of the charges; ty atit was gnite possible that these whom the prisoner ha, I de- frauded in other ways might take proceedings again, t him before the ensuing assizes. Evidence was then if .ven in proof of the three charges. Prisoner in eaeh inst, ,nee re- served his defence, and ho was accordingly ceraw. itted for trial at the approaching assizes. THE _ IN "FOLK-LORE." Sir,—Some young folli I know have been hunting among roy books, and have discovered some curious Chinese super- stitions in connection with the hare, taken from a book entitled "The Folk-lore of China, and its affinities with that of the Aryan and Semetic races," by N. B. Dennys. Lan- cashire and north country superstitions and legends are in I the pages of the same book alluded to, and compared wit'. Chinese and Indian ones. Here are the extracts, as quof.ed by the young folks in question:—" There are in Chima a large number of generally-believed superstitions, whica it is iifficult to class under any particular head. The myste- rious properties ascribed to the hare are peculiarly Interest- ing.. A prejudice against eating its flesh is rJoeval with Chinese history. In the Erh-ya we find it stated that the people of Yo-yang considered the hare to be a telluric genius, so that nobody dared to hunt it. And throughout China it has always been looked upon (especially the red variety) as a divine animal. Albina hares are regarded as omens of good, and their appearance a mark of heavenly approval. In Dr. Eitel's 4 Handbook of Chinese Buddhism,' article Sakchi, we read that an unselfish hare, who threw itself into the fire, to offer its flesh as food for others, was transferred by Indra to the centre of the moon. The superstition concerning hares is common to China and India. Nor, though it does not take precisely the same form, is a belief in the portentous attributes of this animal wanting at home. For a hare to cross a man's path early in the morning is an ill omen throughout Europe. And a Highlander of the 42nd Regiment, in his printed memoirs, noticed the same harbinger of evil as having crossed his own path on a day of personal disaster in Spain. It is note- worthy that fte Goddess Freya is represented as attended by hares, who act as train and light bearers." "As regards the legend concerning the hare, it is purely of Indian origin, having been introduced into China with Buddhism. Sahyamuni, the founder of Buddhism, is related to have been a hare in one of the early stages of his existence, living in friendship with a fox and an ape. Indra having sought their hospitality, the fox and the ape procured him food, but the hare could find nothing. Sooner than be inhospitable, the hare cast itself into a fire in order to become food for his guest, in reward for which Indra trans- ported him to the moon. The lnnar hare, as Mr. Mayers notes in his manual, is said to squat at the foot of the cassia tree of the moon, pounding drugs for the genii (article Kwei)." So it will be seen that the hare will supply as interesting reading for indoors as it will sport in the fields. I may add that among the Lancashire and north country Superstitions and legends alluded to, it is remarked of the Lancashire superstition as to the "first foot" on New Year's day, that it finds its Chinese counterpart in the dis- like expressed in the flowery land at meeting a woman (poor woman! every nationality has its sarcastic remarks about her!) or a Buddhist priest under such conditions. And it would gladden the heart of " Newtonian " to read the pages devoted to what are termed lucky numbers, " seven " included. Thus the Chinese speak of the seven passions (I hope my critic has none) and the seven spirits. They wish a bride seven children, and they have seven law- ful reasons for divorce, dm., &c. It may interest Newto- nians and Earlestownians who are disciples of Fast, Guten- berg, Jan Ammost, &c., to learn that the type-setting, printing, and binding of the beok in question bas been entirely executed by Chinese workmen.—l am, sir, dtc., ANGLO-SCOTUS. Newington, London, S.E., Oct. 13, 1882.
HARE

P.S.—Perhaps the following "query," sent to the editor of The Lancet by Dr. Pratt, of Appledore, 'North Devon, will interest "Mac's Merry Man" in particular, and the readers of The Examiner in general.—Sir,—Can any of your readers throw light upon a case where there is a discharge of printer's ink from the great toe near the nail, the lesser toes being inflamed at the top on the palmar aspect. The lesser toes of the other foot are also affected—red, and with a severe pricking pain. It is thought to be an exceptional case. Is it so? How is this discharge produced? There is no rector." How, indeed! There's the rub. How did the Bishop's rabbit get it's long tail ?—AS.

div.p: WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY DE BATING SOCIETY.

Sir,—One of onr most entertaining books, "The book of snobs," tells us "it is among the respectable classes of this vast and happy empire that the greatest profusion ef snobs is to be found." Mr. Thackeray had:a great knowledge of the world; no donbt he had often come across the religions snob who, with arms folded across his gentle bosom, turned the white of his eyes upwards and thanked God that he was not as other men. Had he been acquainted with "One of Mr. J. Bright's curiosities" he Would have said "Curiosity indeed! nay, rather a cowardly snob who, slinging slutch, hides thyself under an anonyma. If thou bear a respectable name sign it." I also would refer those who are interested in this question to a source whence may be gained a true and faithful account of what passed during the last session of this society, viz. The Warrington Examiner file—the last two speeches delivered by the leader of the house, and the apology offered by the real leader of the Opposition. In addition, I could give the opinion of a Church of England minister expressed to myself respecting the whole fiasco. Allow me, Sir, to tell this respectable and cowardly insinu- ator that all being well I shall offer myself as a member of any society that may be attempted to be formed in War- rington under the above heading, with a full conviction that no body of amateur politicians will in this nineteenth cen- tury be so narrow-minded as to exclude, yours respectfully, Warrington, Oct. 16, 1882. H. WHITHAM.

Sir,—" One of Mr. John Bright's Curiosities" is deserv- ing the thanks of the local Conservative party for so con- fidently bespeaking their gallant behaviour in the event of the above society reviving. For the sake of the society, I hope his friends will not be backward in meeting their opponents again. We want an "Opposition," or where is the virtue in a Parliament? The chief thing to avoid in societies of the class in question is that spirit of antagonism which a lady once wittily exemplified by stating that she did not know bow it was she and her husband could never agree, "for," she exclaimed, "we are both of one mind; he wants to be master, and so do I!" We can almost pardon the feminine vote for mastery; it denotes a sex with whose weaknesses we ought to deal tenderly. But i in men, conten- tion for conquest merely is ignoble, and s a symptom of latent pugnacity upon which the moral forces. of educa- tion and refinement should be brought to bear. It ma coarse- ness of character which ought not to exist in any body of men, least of all in those who propose to deal seriously, and, in a public manner, with subjects which affect the in- terests of a country like ours. A local Parliament should be free of any sympathy with the "spirit of conquest." It should be well seasoned with debating powers to support the views of each side. The disideratum of the society should be the development and defence ef sound political prin- ciples, and the explosion of unsound ones. With these objects in view the revival of the "Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society" would be a success. To be a success it must be on a basis that will exclude bigotry from debate. Bigotry is intolerable in a deliberative assembly. It is worse than "whispering tongues" which "poison truth," inasmuch as it breeds enmity and prevents the birth of truth. I regret that your correspondent has a tinge of bigotry in his opinions, of which anon. To be of service, the society should be a fair representation of local opinion. In this case, Conservative aspirants to amateur M.P.-ships must be prepared to occupy the . opposition benches. If they have the pluck of a sensible minority they will not only do this, but subject the policy of the Government to a searching criticism. If the society were reformed on a basis of this kind there would be some encouragement for local thinkers to step into the arena of debate and give vigorous countenance to their respective views. As a means of bringing this about I should suggest that the friends of the society send iu their names to the secretary of whichever club they are members of, and as soon as a sufficient number of names were forth- coming the secretaries might arrange for a preliminary meeting. Let this be dose at once, and it will not be long before Warrington possesses what other towns of less size and pretensions make good use of. Your correspondent has, I observe, some respect for 'respectability—a very natural relish on his part, no doubt----and an equal antipathy towards atheists. In the latter he inclines to bigotry. He would exclude atheists from Parliament. "No atheists allowed here" is the card he would bang on St. Stephen's Gate. This is lamentable, for it proves that if he be one of . "John Bright's curiosities" he at any rate is not one of John Bright's followers. Neither John Bright, Mr. Gladstone—second to none—nor any true Liberal carries his religious principles to such an extreme as to prohibit a fellow-being the enjoyment of electoral freedom on the score of theological delinquency. I have such confidence in the late Lord. Beaconsfield's character as to believe he would not be guilty of a similar injustice to any man, friend or foe. But there is one way in which this fr,ilty of feeling in your correspondent can be met. Th etaking of the oath is as formal and necessary a proceeding in a properly conducted Parliamentary Debating

Society as in the House of Commons proper. No atheist with moral stamina will take that oath. As soon as the society was in working order the Abolition of Oaths Bill might be introduced—l should not object to defend that bill myself, sir—when the votes of the majority would concede or refuse that right to the atheist which "One of John Bright's Curiosities" curiously enough would deny him. There must be something dreadfully abortive in an atheist! I have heard of people fainting at the sight of spiders, and going into hysterics over a playful little mouso. But for a big man, with a whole party at his back, to shudder over an atheist is incredible. Surely there is an absence of mental strength in one whose method of dealing with the atheist is to make a leper of him, or a kind of Pariah whose caste affords an excuse for political boycottism ! Or does our friend view him as a sort of giant, against whom he dare not pit himself as a David? lam afraid "One of John Bright's Curiosities" is too delicate for hand- ling, and ought to be placed on the shelf of some religious museum, where the many-phased gods of modern Christendom are exposed to view, which all but the Atheist are permitted to inspect, and he withheld lest he should laugh at a theological creation with such mar!,fn:id complexions. I am no Atheist, sir, but an el.ociaent, preacher of Atheistical doctrines, reverse",, a wll-:ancoatt phrase of Pope's, and says "An honest, god if. the notleitt work of man." If men will produce worship them, at any rate they ' - o".graven images ), and B,Luld not act .'carcively towards those whose consistenr4 preventYitheih adopting the same extreme. We muse. have freedrAn of opinin, and fread?m of action; while f.,0 bring the 'prejudices ol religion into juxtaposition ! indicapolitics is at once unprintipled and wrong. It also o with ties absence of intellectual prudence not excusable in ev.4,1 "one of Mr. John Bright's curiosi- ties." I hope .V,te. "no Atheists" cry will not deter our local Consira%fves from steeping forward and combining with the Lib'erals to revive the Warrington Parliamentary Debating mciety.—l am, sir, yours truly, BENJ. THE LATE 'VICAR OF FRODSHAM. Sir,—Your correspondent "In Memoriam" has struck a happy chord in advocating a public memorial to the Rev. William Charles Cotton, late vicar of Frodsham. Mr. Cotton was our 'vicar for the period of twenty-two years, during which time he discharged the manifold duties of his office with all love and meekness, the natural reserve which usually concealed his inner thoughts and inner self causing him to to be really known to but few. But to these privileged few who knew him living, and knew him well, their sorrow will be long, and these are they who will cordially endorse in a substantial manner the statements so ably propounded by "In Memoriam." Truly was it said of our late vicar, by an , able coadjutor in the parish at the time of his death, "That ' a great man, a king amongst men had fallen, and well did be merit the well-known but proved encomium passed upon the noblest of the Romans." His life was gentle, and the elements so mixed in him that nature might stand forth and say to all the world, "This was a man." We do not only wish to commemorate the strength of his gigantic intellect, of which there are but few in a century, and talents seldom equalled in their marvellous variety. Nor do we desire only to commemorate the astounding depth and accuracy of his learning, his knowledge of almost all left to us by the ancients, his comprehensive acquaint- ance with nearly every department of modern literature, his scientific acquirements, in a word, his universal genius. No, not even these when all put together to make up an extra- ordinary man,—it is something more valuable, and which we, once his parishioners, appreciate more truly than all our late vicar's learning. It is the natural goodness of his heart, without distinction of rank or station, his unvarying kindness, his goodwill to men, his self-sacrificing generosty which loved to shew favours, which yearned to relieve dis- tress, and which pitied every instance of sorrow. Surely we, his once admiring friends, have not so:soon forgotten the rich intellectual feasts which he so often provided, and which we relished so keenly; have not forgotten his ready wit, his pungent satire, his power of illustration, his bound- less wealth of anecdote, and his amazing fertility of inven- tion. But what we most admired in our late vicar was his genuine humility. His gentleness and goodness to children was an apt illustration of this. He loved to teach them, he loved to gladden their young hearts with presents, he loved to make them wise and happy. But even this did not proceed altogether from the natural goodness of his heart. It sprung from a purer soil than the best man's natural heart; it was the copy of a nobler and holier example than that of any mere man. It was the consequence of a ready and cheerful obedience to a voice he had ever been accustomed to obey, and which had said, in words in harmony with his nature, "Feed my lambs." We all lost a good frieed and an able counsellor in our late good pastor, and it will be a long time before we shall meet with anyone who will so naturally care for our state. From whom again can we expect to receive such good lessons as his life afforded? Lessons of truth- fulness, lessons of honesty, lessons against those common and hateful vices of the world, petty weariness and selfish- ness—in a word, lessons of true manliness. We ought there- fore at the present time to arise to the contemplation of our bounden duty, to a sense of our deep responsibility, and to , the full recognition of our need of some memorial to the man from whose big manly heart used to come those kindly greetings, which we shall never hear more, unless it be in the ear of memory. The restoration of his old parish church is rapidly approaching completion. The opening is fixed for the 23rd of next month. Can be do better, then, than erect some testimonial in this renewed pile to the memory of a labourer in God's vineyard, who was so manifestly worthy of his hire ? The east window is ap- propriated to the memory of another late parish worthy, who richly deserves such distinction ; but so far as is at pre- sent known, nothing has been done in the way of a reredos. The pulpit, font, lectern, screens, and subordinate stained windows are already appropriated. The reredo, that cowning attribute to the "Holy of Holies," and to that table from which the late Mr. Cotton so faithfully and reverently dispensed the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, would be a fitting memorial to him. If properly started, a really handsome structure might be erected, which would remind us of our late friend at every service. Money would be forthcoming in abundance, and all that is required is a little energy on the part of the restoration committee. A vestry meeting should be immediatety called to properly consider that question, and a small committee appointed to take charge of the funds, which, as a matter of fact, are
alrealy offered and held out to them. An by so doing we shall not have it laid to our charge that we have failed to _ _ _ _ _ _

recognise real worth and the higher attributes of Christian love and duty. Thanking "In Memoriam" for his letter, apologising for the great length of my letter, and with an earnest wish that older pens and wiser heads than my own may take the matter up, I ana, sir, yours, (cm, "HONOUR TO WHOM HONOUR IS DUE." Frodsham, October 12th, 1882.

div.head: BLUE RIBBON MISSION.
div.p: BLUE RIBBON MISSION.

Sir,—Those of your readers who are looking forward with interest to the forthcoming " Bine Ribbon Mission," to be conducted by Mr. T. E. Murphy, will read with pleasure the following extract from a letter which I received last Saturday from the Rev. Adam Scott, Congregational minister, Lancaster. He says :—" I understand that Mr. T. E. Murphy is likely to hold a Blue Ribbon mission in your town soon, and I have felt that I should like to write and say to you that be has been with us now for nearly a fortnight, and that no work has ever produced such an effect upon the Lancaster public as his has within the memory of the present generation. The whole town is moved, and 5,000 have put on the ribbon. . . . I can assure you we are having a great blessing, and I trust you may have no less.", Why should we not ? I believe we shall. Mr. Murphy will commence his work in the Tolunteer Hall on Sunday evening, October 29th, at a quarter-past eight o'clock.—Yours truly, R. J. WARD. St. Helens, Oct. 19, 1882.

Viand iiingdom, and especially to the electors of Various con- stltitencies, yet more earnistly arAd unitedly to eantrOise their soda' and political influence, to secure through their represen- tatives in Parliament to stippolt immediate and effective legisla- tion to suppress the traffic in intoxicating liquors, as the main source of that appalling flood of intemperance, the results of which are more calamitous and ruinous than the ravairs and horrors of war, pestilence, and famine combined. He said there was no one in that room who was not convinced of the evil of intoxicating liquors—the evil of the abuse of intoxicating liquors he would say. He did not think in- toxicating liquors in themselves were an unmixed evil, and he was sorry to say he could hardly agree with the last speaker in tot o. There was no doubt that if they could banish intoxicating liquors from the land it would be an advantage; but he believed that there evil would be tempta- tions in this world, and that it was necessary there should be temptations in this world to make men strong that they might resist the temptations that were around them. But there was no doubt that public-houses did offer temptations to the weak in an abnormal degree,—to a fearful extent, and that they might be lessened very considerably. He was very glad that this question was being taken up as it was to-day, that the evil of intoxication was seen on every hand, that they had so many movements at work to mitigate this evil; and he believed that this question was in the van. There was no doubt that the revenue indicated that there was a lessened consumption ef intoxicating liquors. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that the time might come whea intoxi- cating liquors would be used—if they were to be used at all —in moderation. There were some people who seemed to think they could gain benefit from intoxicating liquors, and they used them in moderation. He knew that would not gain the sympathies of some who were pre- sent that night—(hear, hear)—but it was his feel- in in reference to this question. It had been used in'all ages, and he dared say the pure juice ef the grape and, it might be, intoxicating liquors, would be used in moderation in times yet to come. That was hardly the platform on which to make these observations, but he did not come there to speak. He might say tjrat meeting did not represent the sympathy that the temperance friends and the inhabitants of the town had for this great question. Many would have been present, but they were unavoidably absent. He should be very glad to see :public-houses lessened very considerably. He should be very glad to see them conducted on better principles than they were con- ducted to-day. He should he very glad to see the people of this country becoming more sober, and he believed they were becoming more sober. He thought that this country, if it were to go on as it was going a few years since, would have been ruined, for the drunkenness of the people pre- vented them from doing that work efficiently and well which they would have done if they had not used intoxica- ting liquors. He was very glad to think that this movement was gaining ground, that there were many who could not use intoxicating liquors moderately who had taken the blue ribbon, that there many giving it:up altogether who felt it to be a snare to them, and he trusted the time might come when those who felt that they could not use intoxicating liquors 'moderately would give it'up altogether. He was a teetotaller himself, and had been for something like 24 years, arid he had certainly not suffered from the disuse of these intoxicating liquors. Mr. R. Gedemerr, in seconding the resolution, remarked that there was something in what that Bachelor of Arts said that was hardly the thing. (Applause.) He had yet to learn that temptation was needful to strenthen a man, or to produce force of character. He thought it was an Englishman's duty to do all he could to make temptation as small as possible—(applause)—and he was quite sure Mr. Guest would endorse that sentiment, and feel with him that it was their duty to make it difficult to do wrong and easy to do right.' (Applause.) Mr. TORRENS supported the resolution, and said he could assure Mr. Guest that public-houses were a very severe temptation—(hear, hear)—and if he had sat upon the Bench for as many years as he had done he would have seen what the temptation did. (Hear, hear.) After speaking of what temptation had done, he said in Scotland they were further advanced than they were in England. (Hear, hear.) They had Sunday closing in Scotland, and had had it many long years. The sooner Englishmen began to think of this question as they ought to think of it the better, and he hoped they might have not merely a reduction of public- houses, but a removal of them. The Rev. Demsoez BURNS, D.D., who arrived during the course of the evening, also supported the resolution, and gave the history of the local option movement. The resolution was carried. The Rev. J. YONGE said the resolution which had been put into his hands was of the simplest character, but he should like to say, before he submitted it, that he felt com- pelled to come that night in order to testify his interest in the project of the United Kingdom Alliance—(hear, hear) —and also to let his temperance friends know that his fer- vour and zeal in the temperance cause had not evaporated. (Applause.) He was unfortunately prevented being there last Wednesday night, when some of them were led to ex- pect his presence, by one of those fits of exhaustion which had bothered him a great deal lately; and he felt he must make an effort to come that night to let them see that he was still alive, and that his interest was still alive in this great cause to which so recently he had pledged himself. It had been said, by some enemy, he supposed,:that in this par- ticular case that his recent failure in health had been pro- duced by that little bit of blue ribbon. (Laughter.) He wanted them to understand that he did not believe it—(hear, hear)—and he wanted them to understand still farther that his doctor, who had known him for the last 16 years, did not believe it; and therefore the probability was that he would be able to stick to teetotalism and help them with all the strength which God might give him in days to come. (Applause.) After stating that they must not judge of the interest people felt in that movement by the number who had attended the meeting, he proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman for his presence. (Applause.) Councillor GREENING seconded the proposition, which was carried, and The CHAIRMAN, having briefly replied, the meeting separated.
