was not opposed to that course; but, With regard to the interest derived _from the treasurer, whrzh was called the

"Interest Fund," he did not suppose the Local Government Board or anyone else would interfere with it if the treasurer I thought proper to hand it over. He thought it would save a great deal of bother if there was an interest fund, out of which the cost of deputations could be paid, or out of the rates, subject to the auditor's approval.—Major CART- /FRIGHT asked the Clerk how he knew that the proceeds of the sale of the hospital were handed over.—The CLERK said his brother sold it, and the money was undoubtedly paid over to the Union account. Mr. Knott admitted that to be so in his report to the Local Government Board. —Major CART/FRIGHT: You know, Mr. Clerk, I never interfered with the interest fund in the slightest.—The CLERK: Well, I wish you never bad done.—Major CART- WRIGHT said what he had always contended was that this money that was expended on the hospital was the rate- payers' money, and that the receipts for the use of the hospital belonged to the common fund of the Union. But the Clerk wrote in the letter that the accounts paid out of this fund were accounts approved by the Guar- dians, and that they were so approved because the Board considered there was nothing unfair and no objection. Now if the Clerk were alluding to the interest fund, there would have been no objection whatever to that, but they were not only spending the interest fund but money belonging to the common fund of the Union. Then the Clerk turned round upon him in a way which he did not think was fair, and said that he was the means of stopping the payments which the Board were making for luncheons; but now he said the luncheons were required at long sittings and there was no objection. Why had not the luncheons been provided? They had the fund in their hands, and had made payments out of that fund for other matters which would not pass muster with the auditor if they had been brought before him. He asked, whether in common fairness to him, the Clerk should saddle him with having stopped the luncheons of the Assessment Committee He knew the reason that was done. It was to set those gentlemen who were members of that committee against him, simply because "the Major has stopped our beef and beer." (Laughter.) He declared that "the Major" had done nothing at all of the sort. ("Oh," and laughter.) They might laugh, but their laughing and sneering was contemptible beyond measure. They sneered and laughed as if they knew everything, but they did not. [Mr. GARNETT : That's personal.] He never objected to the luncheons. What he objected to was to sit down with them, and he gave his reason why he would not take luncheon.—Mr. °weer: You did sit down with us.— Major CARTWRIGHT: Did I P—Mr. OWEN: Yes.—Major CARTWRIGHT : Well, it was during somebody's absence, whose name it is not worth my while to state. He did not see why the blame should rest upon his shoulders of having been the means of stopping the luncheon, when be did noth- ing of the sort. Mr. Derbyshire might sneer and laugh, but he told him flatly, and withouc fear of contradiction, that it was totally untrue that he had done so. He had named the matter since that time, and not a member of the Board got up. It had emanated from the clerk :—" lam afraid the Major has stopped your luncheon." He was afraid to give the caterer, Mr. Cooper, the order, and he said, "I wish you would move that the committee should have their luncheon as usual." He (the Major) said he would do nothing of the sort, as they could have their luncheons so long as they had the interest fund. His version was the truth and nothing but the truth.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE : I don't believe it.— Major CARTWRIGHT: You don't believe anything. You are one of those spurious imitations of the gentleman I know. —Mr. GARNETT : That is personal.—The CLERK put it to the Major as being ungenerous to accuse him of having stopped the luncheons. He said it was the clerk who had stopped them,—[Major CARTWRIGHT : Yes, I do.]—and it was upon that that he got up to give an explanation that all he had done was to ask the auditor how he had become aware of this fund and these luncheons, and be said that Major Cartwright had told him about them.—Major CART- WRIGHT: Was this explanation given in my presence?— The CLERK: Yes.—Major CARTWRIGHT: That I told him you were spending the interest money P—The CLERK: Yes. —Major CARTWRIGHT : I did nothing of the sort.—The CLERK said he was repeating exactly what took place, be- cause if Major Cartwright said he saddled this upon him at all he was mistaken. All he said he said in the Major's presence, and in explanation of his statement that be (the clerk) stopped the luncheons. He had always believed the luncheons were most reasonable under the circumstances' and he should have been sorry to have raised his hand against them. But he was placed in this position: An independent authority of the Local Government Board—a somewhat high authority— spoke to him officially, and said he might not be the respon- sible person, but it was his duty to call his (the clerk's) attention to the fact that these luncheons could not be pro- vided out of the rates, and to say the least this fend partook of the nature of the rates if not exactly the product of the rates. He had to tell the Board the cost of deputa- tions to the Conferences was not lawfully charged upon the rates, and they had better not attend until the Local Govern- ment Board had said whether they were entitled to do so or not. For the first time in his experience the Board did not send a deputation to the conference; but then the question arose as to whether they ought to attend. It was said "the money is not taken from us at present. It is right we should attend this conference, and we will." He had done then. He had pointed eut to the Board the illegality ef the thing, but he must not dictate to them. Therefore they attended the conference, and he attended with them. The same thing would have followed if Major Cartwright had requested Mr. Cooper or any other member to move that the luncheons be continued until the money was taken away from them. He had no right to interfere. He could only say it was not a lawful charge, and explain the position they were placed in in regard to it. It appeared to him the letter properly put their positicn to the Local Government Board.—Major CARTWRIGHT : Have you written out a cheque for any payment, since the stop- page of these luncheons, for purposes connected with this Board ?—The CLERK: Only by order of this Board.—Mr. GARNETT thought it was time they had done with the matter, and proposed that the letter be sent to the Local Government Board.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE seconded, and the CHAIRMAN having remarked that Major Cartwright was indirectly responsible for what had taken place on the sub- ject, the proposition was carried. TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS.

The CLISRIC said he wrote to the Local Government Board asking them to issue an order to enable them to take a poll of the owners and occupiers of property in the Union with a view to having the election of Guardians made for three years instead of one as at present. The Local Government Board wrote to state they would consider the application, and he had since received the order. After reading extracts from the order, the Clerk brought under the notice of the Board the question of remuneration to be paid to him, and said there was no doubt the new arrangement would materi- ally interfere with his ineome. In several unions the clerk had been paid 3d. per assessment on the rate book for con- ducting the election.—Mr. OWEN said it was evident the Clerk had made up his mind what salary he should like. (Laughter.)—Major CARTWRIGHT : You want to contract with him for the job, do you? (Laughter.)—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE was sorry the Local Government Board had issued the order so soon.—Major CARTWRIGHT pointed out that the Warrington Board of Guardians was the first to move in the matter of triennial elections five years ago, and every time it had cropped up the Clerk had opposed it. He moved that the Clerk be remunera- ted on the same principle as he was when he conducted the poll for the election of Guardians.— Mr. LONGSLIA.W asked if it was not possible to postpone the poll until next April.—The CLERK: No, as the order has been received from the Local Government Board.—Mr. OWEN seconded Major Cartwright's motion, but subsequently expressed his desire to withdraw, but this the Major would not consent to.—Mr. GARNETT proposed that the Clerk be paid 3d. per assessment throughout the district.—This was I seconded by the Rev. G. F. ROBERTS, and carried by a large majority.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. H. S. Hall. John 'Brock, and Holbrook Gaskell, jun. A BATCX or BEGGANS.—John Burke, John McGovern, and George Totterill, elderly men, were charged with bogging in Widnes, on the previous day, and were each sent to prison for seven days' hard laboar.—Burke had 4d in his possession, and McGovern 2s 51d. The cases were proved by P.O. 'a Thompson, Almond, and Skinner. MISCELLANEOUS.—JAn McGee, a young mark,, was charged with sleeping in a chemical works on the previous night. with- out any visible means of subsistence, and on the evidence of P.S. Strickland he was committed to gaol for seven days.—The following persons were fined for drunkenness :—Alfred Hunt, John Riley, Thomas Ward, John Bee, Jaboz Rostrance, Catherine Foyden, Lien White, Elizabeth Oates, John Rowe, Peter Moylan, Thomas Leash, Dennis Burns, Edward Wilding, and Thomas Mitchell.—Thomas Scailey and Thomas Burns, young men, were charged with being drunk and disorderly on licensed premises. P.C. Skinner stated that at a quarter to seven o'olock on Saturday, the 9th inst., the defendants were drunk and creating a great disturbance in the Tine Inn, Waterloo-road, Widnea. Witness entered and requested them to leave, bat they refused to do so, and he forcibly ejected them. Burns was fined 10s and costs, 7s 6d; and Scally,:who did not appear, was fined £1 and costs, 71 6d, or a month's hard labour.—For a similar offence committed in the house of Phillip Dutton, Waterloo-road, Widnes, on the Bth inst., Robert Durham was fined 103 and-costs, on the evidence of Inspector Barnett.—James Roach was charged with commit- ting a breach of the peace La Waterloo-road, on the 7th inst., and was bound over for his good behaviour for two months, himself in £lO and one surety of 25. A DANGEROUS FRACTION. Bernard Canninghan,' James McKenna, Joseph Trainer, and Henry Farmer, boys, were summoned for discharging fireworks in the street.—Mr. Super- intendent Barker remarked that as these were the first cases for the reason he would not press for a penalty, but :he should ask the Bench to deal severely with offenders in the future. The Bench ordered the defendants to pay costs U.—Mr. Barker observed that one or two of the boys were nnder 13 years of age, and he wished it to be understood that shopkeepers could be proceeded against for supplying such boys. CHIMNEYS ON FlRE.—James Condron and John Cowley were fined Is. and costs each for allowing the chimneys of their I houses in Elizabeth street to be on fire.

STRAYING ANIMALS.—Robert Hoy was charged with having on the 10th List. a.lowed his two donkeys to stray in Page. lane, and on the evidence of P.O. 1040. who slated that he had often warned the defendant, he was fined bs and c3sts.—For allowing his horse to stray on Widnes-road, on the 10th inst., George Hewitt was mulcted in a similar sum.

div.head: UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.
div.p: UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.

MEETING AT WARRINGTON. Under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance, a meeting was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, on Mon- day evening. There was a moderate attendance. The chair was taken by Mr. Councillor Monks, who was supported by Mr. R. Swann, of Sunderland, and Mr. Bailie Torrens, of Glasgow, deputation; Rev. W. Pilling, Bev. J. Warnock, M.A., Rev. J. Yonge, Councillor Greening, Councillor Guest, 8.A., Messrs. R. Garnett, John Green, C. Plinston, and C. H. Murray (Preston). Mr. MURRAY explained that a number of gentlemen who were expected, and some who had promised, to be present, were prevented from being with them. He apologised for the absence of the Rev. C. Mansfield Owen, of Southamp- ton, and the Rev. Dawson Burns, of London; and explained in regard to Mr. W. Long that his name was printed as chairman of the meeting without his knowledge and con- sent, and he desired that to be stated in justice to himself. In the difficulty Mr. Monks had consented to act as chair- man. He had letters from the Rev. W. Mules, Mr. Naylor, and others, expressing great regret that they were unable to be present. The CHAIRMAN did not think they would consider it necessary that he should make an introductory speech, be- cause the deputation was present to advocate the cause of the Alliance. He thought the meeting did not fairly repre- sent the feeling in Warrington on this question. Judging from recent events, he was inclined to think that the feeling in reference to the object of the Alliance—which was to give the inhabitants of towns local option—was strengthen- ing in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that the feel- ing would be further strengthened, and that the residents of any neighbourhood who felt themselves aggrieved by the action of any publican would do as some of the residents in Bewsey-road had done—make such representations to the authorities who had the granting of licenses in their hands as should ensure a fair consideration of the whole question. (Applause.) This was not a matter to be forced down the throat of the people, but he believed the conviction was gaining ground throughout the country that this questism of drunkenness was one which must be dealt with, and he was not sorry to see in recent legislation the attempt to throw the responsibility to a large extent of what were called "off licenses" on the shoulders of local magistrates. (Applause.) It was quite evident that the Legislature felt themselves in a difficulty on this matter, and he thought they might take their action as indicating that they felt that those who had a knowledge of all the local circum- • stances were perhaps after all as well qualified to deal with Ithe subject as an irresponsible licensing board in the form of the Excise; and, being so, it remained to a large extent with the inhabitants of Warrington to take the matter into their own hands. He must say that every licensing case that had come before the Warrington magistrates, as far as he was able to judge, had received fair consideration, and he did not think either side had any right to complain. (Applause.) Mr. Councillor SWANN remarked that he was glad to meet them upon the temperance question, and to be able to con- gratulate them upon the position that had been attained in recent years by this great reform. He was very happy to recognise that this temperance question had come to the front, and that it had attained the position its advocates desired it should attain, namely, that the great evil against which they contended was acknowledged on all hands. He looked upon that acknowledgment and that conviction as tothe existence of the drink evil as being a very great accomplish- ment. Some years ago they could not congratulate them- selves upon this matter. Many people disputed the position they held in relation to it. Now everywhere, it did not matter where they looked, they would find the drink evil was acknowledged as a very great evil. If they went into the House of Commons and House of Lords, or throughout the length and breadth of the country, they would find some- times pointed and frequently indirect allusion made to this great evil. Not only was there the conviction of this evil existing in our midst, but there was a growing and earnest desire for its abatement by some means or other, and he,had been glad to recognise within the last few years various socie- ties had been instituted for the purposes of grappling with this evil with the view of its abatement. They had had some- thing rather new upon a large scale in this respect—namely, denominational temperance societies. They found that the churches had taken this matter up, and he looked upon all these societies as a manifestation of the great desire for this drink evil to be abated. 7ie referred to the establishment of coffee shops, AC., adverted to the feeling in Parliament on this subject, and spoke of the progress of the Sunday Closing movement. The supporters of the Alliance were not only in sympathy with all these efforts that were being put forward, but he did not know that there was any form of temperance which Alliance men were not fully in accord. They would find the earnest supporters of every department of temperance wo:k were men prominently connected with the United Kingdom Alliance. The Alliatfce had a special work which it was seeking to promote. Some had hesitated a little on this matter, but he was very glad indeed it was now i nearer a settlement than ever t was before, and that there was almost perfect unanimity amongst temperance reformers in relatiOn to it. The Alliance men did not take a utopian or imaginary view of this question.. They did not ignore the vast amount of capital involved in the liquor traffic, and they wanted to deal with it in a practical way—the way Sir Wilfred Lawson had eu,ggested, which was to his mind the most moderate, most reasonable, and. most constitutional mode in which they could deal with it. He pointed out that as public-houses ostensibly existed for the convenience and benefit of the neighbourhood the present law was eminently a local option law, and they did not want to go contrary to the spirit or to the letter of the law as it at present existed. They simply wanted an amendment of the law, so that the people could decide whether they would have public-houses in their midst. They had confidence in the heads, hearts, and other feelings and principles of their fellow countrymen that they would come to it, and although it might involve a little self-denial in the spirit of the Master, who said, "If any man will be my disciple let him take up his cross .daily and follow me," in that spirit of love and magnanimity and humanity they believed that they very soon would find this otherwise happy land of ours rid of this terrible evil that had so blocked our nation. (Loud applause.) Councillor GUEST moved the following resolution : That this meeting appeals solemnly to the citizens of the 1

div.head: WARRINGTON B OA RD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: WARRINGTON B OA RD OF GUARDIANS

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday. Present—Mr. G. Blackhurst (chairman), Rey. G. F. Roberts, Major Cartwright, Messrs. Darbyshire, Cooper, Brown, Hunt, Houghton, Greenall, Longshaw, Swinton, Appleton, Wallington, Woolfall, Hum- phreys, Marsh, Owen, Greening, Garnett, Caldwell, Hall, Gibson, Kilshall, and J. C. Sutton (clerk).

div.head: PAUPER LUNATICS.
div.p: PAUPER LUNATICS.

Mr. DARBYSHIRH said in looking over the accounts on Tuesday he noticed there were 80 or 90 pauper lunatics in the asylums, whose maintenance cost £430 a quarter or £1,720 a year. He was rather astonished to find so many lunatic paupers in the various asylums, and if there were any in a fit state to leave he thought it was the duty of the Board to see that they were released. What the Board could do to stop the current of issadity he did not know, but it seemed to him lunacy was on the increase and was bccoming very expensive to the Union.—Major CART- WRIGHT: I presume it is the duty of the Visiting Commit- tee, who visit the asylums, to see whether these cases are dischargeable or not. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. APPLETON : That is the dutyof the Visiting Committee.—Major CARTWRIGHT had no doubt it was quite true the pauper lunatics were costing the Board £l7OO a year, but his impression was that the medical officer ought to visit the asylums with the com- mittee. He was, or ought to be, a judge as to whether the cases were retainable or dischargeable. He agreed that the cost should be curtailed if possible, and he would, move that the medical officer accompany the Visiting Committee in future.—The CHAIRMAN said it had occurred to him that it was a great mistake not to take the doctor with them to the asylums.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said it appeared he was wrong in his figures. The cost was £l,BBO a year. The reason he mentioned the matter was that there were two cases in which he interested himself, and was instrumental , in getting them discharged.—The subject dropped.
THE INTEREST PIINIE): THE BOARD'S REPLY TO THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.
The CLERK read the following reply of the Board to the letter from the Local Government Board on the interest fund:—

My Lords and Gentlemen,—ln reply to your honourable Board's letter of the 9th ult. enclosing extract from assistant auditor's report, I am to sty that Major Cartwright having, as he explained to Mr. Knott, filled the office of chairman of the Board when the monies forming what is in the extract termed the" Nemo fund," were received, he is probably correct in his recollect ion of the circumstances. In the absence of any minute explanatory of the purposes for which the two cheques for £145 were drawn in favour of their clerk, and cashed by him or his assistant, it is impossible to add to what has been already written thereon. Payments from the fund in recent years are explained by the vouchers and by the minutes. Major Cast- wright was mistaken in saying the proceeds of sale of the hos- pital building were applied to the Nemo fund ;" such pro- ceeds were duly passed through the Union accounts. The Guardians consider the intention of the persons who in 1868 paid for use of the building was to compensate the Union for the use thereof, and they are prepared upon hearing that you approve their intention to transfer the balance of the " Nemo fund " or special account with their bankers, to the treasurer's account. As regards the"lnterest account," I am to say it consists of ac- cumulated gifts by the treasurer, who made the gifts for reasons explained in my report, and who continues them with the in- tention that they are to be considered a private fund, the use whereof is at the Aiscretion of the Guardians. It is not, nor has it ever been, customary to allow on municipal, parochial, or Union funds in the hands of treasurers or deposited with bankers in Warrington interest, and on the other hand no commission is charged. The terms of appoint- ment of the present treasurer were similar to the terms made with his predece,sor who allowed no interest of money and contributed to no private fund. The treasurer at the last audit asked Mr. Haselhurst to say, if he volunteers to contri- bute to expenditure by Guardians for purposes not chargeable upon the rates, by what law he is prevented from doing so ? The Guardians desire to put the same question to your honour- able Board, and they submit that no illegality, and, in the ab- sence of unworthy motive, no impropriety exists in their use of m^ney expressly meant by the donor to be used at their dis- cretion. The Guardians think it impossible for your honour- able Board to dissent from their view of this matter. Were it otherwise, they suggest that no possible advantage can result from interference with the fund, which is already largely used for purposes the auditor would find to be lawful and rersonable if the expenditure came under his supervision, With regard to expenses of attending Poor Law Conferences and luncheons at long sittings of the Board, and of committees, and not lawfully chargeable upon the rates, I am to say that the expenditure is moderate and reasonable, and that no objection has been made in respect thereof by any person. If your honsurable Board think it necessary to take further steps in this matter the Guardians request your consent to meet a deputa- tion thereon at Whitehall, when the whole subject may be dis- cussed, and a satisfactory settlement thereof arrived at. Mr. OwErT : What do you think of that, Major ?—Mr. APPLETON said it appeared to him that the money derived from the use of the hospital was what was called the "Nemo Fund," and that if the amount was paid to the common

div.head: SALARIES OF OFFICERS.
div.p: SALARIES OF OFFICERS.

'Applications for an increase of salary had been reclived from Mr. T. Garnett, relieving officer, and Mr. B. Shearer, collector and assistant relieving officer. The officers were called before the Board, and in reply to questions, stated that they applied on the ground that they did not consider themselves sufficiently remunerated for their services. Considerable discussion took place as to the officers' duties, and even- tually it was decided not to entertain either of the applica- tions.

SCHOOL COMMITTEE—RESIGNATION OF THE CHAIRMAN. The minutes of the School Committee, which wre passed on the proposition of Mr. BROWN, contained the following: —The committee have before them the resignation, in writ- ing, of the Rev. John Yonge, of the office of chairman of the committee. They much regret that the health of the chairman has not of late been good, yet they lE4pe he may be induced to continue his valuable services in the capacity of chairman for the remainder of the official year, and with the hope that arrangements to this end my be made the superintendent is instructed to call a special meeting of the committee.

div.head: HAYDO(TK COLLIERS.
div.p: THE HAYDO(TK COLLIERS.

Last week several " sectional " meetings of the men em- ployed by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. were held to consider the present position of the wages question, but no definite clecision was come to. No further steps have yet been, taken towards demanding an advance of wages, beyond those reported a fortnight ago, when the notice served on the firm asking] for an advance of 15 per cent. was postponed for a ,month. The men, however, appear pretty unanimous and determined in their intention to press for an advance in a week or two.

On Tuesday evening a man met a Bootle constable, and asked to be arrested as a deserter. He gave his name as Samuel Love, and said that he belonged to G Battery 7th Brigade Royal Artillery; that in December, 1870, he had twenty-eight days' leave of absence, and that he availed himself of that opportunity to abscond to America. He seems to have been fairly prosperous. He was respectably dressed, had money, and also a costly gold watch and valuable chain. Why he -should have given himself up to the police twelve years after his desertion is a matter which he can best explain himself ; but he has, at all events, been remanded until the military authorities are communicated with.

AUTUMN DANGERS.—Pestilential fogs and vapours always follow excessive summer rainfall, and infectious diseases are at no time more prevalent than in the autumn. Every house- holder should be on his guard, and provide in every bedroom, bathroom, and nursery, "Wright's Coal Tar Soap." It is a simple but efficacious prevention of infectious disease. Pur- chase only " Wright's Sapo Carbonis Detergens," as prescribed by the medical profession, ;and see these words w e on every wrapper and tablet.—Advt.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.

ALTRINCHAM. The advocacy of temperance principles on Gospel grounds has been extended to Altrincham, where a crowded meeting was held on Saturday. FRODSHAM. HARVEST FESTIVAL.—A harvest thanksgiving service was held in the Iron Church, Frodsham, on Friday evening, when the church was crowded. The decorations this year were even more artistic than in previous years, and the taste displayed by the decorators shewed to advantage when the church was lighted up. The communion table was perhaps the more pleasing feature, and a very happy effect was produced by a cross of pure white lilies with tastefully arranged vases of flowers on either side, and round its base a magnificent bunch of grapes and other choice fruits, while fine specimens of cereals were suitably placed. The altar rails were entwined with climbing ivy and other seasonable decorations, and gave evidence of the careful attention which had been bestowed. The reading desk and choir stalls were artistically draped with a fringe of oats, sur- mounted by dahlias and interspersed with maiden hair fern. The ectem was entirely hid by some splendid variegatedlili s arranged to form a cross. The chancel arch was ornamented with the esthetic sun flower,-and showed to advantage. The other parts of the church were prettily decorated with flowers, ferns, corn, and evergreens, and the bannerettes were very tasteful. The musical portion of the service:had been well rehearsed, and Mr. Riley, the organist, accompanied with his usual good taste. The anthem was taken from the 65th Psalm, "Thou visitest the earth and blessest it," and was very well rendered by the choir. The preacher was the Rev. Samuel Wilkinson, of Warrington, and an appropriate sermon was given from the words, "The Lord of the har- vest." We must not omit to mention that the fruit, ikc., was liberally supplied by Mrs. Thomas, Mrs. Reynolds, Mrs. Sutton, Messrs. E. A. Wright, Thomas Davies, J. E. Bate, R. Bate, /ec. The ladies and gentlemen who kindly undertook the decorations were: Mesdames A. Thomas, H. Reynolds, F. W. Dunsford, J. C. Sutton, R. Holland, Misses Thomas, Eliza Davies, Astons, Sutton, Holland, Coke, and the Vicar, Rev. A. P. Reynolds, Rev. A. Grier, Messrs. Henry George Linaker, D. Ashton, R. Andrews, and Dr. Robinson. The collection was in aid of the Chester Infirmary. DIOCESAN TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. Two sermons were preached by the Rev. Lionel Garnett, Rector of Christleton, in the Iron Church, Frodsham, on Sunday, when the church was filled by a large and fashionable congregation. On Monday evening a public meeting was held in the girls' school, Church-street. Frodsham, when the Vicar presided, and addresses were given by the Hon. Conrad Dillon and the Rev. Lionel Garnett, rector of Christleton. The pro- ceedings were enlivened by a programme of temperance melodies rendered by the children. LYMM. LYMM LOCAL BOARD.—On Monday evening, a special meeting of this Board was held for the purpose of passing a resolution, or otherwise, to reduce the price of gas. Present —Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Rogers, Appleton, Foster, gibbon, Bailey, Taylor, Dewhurst, Callendar, and Ridgway (elerk).—The Chairman said he was very sorry to have had to call them together that night, but he supposed business must be done. A resolution was brought forward at the last meeting, which was broken up, that the price of gas be reduced from 5s to ds 2d per thousand cubic feet on and after the 30th September, 1882. That was moved by Mr. Rogers, seconded by Mr. Bailey.—He then put the resolu- tion, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Rogers moved the next resolution that four additional lamps be fixed in Higher-lane.—Mr. Bailey seconded the motion.—Mr. Taylor thought there were other districts quite as deserving of being lighted as Higher-lane. If they went to light "those out- landish places" why not go as far as2Mr. Mr. Stubs's and the canal arches in Burford-lane? Those places in the village ought to be attended to before anything else. He moved an amendment that the lamps be not placed in Higher-lane.— Mr. Gibbon seconded.—Mr. Rogers said there was a gas-lamp close to the arches. There was a considerable population about Higher-lane, and he thought they ought not to be kept in darkness.—On a vote being taken, the original motion was declared carried. DRIVING A LOCOMOTIVE AT NIGHTTIME THROUGH LYMM. —A man named Edwin Griffiths, a driver in the employ of Wm. Mitchell, swing boat owner, of Oldham, was brought up at Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, charged with driv- ing a locomotive along the highway at Lymm, at 10 p.m. on Sept. 27th, contrary to Act of Parliament, which states that a locomotive shall not pass over a highway between the hours of 7 p.m. and 3 a.m.—P.C. Chatterton said that on the night in question he saw the defendant driving a traction engine, attached to a number of swing boats, through Lymm, about 10.10 p.m. Defendant, on being questioned, gave his name, and said that he did not know he was break- ing the law. Defendant, when before the court, stated that he had travelled through the district about two years, and had been acting under the bye-laws of 1878. During the time he had travelled through the district he had not seen any bye-laws.—PS. Harrington remarked that large placards were posted in every township in Cheshire stating the hours when a locomotive was NC pass along the roads—Defendant: We did not know that there was a bye-law or we should have applied for one.—ln answer to the clerk, defendant said he or_ly travelled in Cheshire and Lancashire, and had gone through Altrincham and Stockport several times.— The Bench fined him 20s and costs 14s 6d. A NEGLIGENT FATHER SENT TO G-AOL.—At the Lymm Petty:Sessions, yesterday, before Messrs. G. Dewhurst, Henry Stanton, and A. Milne, Mr. W. C. Moore, relieving officer for the district, appeared to prosdcute James Moore, a tailor, who did not appear, for _neglecting to comply with the magistrates' order to support his child.—Mr. Moore said the case was adjourned two months ago because the defendant promised to pay 4s. until arrears amounting to .£1 12s. were paid off. Since that time he had paid in all 16s. He had seen the defendant, who was working in Lymm, and had told him that unless he paid 12s. that morning he should go before the court. The defendant had not paid the money, and he was instructed by the Board of Guardians to ask that hp be committed to gaol. This case had given them more t ,-;uble than any other case they had on their books.—ln answer to the clerk, P.S. Harrington said defendant hadf neither house nor furniture. He had been sent to gaol for a month previously, and was a lazy fellow.—The Bench con- sidered it a very bad case, and committed defendant for a month, with hard labour.

NANTWIC H. To suppress the nuisance of stone-throwing, the Nantwich Highway Board has instructed its surveyor to issue cautionary notices. Damage to the extent of £lOO has been sustained by a farmer of Doddington, near Nantwich, through the burning of his shippon. The estimate of the expenditure of the Local Board of Nantwicb, for the half-year ending March 25th next, amounts to £1,327 3s. Bd. The number of persons sleeping in the different lodging- houses at Nantwich during the past fortnight was: Males, 302; females, 106; a totaLof 405. Two persons have died suddenly at Nantwich within the past few days from heart disease, one being a labourer in Crewe works and the other a married woman. BE-ASSESSMENT OF RULWAY PROPERTY IN THE NANT- WICH UNlON.—Sometime ago the Assessment Commtttee of the Nantwich Union decided upon a re-valuation of the whole of the railways, works, canals, and manufactories using motive power in the Union. The Crewe steal works of the London and North-Western Railway are comprised in the Union district, and the Company, after some correspon- dence, offered to compromise with the Committee by sub- mitting to an increased assessment of £B,OOO. This offer I was net accepted, and Mr. Marshall, of London, who has made the re-valuation, has just completed his report. Ihe re-assessment shows an increase of nearly £50,000. The property of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany in Monk Coppenhall has been increased from £20,000 to £34,000; in Church Coppenhall from £4,000 to £7,500; in Crewe (borough) from £4,000 to £lO,OOO. The re- assessment has embraced over 30 adjoining townships, in all of which the assessment had been considerably increased, it being in some cases more than double the old valuation. The North Stafford Railway property in the Union has also been increased for rateable purposee by over £1,500. It is expected that the result of this great increase will be to reduce the Union poor rate by sixpence in the pound per year, and the general district rate (Crewe) by a similar amount. The agriculturists will benefit very considerably. CLUB DINNER AT WINWICIC.—The members of the Win- wick club celebrated the anniversary of their institution on 'aturday evening last by a dinner at the Swan Inn. After ~inner the prizes of the club bagatelle handicap were pre- sented, and the usual loyal and patriotic toasts were pro- posed. The society are endeavouring to raise funds for the purchase of a library. BAGATELLE HANDICAP AT WINWICIL—During last week the members of the Winwick club were engaged in playing off a bagatelle handicap, which has excited considerable interest among them. The game was 150 up, 24 members competing. Mr. H. J. Longton (scratch) was declared the winner, having beaten five successive opponents, Mr. J. Pen- nington (70 start) being the runner up. The third, fourth, fifth, and sixth prizes were taken by Messrs. J. Greenhalgh, S. Straw, T. Straw, and W. Sweetlove, in the order named. The seventh prize was competed for by the twelve men beaten in the first round, and was won by J. Shaw (50 start). Mr. Gibson, from Manchester, gave the first prize, and Messrs. Crawford, P. Langton, H. J. Longton, Green- halgh, and Sweetlove each gave a prize. WIGAN. Mr. Algernon Egerton was on Wednesday afternoon raited upon by a deputation from the Wigan Conservatives, who asked him to become their candidate at the election for that borough. Mr. Egerton accepted the invitation. THE WIGAN VOTING LISTS —The new parliamentary and municipal voting lists for the borough of Wigan were issued on Saturday. These give 0,172 voters on the par- liamentary list, and 7,054 on the municipal register, being an increase of 75 on the parliamentary and 105 on the municipal list. WIGAN TOWN Couxem—A special meeting of the Wigan Town Council was held on Saturday, for the purpose of electing a successor to Mr. Alderman Thomas Byrom, the "father of the Corporation," who died last week. Mr. Councillor Henry Park (C), iron merchant, of Wigan and Southport, was elected. Mr. Byrom was also a Conserva- tive.

CHURCH EXTENSION IN THR NEIGHBOIMITOOD OF WIGAN. —The Earl of Ellesmere, on Wednesday afternoon, laid the foundation stone of an extension of the Bridgewater School Church, Newtown, near Wigan. Some months ago.a move- ment was inaugurated to extend the church and school accommodation in the parish of Pemberton, and the Bridge-

water trustees, towards the cost, which is estimated at £4,000, contributed £6OO, and the other landed proprietor, in the neighbourhood have promised liberal subscriptions., The scheme is to erect school churchea in various parts 01 the p .rish. _ _
