div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

TtnesDev.--.l3efore Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. ACTION AOAINST A WARRINGTON VETERINARY StinCMON. --George Mock, of 32, Bridge-street, Runcorn, sued Fredk. Wall, veterinary surgeon, Warrington, for the sum of £1 Us. for rent -due.—From the evidence adduced by the plain- tiff, it appeared that Mr. Wall engaged a room in the defen- dant's house as a branch surgery, in which he stored his bottles, at a Te.onthly tenancy of 16s. He had paid two months' rent by an order of the court, and he was now sued , e for the remainder.—Mr. Wall said he had had no epplica- - - don for the rent, and the defendant had had notice given him two months ago. He took the room at a weekly emaeoze.—Mrs. Wall, who was called, deposed to giving the defendant's wife notice on one day when the latter called at her house for the rent.—Mrs. Mack denied this, and said Wall's bottles were still in the house, and his bill also In the window.—His Honour gave judgment against the defeniant. He thought the room was let at a monthly ten- ancy, and Mr. Wall was still in occupatien. A FRODSHA3I PICT-CU:2 TRINSACTION.—Mr. Hitthen ap- -12 'peered for the plaintiff, and Mr. Little (instructed by Mr. Burton) appeared for the defendant, in a case brought by Wm.Strickland,photographer,Frodshaireagainst Mrs.Prouse, Of the same locality, for the sum of £3, being the balance due on two pictures supplied by the plaintiff to the defend- ant.—lt seems that Mr. Strickland purchased the business ' of Mr. Harvey, of Frodsham, early in the present year; and shortly afterwards undertook to produce two oil paintings— one of Mr. Prouse, the deceased husband of the defendant, and one of Mrs. Prouse herself—from two small photo- graphs. He was shown a picture to give him an idea as to the size which he was to make the paintings and another as to the style of the frame. The plaintiff took proofs of the pictures to Mrs. Prouee's house at latter end of March when Mrs. Sutton, the defendant's neice, pointed out that Mr. Prouse's portrait wareted studs painting in the shirt front. The plaintiff painted in the studs, and framed the pictures, and on the Ist April again took them to the house of the defendant. The defendant was in bed, but Mrs. Sutton re- ceived them, and took them upstairs to be viewed by Mrs. Prouse. Mrs. Sutton shortly afterwards returned, told him her aunt said the pictures were satisfactory, and that she would call upon him in a few days and settle the account, giving him then, however, 2s. 6d. for his trouble. When he neat went to the house Mrs. Prouse re- fused to pay him tee money, because one of the pictures, that representing herself, was cracked down the face. Plaintiff contended this defect was not in when he delivered them, and alleged that it had been done by laying the picture on some uneven surface.—Mr. Sampson Harvey said the pictures, which ho censidered good ones, were not injured when delivered. The. marks which the picture now bore might be the result of a blow of a fist. In reply to Mr. Little, he said he had seen many a face cracked by a blow from a fist. ee(Laughter.)—For the defence Mr. Little con- tended that the defendant, when shown the pictures which he was to take as patterns (produced), promised that those he should produce would be equal if not better, and £3 was paid on account. Scarcely a day had passed after the pictures had been taken borne before blotches appeared, grew larger, and 'ultimately the picture cracked down the face. This arose from the chemicals used not being properly applied.— Mrs. Sutton said she took the pictures in her aunt's bed- room on their arrival, but she scarcely gave her time to examine them; and her aunt gave her 2s 6d to give to Mr. Strickland, and told her to inform him she would pay him- in a few days.—Mr. Weaver, photographer and picture dealer, Runcorn, was called, and said the pictures were poor ones. In his opinion, the crack and blotches were caused through the pictures not being properly mounted.—His Honour, in giving judgment for the plaintiff, remarked that be was of opinion that the injuries had been caused to the picture by their being laid against some projection. De- fendant agreed to pay for the pictures, and it was now too late to object to do so because, as she set up, certain injuries afterwards developed in the pictures as they hanged upon the wall. CLAIM FOR INJURY TO A HORSE. CURIOUS PROCEEDINGS. William Bentham, boatman, of 36, Shaw-street, claimed £l6 from John Moore, blacksmith, being the damages sus- tained by plaintiff in consequence of the loss of his horse, caused through the negligence or improper shoeing of the horse by the defendant or his servant. The plaintiff also claimed £1 55., being the amount paid for the keep and hire of a horse during the time the plaintiff's horse was unable to work.—Mr. Fletcher appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Thomas Shepherd Little, barrister-at-law, Liverpool (in- structed by Mr. Barton), appeared fer the defendant.—Mr. Fletcher said the allegation by the plaintiff in this case was that the horse was "pricked " in shoeing, badly pricked, and that in consequence of being pricked intim:nation set in in the foot of the animal, which ultimately had to be des- troyed, and became a total loss. The facts of the occur- rence were these :—Mr. Edwin Tuckey, brother-in-law to the plaintiff, was a hay and straw dealer, and also a hauling horse keeper, and the horse in question was left in his charge whilst the plaintiff went to Liverpool. On the 4th August, receiving intimation from Bentham that the horse would be required for use on Saturday, Mr. Tuckey took the horse to the defendant's smithy, and left the horse with the de- fendant's son. In a short time afterwards the son returned the horse to Tuckey'S stable. The horse was apparently all right until the Bth August, when he was noticed to be lame. The horse had not been worked. Tuckey sent to the de- fendant and informed him that there was something wrong with the horse's foot. Accordingly Cooke, the defendant's 113,113, oa the evening of that day carefully removed the shoe Irene the neer bind led, with rispect to which the aetiOn was brought, and next morning Cooke anii defendant's son, who had shoed the horse, examined the horse and endea- voured to cut down the nail holes, but they did not succeed in getting to the bottom of them. They cut as far as they , deemed t 3 be prudent, and then left the foot. By the ' directions of Mr. Coates, veterinary surgeon, Halton, a mode of treatment was adopted.. Coates did not appear, however, to have examined the foot; but said he was under the impression that the horse was suffering from an open joint. On the 3rd August the animal was taken to the field Of a farmer named Ford, and on the 15th, either in conse- quence of the aCtion of the police or the Royal Society, the horse was killed. Not satisfied with what Mr. Coates had said about the matter, the plaintiff thought it advisable to have a post-mortem examination. So far as the leg was concerned, and accordingly Robinson, horse slaughterer, a nun of very considerable experience in matters of this kind, was told to make an examination. He pronounced that the horse had died from a prick. The leg was cut off, and taken by the plaintiff to Mr. Ferguson, veterinary surgeon, of Warring- ton, a man of high repute in his profession. Before doing so, however, the plaintiff informed Moore of his intention, and invited him to accompany him, or informed him that another veterinary surgeon could see the limb, and confer with Mr. Ferguson on the matter. Moore declined the in- vitation, and said he would have nothing to do with the matter. On returning from Warrington the plaintiff and Tuckey called upon Moore with the leg, and told him the result of the examination by Mr. Ferguson, and they asked him also to have an opinion on the matter, but he refused. The consequence was that the plaintiff , kept the leg as long as he could—embalming seemed to have I been a lost art—and be had to part with the leg. Otherwise it was their intention to keep it until after the hearing of this case. Moore made one very extraordiary statement when the matter was first mentioned to him on the day when he and Cooke went to examine the horse. Cooke was con- gratulating himself, aaying "It was a grand good job I did not shoe the horse," when Moore said, " Well. I certainly did touch him in the fore legs, but I didn't know that I had done him in the hind legs. If Moore made that statement, to which witnesses would testify, it was pretty clear that he was not an experienced blacksmith, and ought not to be em- ployed in a smithy ; in fact, he (Mr. Fletcher) was told that ha was not the proper man to drive the nails. Cooke, who was a man of considerable experience, ought to have shod the horse, but Moore was trying his " prentice hand" upon . animals that morning. Edwin Tuckey was then examined and corroborated the advocate's statement.—Wm. Bentham, boatman 36, Shaw-street, Runcorn, also gave evidence.— Peter Robinson, 20, Church-street, Warrington, said he came to Runcorn to remove the plaintiff's dead horse from the field. At the invitation of Tuckey be examined the horse, and cut the near hind foot off at the fetlock joint. When he did so a quantity of matter and blood came from the joint. To the best of his knowledge the horse had been pricked, which had caused death.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Little, witness said he boiled horses down, and sold them for cat's meat, and sent them to London.—Mr. Little : To be made into sausages. (Laughter).—Witness: Well, I sell them most to Sir Gilbert and other gentlemen. I don't know what they do with them. (Laughter.)—Mr. H. Fer- guson, veterinary surgeon, Warrington, said on the 16th August, Bentham and Turkey called upon him with a horse's foot, of which he made a c'ose examination. He got one of his smiths to divide the wall of the foot from the sole, and also divide the wall across the front of the foot from below upwards. He then carefully removed all the outside of the foot—the horn. He found intense inflammation of the sensitive lamera, a portion of which was destroyed ; evidently caused by injuries from nails. Without doubt those injuries resulted from pricks. The horse had net suffered from an open joint. The condition of the horse's foot on the 16th when he saw it was consistent with a prick received on the sth. From the state in which the foot was when he examined it, he was of opinion the horse could not havaenrecioveredijotHpreohpaedr threeaartdmhenowt ft ohre hthoershe ohrsaed, been treated,d t Was but the plaintiff had no proper advice on the matter. It would not be right to take the horse suffering as it was a walk of three-quarters of a mile.—By His Honour: During his experience of 10 years he had only bad two fatal cases from pricks.—This concluded the case for the plaintiff f.— The court then adjourned for lunch; and, on resuming, Mr. Little submitted that no case had been made out against the defendant. There was no evidence to show that the loss of the horse was caused by the negligence or improper shoeing by the defendant. With regard to the claim for the hire and keep of the horse during the time which the plain- tiff's horse was unable to work, this had not been proved. On the evidence of Mr. Ferguson, it could not be said that the loss of the horse was owing to the negligence or improper shoeing. The hors-e was not properly treated. Had it been so Mr. Ferguson's impression, from his experience of the nature of pricks to horses, was the horse would not have died. If a man was to properly treat a horse and then kill tehvehosruspewsiit2hgout the authority of any veterinary surgeon, en po that the defendant had been negligent in the first instance, it would certainly be bad in law. The plaintiff seemed to think all that was required of him in his proof was to prove that the defendant had pricked the horse, but assuming that the evidence which had been offered was correct, he submitted that the plaintiff must do 1 something more—that the mere pricaing of a horse in

shoeing was not sufficient unless there was some evide-joe of negligence. Mr. Little quoted a decision of Baron l'ollock, that a farrier was not an insurer, and Ms. Little, therefore, contended that the plaintiff, In addition to proving that the foot of the horse had beeu pricked, must also prove that there had been negligence in the method of shoeing otherwise the farrier would be made an insurer. —His Honour said a skilled workman was bound to exhibit i reasonable skill and knowledge in the particular trade or work in which he was engaged. He did not undertake to be perfect; but the question in every case of skilled working was had there been a fair and reasonable amount of skill used by the woezman or not. He should say that there was raidence of a .cant of skill, otherwise the horse would never have been pricked. He thought there was prima facie evidence to rapport the plaintiff's contention as far as the case.had gone, but from the evidence of Mr. Ferguson there did not seetea to have been any proper treatment used for the horse; there had been great negligence from first to last; and that '.seing so, it seemed to him that the consequences in the shape of damage for the plaintiff had not followed upon any.negligence caused upon the part of the defendant. With regard to the shoeing, tha plaintiff might be entitled to some trifling amount of damage, but he was not prepared to say from the plaintiff's evidence that the death of the horse had resulted from the injury alleged to have been inflicted by the defendant.—Mr. Fletcher pointed out that a man was only bound to exercise a reasonable amount of care to avoid the consequences of this wrongful act, and he contended that the plaintiff had done so. The plaintiff had used the best means at his disposal since the injury had been inflicted to cure the animal. The death was the result of the prick. —His Honour: I deny that; the evidence shows that it was not. I distinctly deny that:—Mr. Fletcher: It was the not letting out of the matter caused by the prick. It did not follow tkat because a man did not do the best thing sug- gested by science, that the defendant was relieved from lia- bility.—His Honour: I think so; for the plaintiff does not resort to the best assistance he could gee, but merely called in Cooke, when he could have had the assistance of a com- petent veterinary surgeon; which is neglect on the part of the plaintiff, for which the defendant is not liable, particularly when you hear the evidence of Mr. Ferguson, who, during ten year's experience, has only had two fatal cases.—Mr. Fletcher: He has known these. This was such a one.—His Honour: He doesn't say so. There has been no proper treat- ment.—Mr. Fletcher: I can-not carry the case any further. —His Honour If the defendant were to give plaintiff some trifling sum, assuming that there was a want of skill in pricking the horse, and both parties withdraw from the case, I think that would be the best way. I felt very strongly all through the case that I could hardly impute that the death of this horse was caused really by the prick.—After a consultation between counsel, Mr. Little said he had taken upon himself to say that the defendant would give the plaintiff .22 10s, and each party pay their own costs. Mr. Fletcher had assented to that, and he (Mr. Little) thought it was not an unfair settlement.—His Honour: I think it is a fair settlement.

div.head: SHOCKING CATASTROPHE AT WESTON POINT.
div.p: SHOCKING CATASTROPHE AT WESTON POINT.
A BOY AND HORSE DROWNED.

The dock at Weston Point, known as the old basin, was the scene of a sad accident about seven o'clock on Monday night. The road, which runs parallel with the dock, although much used by foot passengers and vehicles, is un- protected by any fence, and as Robert Leyland, a man em- ployed by the Runcorn Co-operative Society, was driving a cart along the road the horse in the shafts took alarm at some object in front. It commenced to back towards the water's edge. The driver, in alarm, leaped from the cart, seized the reins at the horse's head, bet his strenuous efforts to make the horse stop its retrograde movement and go for- ward were unavailing. The horse continued backing, and fresh horror was I ent to the occurrence by the fact that in the cart was a young boy named John Masker, and the night was pitch dark. At length the boy, cart, and horse were in the water, and Leyland sent forth shouts for aid. Aid was quickly forthcoming, but too late to be of any service, for when the cart was raised to the surface, the poor boy was lying in it quite dead, as was also the horse in the shafts. The inquest on the body of the boy was held at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, on Tuesday afternoon, before Mr. Ridgway, coroner. Robert Musker, a boatman, Whitechapel, Weston Point, deposed that the body, of which the jury had had the view, was that of his son, 10 years of age. As he was at Liverpool at the time of the accident he did not know how the deceased came to his death.—Robert Leyland, of 50, Sewell- street, Runcorn, was then called. The Coroner cautioned witness in the usual way, and handed him the testament for the purpose of administering to him the oath. Witness declined to be sworn, and when asked his reasons he said he believed in the New Testament, but the Saviour told them to "swear not at all," but that their conversation should be "Yea, yea, and nay, nay." He had come to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. The Coroner said he was afraid he could not let him off, and asked witness if he was a Quaker. Witness: Not exactly. The Coroner: Well, then, unless you are a Quaker, you are bound to take the oath. If you had been a Quaker I could have adminis- tered a declaration. Witness: If I said I was a Quaker I should be telling an untruth. The Coroner: Then I must ask you to kiss the Testament. Witness: I would like the gentlemen [jury] to say. The Coroner :It does not rest with the jurymen. I sit here as coroner, and it rests with me. lam afraid I cannot help you. He pointed out to witness that.the law compelled him to administer the oath unless he was a Quaker. Witness said he objected to kiss the Testament on conscientious scruples, and he did not care to violate them.—The Coroner said he respected the scruples of the witness.—After a little further consideration witness consented to take the oath, and he deposed that he was a carter in the employ of the Runcorn Co-operative S,ciety. On Monday afternoon he was delivering goods at Weston Point, and he made a call at the house of Mrs. Tatlock. Before he reached that house the boy Masker had been riding with him in the cart. He had followed him some distance asking him to allow him to get into the cart, and he consented. Just previous to leaving Tatlock's a board fell from the cart and Musker go out to pick it up. Witness then told the boy that he must not again enter the cart until he got to the lamp on the dockside. On arriving at that spot witness examined his book by the light shown from the lamp, and whilst doing so the boy, unperceived by him, mounted the back of the cart. Afterwards he started the horse along the dockside a distance of about 50 yards. Then he turned to cross the piece of waste land, known as the Croft, with the intention of going to the schoolhouse. The lhorse shied at something and began to "back." Witness jumped Over the front of the cart, seized the horse's head, and did all he could to prevent the horse backing into the dock. It was very dark and he could not get the horse to move forward. It centinued backing in spite of all his efforts—the wheels went over the dockside, and he (witness) was dragged to the very water's edge before he let go the reins. He was at a loss what to do and called ifor assistance, but nobody came, and he ran for the I police. He met P.S. Dalziel coming out of his house, and ; went with him to the spot. Means were taken to raise up the I horse and cart. Witness waited until the horse and cart were taken from the water. The body of Musker was found dead in the cart.—By the Coroner : The way across the Croft was a short road to the schoolhouse. He could not say whether it was a private or a public road. He had I never been warned not to go across.—A juryman stated that I the road along the dock side had been used by the public for many years, but the road across the Croft was not a I public one, and he considered that it ought not to be used by vehicles.—Another juryman stated that years ago the road along the dock side was protected by fences, which had been broken down. —The Coroner, in sum- ming up, said the evidence was very simple and plain, and he thought the jury would have no hesitation in saying the boy had met his death accidentally. So far as he could understand the evidence of the driver no blame was attach- ing to that individual for the death of the boy Musker. He did not know what the jury felt collectively and individually about the case otherwise. It seemed to him to be a pity that there was no protection at the lane end to prevent any per- son driving into the docks, and it was for the jury to sug- gest that the dock trustees should put up a barrier to pre- vent future accidents of a similar nature to the one 're question.. If the driver had kept on the proper road the unfortunate accident would not have happened, but the jury knew that men— they did so often enough themselves, perhaps—would take the shortest cut in going to any place. He did not think any blame could be attached to Leyland.—Mr. S. Yarwood, foreman of the jury, remarked that this was the third acci- dent which had occurred at the dock side. At the particu- lar spot in question three horses had been drowned, but this was the first occasion on which human life had been lost.— The jury returned a verdict of 'Accidental death," and re- commended that a strong low fence should be placed along- side the dock to prevent horses walking into the water in the dark.

div.head: BIBLE SOCIETY MEETING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: BIBLE SOCIETY MEETING AT RUNCORN.

There was only a moderate audience at Runcorn Public Hall, on Tuesday evening, op the occasion of the annual meeting of the Runcorn Branch of the British and Foreign Bible Society. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. Symons (district secretary), \%T Preston, J. Pickwell, and—. Williams. The CHAIRMAN remarked that while other books had been 'superseded by those of modern date, the Bible still held its place on the bookshelf. There never, perhaps, were so , many men permeated with scripture truth as there were at the present time. He did not say that it all arose from personal reading of the scripture in private, or from hearing , it read in our sanctuaries, but whatever knowledge of truth was conveyed to the mind of man, whether through the preaching of the Gospel, or the conversation of Christian I men' as were the instructors in Sunday schools—whatever good had been derived was to be traced to the foundation and fountain of it all—the Bible. (Hear, hear.) He did not know where they could look without perceiving the universal influence of the Heart of God. The palaces of our merchant princes were adorned with illustrations which were derived from scripture. The painter's pencil had depicted the birth of Christ, His crucifixion, His resurrec- tion, His ascension—all these glow upon the walls of our palaces; and, in fact, the rude stones were by the young ' sculptor's chisel formed not merely into gods and goddesses, fairies, and nymphs, but grew up into preaching apostles and martyrs. And what had music for some of its sub- limest themes but the Bible—where except in the scriptures could they find subjects adegnate to excite the genius of our great musical Composers? It was impossible to say how much the Bible had done for us all, and how unconsciously

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 21. 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 21. 1882.

were so many minds affected by it. When they considered the great good the Bible had done for everyone, he thought they would agree with him tl:at it would be the lesser cala- mity that should withdrar the sun from the firmament and the oxogen from the atmosphere than it would be to rob the Christian of the brk;nt light of the poet art of revelation. The Rev. J. STmorrs delivered an address, remarking that it might have seemed strange that he should succeed the late Mr. Page, 'out he might tell them that he had been a clergy- man of the Church of England for a period of dye years. For a period of 131 years previous to his taking holy orders he was an officer in the Royal Navy, and had visited many quarters of the globe. During the year lately passed the Bible Society had circulated in round numbers 3,000,000 copies of the work of God either in whole or in part. That was at the rate of 60,000 ' per week of six days. The society distributed Bibles to gaols, workhouses, asylums, waiting-rooms at railway stations, bedrooms at hotels, and numerous other places at home. The other day our troops left England for Egypt; of course, they were now returning. The men were going into camp, into action, and were devoid at any rate'of some I of the ordinary means of wors4pping, and so the Bible Society considered that they ought to do something. Through the Thames and Mersey City Missions the society circulated no less than 12,000 New Testaments to the troops on their leaving the shores of England. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The society did not work among any particular class to the exclusion of any ether. Not long ago Prince Leopold was married, and the Bible Society, following a custom which had got fairly hold, presented him and his bride with a copy of the scriptures, accompanied with the respectful request that they would be pleased to accept it, and that God would bless them in their married life. The present was acknowledged by Prince Leopold, who said he was glad the society had not forgot the custom which was initiated when the Prince of Wales was married. Referring to the foreign labours of the society, Mr. Symons said there was a wonderful work being done in France. In France and other parts of Europe there were over 300 colporteurs distributing the Word of God, and the Society had been enabled to circulate over 600,000 during the past year. The Congregational minister, Mr. Weal', had'2s missions in Paris, and the good he was doing was inestimable. A check had been put upon crime there, and the only reason the Prefect of Police could give for the pleasing fact was that Mr. M'Call was civilizing the people. (Applause.) Mr. Symons touched upon the Society's work in Belgium, Germany, Austria, and Spain. In the latter country great difficulties had been met, but recently the minister of public warship had introduced greater liberty of worship, and the society's circulation was increasing. Speakingof.the Rev. Lansdale's journey to Siberia, where he distributed a large number of Gospels, Mr. Symons said there was a grand field which had not yet been opened out, and, although the society had, since its formation, distri- buted 93 million copies of the Bible, the society had scarcely commenced its work.

The Rev. W. PRESTON related a few of his personal experiences in Rome, where he himself had distributed the Bible, and read the annual report, which showed that the subscriptions received were :—Dowager Marchioness of Cholmondeley, £5; Parish Church, £7 us; Trinity Church, £3; Wesleyan, £l7; Congregational, £2 19s 6,1; Presbyterian, £4 15s; Primitive Methodist, £1 14s; Welsh Church, £1 9s; United Methodist Free Church, 17s 6d; Halton Church, £1 10s; Halton Wesleyan, £1 8s 0d ; Weston Point, £1 is; total, £4B 5s 6d. During the year there had been sold 392 Bibles and 383 Testaments, com- pared with 210 and 97 respectively in the previous year. During the past year the depot had been removed to Mr. Humphrey's shop, and he had returned as a subscription the 36s he had received for the use of the depot and commission —(applause)--and Mr. Preston said that the best thanks of the meeting were due to him for his generosity.—The Rev. Mr. WILLIAMS moved that the best thanks be given to the learned chairman for presiding over the meeting.—The Rev. J. Plcawint, seconded, expressing the hope that there would 131 a larger attendance at the next meeting of the society.— The meeting closed in the usual way.

fermed that they had expended £1,070 cpon their beautiful chapel, and towards this the sum of £450 had been raised, leaving a debt of £620, and they hoped to realise £l2O by the bazaar. The sum was not a very large one, but he was glad to see that they were struggling to free them selves from the burden. He sincerely wished that the bazaar might be eminently successful, and they would then have no cause to regret coming together that day. He had great pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. The serious business of the day was then commenced in good earnest, and an inspection of the stalls showed that the friends had bestowed much care and taste upon their' arrangement. There were three stalls, and at the one presided over by Mrs. Midwood and Mrs. James Hough, we noticed an oleograph, wooden cradle, antimacassars, wool- work cushion gipsey table, what-not, and a quantity of children's - clothing. The stall under the management of Mrs. Billingsley and Miss Moore, of Run- corn, and Miss Berwick, of Frodsham, had a number of toilet sets and boxes, dolls' beds, bead work cushions, darnet antirnaccassars, crewel work, tea cosies, miniature ships, dolls, and other fancy articles. The other stall was under the direction of Mrs. Booth and Mrs. Pickwell, of Runcorn, and Mrs. Booth and Mrs. P. Riley, of Frodsham, and had a miscellaneous assortment, consisting of wool wraps, satchels, carved brackets, baskets, doll and cradle, ' stools, children's clothing, &c., &c. It was announced dur- ing tbe first days' sale that Mr. Speakman had kindly given £5 and a waggon of coals towards the bazaar fund, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Speak- man for his liberality. An interesting • document was on sale at the bazaar, being a copy of the first plan printed in the Primitive Methodist connection, and bears the date of 1812. It contains many of the well-known names of the early prisoners of Primitive Methodism, amongst which we observed J. Bourne, H. Bourne, W. Clowes, &c. The last-named gentleman is down on the plan as having preached at Five Crosses, near Frodsham, on the 6th Jane, 1812. The birth of Primitive Methodism in Frodsham, it should be stated, dates from the year 1819, when the town was missioned by Thomas Jackson, and a society of 30 was then formed, but no per- manent place of worship was provided until the year 1870, when the chapel at Frodsham Bridge was erected chiefly through the exertions of Mr. Wm. Booth, who has been a hard worker in the cause at Frodsham for upwards of twenty years. In the year 1875 a school was built in Frodsham, and in 1878 the present neat chapel added, and it is in aid of the funds of the building in Frod- sham that the present bazaar was held. There was a brisk demand for the goods, which we ought in fairness to state were marked in plain figures, and at very reasonable prices. The refreshment stall was presided over by Mrs. Collier and Mrs. Thomason, of Runcorn. and Mrs. J. toud, of Frod- sham, and we can vouch for the excellence ef the good things provided. Mr. Uxworth, of Runcorn, kindly sup- plied the flags for decorating the hall, and the decorations had been carried out by Mrs. Booth, of Runcorn, Rey. D. Schofield, Mr. W. Booth Mr. Peter Riley, and Mr. James Hough. The Rev. D. Schofield acted as secretary, and Mr. William Booth as treasurer. We must not omit to mention that the museum afforded much amusement, and contained some rare curiosi- ties. A musical programme each day was given by Miss Schofield and Messrs. E. Billingsley and James Hough on the piano and American organ.
deliver lectures, and he thought Mr. G. S. Ilazlehurst would do so.—lt was decided that a series of lectures be arranged

A COMMITTEE. Mr. FRITH said the time had come when they ought to have a larger Library, and as a means to that end he pro- posed that a sub-committee consisting of Messrs. Rhodes, Simpson, Handley, Hazlehurst, Lake, and himself should be appointed to seek for, purchase, and deal with the question of lending beoks. There were plenty of gentlemen in the town who would be willing to give books if they were asked.—Mr. BRISCOII seconded the motion, which was carried, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: ROBBERY OF BRASS AT RUNCORN. CHARGE AGAINST A MARINE STORE DEALER.
div.p: ROBBERY OF BRASS AT RUNCORN. CHARGE AGAINST A MARINE STORE DEALER.

Wm. Ball (17), Montrose Abbot (15), Anthony Welsh John Wakefield (13), Martin McDonald, and Ellen Lavelle, were charged at Runcorn Mice Court, yesterday, before Captain Hazleburst and Mr. H. Reynolds with having stolen 26Ibs. of brass of the value of Sc Bd, the pro- perty of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited. They were also charged with receiving the same knowing it to have been stolen.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson remarked on the youth of the prisoners with the exception of the woman, Lavelle, said the brass steps were used at slip, on which boats are repaired, opposite the Belverdere in Runcorn. They were used for hauling boats from the river on to the slip, and were only occasionally in use. From what came to the knowledge of the police on Thursday morning the brass was found at Mr. Harper's, marine store dealer, in the town. It also transpired that the female prisoner, who was a marine store dealer, purchased the brass very much under its value from several of the prisoners. He did not know how far he could carry the case; against the prisoners Welsh and McDonald, and he would consequently ask for their discharge, as he intended to call them as witnesses against the others. He need not point out that it was an in- centive to youths to commit offences of this nature when they could easily dispose of their spoil. He did not wish to be hard upon Mrs. Lavelle, and he was very sorry she was placed in her present position, but he felt it incumbent upon him to bring her before the Bench, as he was only doing his duty, and if the Bench found the evidence insufficient he should be quite satisfied if she was discharged. The charge was of a more grave character, seeing that she had purchased things which were actually in use, and not the slightest sign of rust about them, If there were no receivers there would be no thieves. Under the Act of Parliament a marine store dealer was not allowed to pur- chase a less quantity of brass, copper, or metal of that de— scription than 561bs.,and as the brass in question had been sold to Mrs. Lavelle on three or four different occasions, she had committed that number of offences against the law.— Welsh and McDonald were then discharged.—John Dykes and James Weedall proved that the brass produced was the property of the Navigation Company, and Anthony Welsh Martin McDonald stated that one night about a fortnight ago they went to the yard on the Belvedere with the pri- soners Ball and Abbot, whom they saw unscrew the brass steps with a key which they obtained from a flat. They then hid the brass. Next day Welsh saw Abbot and Ball coming from Mrs. Lavelle's rag shop. He asked what sum they had got for the brass, and they said 3s. Ip.-P.S. Mac Michael deposed to receiving the brass from Harper, the marine store dealer, who had purchased it from Mrs. Lavelle. He then went to the store of Mrs. Lavelle and asked her if she had lately bought any brass or iron castings. ' She replied in the aegative, but said she had purchased some iron, rags, and brass from the three prisoners. He examined her book, but found no entry of any brass. He apprehended the prisoners, who, when charged, admitted stealing the brass. That morning he apprehended Mrs. Lavelle on the charge of receiving stolen property. She made a statement to the effect that she did not know the brass was stolen, and that it ivas mixed with a quantity of of bones and old iron. She thonght it did not therefore need entering in the book.—There was a second charge against Ball, McDonald, and Welsh for stealing iron, but Mr. Superintendent Williamson said he would not proce ed with the case with the consent of their worships.—Capt. Hazlehurst said this was a very serious case indeed. Ball, who seemed to have been the ringleader in the robbery, would be committed to gaol for one month, with hard labour; Abbott for 21 day's hard labour i and Wakefield would receive 12 strokes with the blrchrod. Mrs. Lavelle's statement that she believed that the brass had been taken from the river was preposterous, seeing that it was clean. As Superintendent Williamson said, if there were no receivers, there would be less thieves. She would be committed to Knutsford Gaol for six weeks' hard labour.— Walsh and McDonald were cautioned.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CH A.PEL BAZAAR AT FRODSFIAAI.
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CH A.PEL BAZAAR AT FRODSFIAAI.

A bazaar was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Wed- nesday and Thursday, in aid of the Building Fund of the Primitive Methodist Chapel. The opening ceremony took place, on Wednesday morning, at 11 o'clock, when the bazaar was opened by Philip Speakman, Esq., of Runcorn. There was a fair attendance at the commencement of the proceedings, amongst whom we noticed the Revs. D. Scho- field, J. Pickwell, and J. R. Trotter, Mr. and Mrs. Philip Speakman, of Runcorn, Mr. and Mrs. Midwood, Mr. and Mrs. Booth, W. B. Gibson, Esq., Mr. J. Diven, Mesdames Rothwell, Hough, Booth, Jones, and Messrs, Edwards, Clarke, Borwick, and others. After singing a hymn, prayer was offered by the Rev. D. Schofield, the resident minister. The Rev. J. PICKWELL, in introducing Mr. Speakman, said he was a neighbour of his, and when he was requested to select a gentleman to open the bazaar he quickly succeeded in securing the services of Mr. Speak- man. Personally he was unknown to him; be had heard of him by the hearing of the ear, and what he had heard gave him hope to believe that he would consent to open their bazaar. In order that be might be the more successful he 'took with him a gentleman well known to their connection in Runcorn and intimate with Mr. Speakman, and they succeeded in obtaining Mr. Speakman's consent. He thought Mr. Speakman felt as much interested in the bazaar as they did themselves. They knew what their object was —to lower the debt on their beautiful chapel. There was a debt upon the premises which was too heavy for their friends, and they were anxious to reduce it by £l2O, and he hoped they might succeed; their friends had done their best in making a good provision for buyers, and he hoped that there would be a good many willing and able to purchase. Mr. SPEAKMAN-said that Mr. Pickwell had laid the case so fully before them that if he had gone on a little further and declared the bazaar open it would have been all that was required—(laughter)—and having said so much with regard to obtaining his consent to open the bazaar, be need not dilate upon the matter ;.but he might say that in all that he took in hand for which he had the time and disposition, he looked upon as a great privilege when the object was to further the cause of Christ. A great many people talked about bazaars, and some condemned them, while others said they served a very useful end. For his own part he liked bazaars. A gentleman had given him a sovereign towards the present bazaar to show his appreciation of the work, and he began to think he had male a great mistake in not com- mencing. to talk about the bazaar to his friends a little earlier. (Laughter.) However, be had done the best he could for them. He was in-

div.head: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.

The usual monthly meeting was held in the Commis- sioners' Board-room, on Thursday. The Rev. Canon Barclay, the chairman, presided, and there were also present Messrs. John Simpson G. S. Hazehurst, T. Riley, —. Rhodes, Lake J. R. Simpson, Peter Briscoe, Wm. Handler, and W. Brookes (secretary).
THE LIBRARIAN'S REPORT.-PRESENTATIONS.

The LIBRARIAN (Mr. J. D. Jones) reported that 1,572 'mks had been borrowed from the lending library during September last, consisting of—Theology, 52; philosophy, political economy, Jr.c., 21 ; history, travelling, and biography, 310; science and art, 55; poetry and drama, 27; prose fiction, 1,015; miscellaneous, 92. He had received in fines, 165.; for the sale of catalogues, 9s. 9d.; sale of tickets, 13s. 2d.; total, £1 Hs. 11d. The books presented were— Subsidence at Northwich and Winsford, the cause and cure, by Mr. G. S. flazlehurst ; reference catalogue of current literature, by Mr. G. Bellamy; I've been thinking, by Mr. Wm. Handley.—The SECRETARY read the following letter, dated the 26th September, from Emmanuel Schools, Bolton, and addressed to the chairman :

Dear Bir,— Might I ask you, on behalf of the committee of the Runcorn Free Library, to accept the accompanying works of one of England's greatest painters—Wilatim Hogarth. It was with the.grea' est interest that [read in the local papers of the establishment of a Free Reference and Lending Library in my native town, and if Runcorn in the future should receive but a tithe of the advantages derived from a similar institution In the town in which I hs.v,3 now resided for over 22 years, the promoters of the scherce will have every reason to be more than gratified.—l am, dear sir, y,9urs faithfully, W. MooRE.

Mr. P. Cowell, Librarian to tite Liverpool Free Library, wrote as follows :—" Dear sir,—l have pleasure in forward- ing you by request of the committee of this Library a list of 45 volumes of duplicate works which they will be pleased to present to the Runcorn Free Library, provided you do not already possess copies. The books are in good condition, and many of them usefully bound. If your librarian would kindly go over the list and mark off such as you do not re- quire I will forward the others without delay. Hoping your Library is prospering in its good work."—None of the books offered, which were of a miscellaneous character, it appeared, were in the Library.—On the motion of Mr. Wm. HANDLEY, the Secretary was instructed to forward the thanks of the Committee to the donors of the books. THE LOCATION OF THE LIBRARY: MR. HAZLEIMRST'S OFFER. The following letter was read : _ _

The Elms, Runcorn.—Dear Sir,—l have pleasure in inform- ing you that I have offered to rent the Commissioners' rooms for the sum of £2O a year in order that a reading room may be opened daily f_r the benefit of the town for the space of three years. lam willing to guarantee that no financial difficulty shall arise therefrom. Believe me, dear sir, faithfuly yours, GEo. S. HAzLEaultsP. If you can see your way to accept this ofler, please n )tify your willingness to the next monthly meet- ing of the Board. The CHAIRMAN also read a communication from the Board of Commissioners, which stated that they agreed to the opening of the Library on Thursday evenings, but were advised that they had no power to rent the Commissioners' rooms to the committee.—Mr. HAZLEHURST said he had received a letter from the Highway and Sanitary Com- mittee, thanking him for his offer with reference to the Library, and informing him that they could not come to any decision on the subject until after the next meeting of the Board. He (Mr. Hazlehurst) should be glad if the Library Committee could see their 'ivay to accept his offer and notify the fact to the Board of Commissioners.—The CHAIRMAN inquired if the only way by which the town could have the Library open daily was by private occupation.—Mr. HAZLEIIIIRST : That we can have a reading room at all. The funds of the committee were not sufficient to enable the Library to be open daily.—Mr. SIMPSON : Supposing in several years yoa had to give up the place, the Commissioners could not rent the rooms to the Library:Committee.—The CHAIRMAN: No; it would always have to be rented to an individual. They may let it to an ißdividual member of the committee.—Mr. RHODES: But they can allow the committee to occupy with- out rent.—Mr. BRISCOE I think it is not the feeling of the Commissioners to do so.—Mr. HAZLEHURST : That is cer- tainly not the present feeling of the Commissioners.—The CHAIRMAN observed that a change of feeling might take place amongst the Commissioners in three years.—Mr. RHODES said if the committee accepted Mr. Hazlehurst's generous offer, there would be absorbed in working expenses an amount of money which ought to be devoted to the pur- chase of books.—Mr. HAZLEHURST: Mr. Rhodes' objection is covered by my offer, which says that no financial difficulty shall arise. I don't mean in any way to restrict the purchase of books.—Mr. HANDLEY thought the committee had better accept, And strongly endorse, Mr. Hazlehurst's generous offer, seeing that it was carrying out what was suggested at the earliest meeting of the committee—that the present rooms were the best suited for the purposes of the Library. The Commis- sioners would then be freed from their difficulty ; because they would have a tenant for the premises, and they had bound themselves to remove when they got a tenant. The Library Committee would have rooms-which could be at once adopted for the requirements of the Library, and also of a reading room sufficient for Runcorn for several years at any rate ; and he thought by that time those who thought the committee was moving along too hurriedly would come round to the opinion that they were only acting in accordance with the wants and wishes of the town. He had great pleasure in proposing that Mr. Hazlehurst's offer lie accepted, and that the Commissioners be notified to that effect.—Mr. SIMPSON seconded the rnoticn, which was carried unanimously.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that Mr. Hazle- burst said in his letter "in order that a reading room may be open daily for the use of the town." That would involve the expense of a keeper of the Library.—Mr. HAZLEHURST : I think if it were open each evening it would meet the case. Of course, the working class cannot come in the day time. However, that is a matter for future consideration.—Mr. BaiscoE observed that the Commissioners objected to the present ',room being made into a reading room on account of the noise from the street.—Mr. HAELEHURST pointed out that this could be remedied by means of double windows.

div.head: GOOD SUGGESTION.
div.p: A GOOD SUGGESTION.

Mr. HAZLEERMST said at the last meeting of the commit- tee he wAs requested to inquire whether the 'committee could obtain any advantage from Messrs. W. H. Smith's station libraries, in the way of hiring books which it would not b 3 desirable to purchase. He had gone into the matter, and found that the committee could have 24 volumes a time, changed twice a week, for £5 ss. for six months, asd he moved that the committee adopt this course. It would be the best expenditure they could make.—The consideration of the subject was deferred a month, until some informa- tion as to the method of working could be obtained.
A COURSE OF LECTURES DECIDED UPON.

Mr. WM. HANDLEY presented the report of the sale- committee appointed to consider the advisability of a series of lectures being delivered under the auspices of the Library. He said the committee had come to the conclusion that it was desirable that a series of lectures should be delivered, and recommended that a course should be at once instituted, that they should be given at intervals of three weeks, com- mencing on the first Thursday In November, that they should be free as they were in connection with a free Library—(hear, hear,)—but that a box be placed in the lecture-room, so that any person who wished to contribute towards the expenses could do so. The whole of the lectures would be illustrated by either experiments or diagrams. Mr. John Simpson, Mr. Rhodes, and Mr. Frith had consented to

div.head: 31 iNCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE 31 iNCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

The Times says :—" Cannot the sea be brought to Man- ches'er ? For every kind of communication with the outer world it is a mere suburb of Liverpool, and, for a suburb, a very distant one. Five millions and a half are at the mercy of a combination holding the pass between them and the rest of the human race, and making the same use of their coign of vantage as the medifeval barons did of their em- battled tollgates thrown across the world's highways. City, port, dock, and railway vie in extortion, and levy duties to the extent of human forbearance. Many millions of tons of material and of manufactures pass annually to and fro between the port and the industrious region at the back of it, and on every ton Liverpool has its profit. It cannot be expected that a large population placed at the mercy of a single port should sit quietly under it. It now appears, and it cannot be a matter of surprise, that there are several alternative ways of bringing the sea to Manchester and making it a port, and that these are so independent, and have each of them so much to say for themselves, that it is possible they may one day be all in operation. Not only do the schemes multiply, they even expand in their aim. It is now hoped that Manchester may be one day inde- pendent both of Liverpool and of the Mersey, the bar of which is continually causing the most vexatious delays. Ocean steamers that count the minutes of their passage lose hours, and one train after another, waiting outside the bar. This, it is now said, is quite unnecessary. The Manchester Ship Canal is the project which has been longest before the public in a form to challenge criticism. This it has encountered, chiefly on the ground that it is not likely to pay. As the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal more than century ago, and the Manchester and Liverpool Railway half a century ago, were met with the same objection— indeed all our canals and all our railways to begin with—we need not think very much of it. If the canal is ever made, it is quite sure to be used to the full extent of its capabilities. The question is whether it can be made. The projectors prastically, and as they are to be understood, decline to estimate the cost. The revenue and the annnal expenses are more within calculation, especially by the light of other works, and they leave a margin itself large enough to pay interest on a very great expenditure, and certain to increase every year. Even if the outlay were 14 millions—better say at once 20—the saving to the manufacturing district would be such as to secure a good return to the shareholders. No doubt, once begun, the work would be proceeded with, and that to completion. No doubt, too, it would be a great gain to the manufacturers, and, in the long run, it might prove a paving and profitable work. But we must confess to a mis- giving that the first shareholders might find themselves paid rather by the glory and grandeur of their work than in solid coin." -

The Daily 2Vews asks :—" But is there traffic enoagh for the proposed canal? The promoters are sanguine, but they have not published the basis of their calculations. Until they do so, scepticism is allowable. Assuming, however, that there is traffic, if the canal were made Manchester mer- chants would be able to put their goods on board ship at their own quays, and the goods would be conveyed directly to their destination, whereas at present they have to be sent by railway to Liverpool, and there transhipped to ocean- going vessels, thus exposing them to risk of damage and in- creasing the cost of carriage. It is notorious that trades of all kinds are migrating from inland districts to the seaside, even a very short distance of railway carriage placing the inland manufacuturer at a disadvantage. Manchester mer- chants complain that their trade at present is being injured by the heavy charges for conveyance levied upon their goods; nor is it merely upon the goods for export that a saving would be effected were the canal constructed. The raw materials of manufacture would also be brought to Man- chester instead of as at present being landed at Liverpool, and then sent on by train. The cotton used by cotton spin- ners, for instance, would be brought direct from Bombay, New Orleans, or Alexandria; and so would the wheat con- sumed by the operatives. There Would thus be a double saving—on the goods sold and the goods bought—aid doubtless the trade of Manchester would receive a new im- petus. In the same way, the towns all along the canal, such as Warrington, would benefit. To same extent so likewise would such places as Oldham, Staleybridge, and even towns further eist."

The Manchester Guardian of yesterday published the first of a series of articles on the commercial prospects of the ship canal, and it dealt chiefly with the geographical question. From that article we take the following :—" In connection with the question of geographical position, there is another circumstance which cannot fail to impress anyone who will look at a geological map. The southern edge of the Lancashire and Cheshire coalfields (which may be regarded as one continuous coal area), sweeps round in what may be roughly described as a semi-circle from St. Helens to Macclesfield. and at the central point of this sweep stands Manchester. Between Liverpool and the western extremity of the coalfields there is more or less wide strip of the Bunter sandstone wrapping all the way round the coast edge to Preston. For a considerable distance the Irwell almost touches the southern edge of this coal- field. Thus, while Liverpool stands at some dis- tance from the majority of the pits, we in Manchester may paraphrase the Laureate's words and say that we have coal to right of us, and coal to left of us, and also coal behind us. Going further east there is the Yorkshire coalfield, with its extensions into Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire, near the western edge of which—that is, the side next to us—stands Bradford, Huddersfield, Barns- ley, Sheffield, and Chesterfield. That all this coal-field is nearer to us than it is to Liverpool goes without saying; but what is perhaps more to the purpose is, that the dis- tance between Manchester and the nearest point on its western edge, say Huddersfield, is less than the distance ba- tween Hull or Grimsby and the point on the eastern edge of the coalfields, say Pontefract, most adjacent to the eastern ports. Even if we take Goole as the point for com- parison, so far as the east coast shipping and coast- ing trade is concerned, we find that the distance from Manchester to Huddersfield is only 26 miles, or about nine miles greater than the distance from Pontefract to Goole, the distance from Pontefract to Hull being over 41 miles. 'A far better idea of the favourable position of Man- chester even as regards this, the most extensive coalfield of Great Britain, which, excluding the Durham coalfield, might be regarded as the natural source of supply for the east coast, can be obtained, if we lraw an imaginary line in a north south direction through the centre of the coalfield. Every portion of the western half will then be seen to be as near or nearer to us than to Goole, and this half includes the great majority of the more important centres ,of manufacture, such as Bradford, Dewsbury, Huddersfield, Barnsley, Sheffield, and Chesterfield., If we take Barnsley as a central point, we find that it is' about equi-distant between Manchester and Goole. To sum up, with the exception of a very small section, every part of the Yorkshire, Derbyshire, and Nottingham coalfield is nearer to Manchester than to Hull or Grimsby, and the greater-and most important part of it is nearer to Manches- ter even than to Goole. 7 The importance of these considera- tions comes out more clearly when it is remembered that if we add to the distance from Manchester the 31 miles be- tween Liverpool and this city, the advantage would then be entirely on the side of the east coast. Thus, the distance from Liverpool to Huddersfield, the nearest point on the western edge of the coalfield, is 57 miles; while the distance from Huddersfield to Goole is 40 miles only, and from Hud- dersfield even to Hull is only 63 miles." The Manchester correspondent of the Times, in an article in which other projected schemes are discussed, observes— "It may surprise most people to hear that the neighbour- hood of Northwich has been thought of as the site of future docks, in which the largest imaginable steamers from all parts of the world might find themselves at home. But this is not a scheme put before the public. The data for calcu- lation are in the hands only of people supposed to be fully acquainted with the natural features of the district, its exist- ing waterways, and its latent capabilities. Geographers have described the whole surface of Cheshire as having the appearance of a delta, formed by some large river which has vanished. But as long as there is no published report upon levels, quantities, or costs, the question of an ocean port in Cheshire may figure as no more than a phantom in the eyes of the advocates of the port of Manchester. If there be any substance in it its reality ought certainly to appear when the various interests stirred by the Manchester scheme come to wage their Parliamentary war."

CONCEUT IN AID OF THE INFIRMARY.—We would remind our readers of the concert to be given this (Saturday) even- ing, in the Public Hall, in aid of the Warrington Infirmary and Dispensary. The concert is under the patranage of his worship the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), and the vocalists are all local amateurs of well-known ability.

MR. H. A. LAMBETH'S CHOIR AT WARRINGTOW.—This talented company visited the town on Wednesday evening, and gave a grand concert in the Public Hall. The eight or ten vocalists brought together and trained by Mr. Lambeth —himself a skilful musician and coniposer—form, without doubt, the finest select choir we remember to have listened to, and well may they be said io have earned their right to announce themselves under royal patronage, having had twice the honour of appearing before her Majesty at Balmoral. As may be guessed, the company is essentially Scotch. Nevertheless, music of all leading nationalities is introduced, and English and Irish fiongs, ballads, ttc., are amongst the most enjoyable items performed. We have not space at disposal to speak of the concert in detail. We can only say that the audience were enthusiastic in tokens of approbation of the tasteful singing both of solos and con- certed music. In the latter especially, Mr. Lambeth is singularly successful in eliciting from his choir the most subtle distinctions of light and shade. Some of the un- accompanied anthems, part-songs, Ste., were marked by the observance of a pianissimo than which we have not heard anything more exquisite. We trust to have another op- portunity of listening to these accomplished artists at no very remote date.
SUNDAY CLOSING. MEETING AT RUNCORN LAST NIGHT.

Under the auspices of the Central Association for Stop- ping the Sale of Intoxicating Liquor on Sunday, a public meeting was held in the Runcorn Public Hall, last evening, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Norman. He was sup- ported on the platform by the Revs. J. Preston, J. D. Thomas, George Hack, John Billington J. Pickwell, Evan Williams, and Messrs. Edward Whitwell (of Kendal, secretary of the Association), John Simpson, Robert Shaw, J. K. Digges, Joseph Bridgewater, and J. D. Jones. There was a large audience present. _

The CHAIRMAN, in openiag the proceedings, said he con- sidered it an honour as well as a pleasure to preside over the meeting, especially as its object was to promote the closing of publichouses on Sunday. He did not see why a publican and his wife should not have the same privilege as the grocer and draper—of seeing his little children dressed up, and take them to a place of worship, church or chapel as the case might be. It was a thorough disgrace for Christian England not to have the Sunday traffic in intoxicating liquor pelt' down altogether. Ireland, Scotland, and Wales had a Sunday Closing Act in operation, awl he believed it worked very well. He trusted the meeting would be unani- mous in doing all they possibly could towards obtaining a a Sunday Closing Act for England. (Applause). The Rev. W. PRESTON moved the first resolution as follows :—"That the rapid ripening of public opinion through- out England in favour of Sunday closing of public houses, and the recent carrying of an Act for Wales through Parlia- ment by overwhelming majorities, are subjects for gratitude and hopefulness; and that as the testimony of Scotland in favour of Sunday closing after 28 years' experience of the Act is so remarkable, not a single petition having been presented against it for many years, and as the Sunday Closing Act of 1878 for Ireland has been productive of such great and undoubted good, that its extension to the five exempted towns is now being loudly demanded, this meeting authorises the chairman to sign on its behalf petitions to both • Houses of Parliament in favour of a measure which will bestow a similar boon upon the whole of England." The traffic in intoxicating liquor on the Lord's Day, remarked Mr. Preston, he considered nothing more nor less than a blot on the Legislature of the country and the national escutcheon. He would go even further, and say it was a sin and a national disgrace—a dis- honour to the Almighty God. The effect of the public- house being open on §unday was demoralising in the extreme, and he was sure they had had such proof of that in Runcorn, without mentioning towns of greater import- ance, such as Liverpool and Manchester. It was a direct foe to religion, as he, as a minister of the Gospel, had ever found it to ha. Mr. Preston touched upon the greater temptation the public-houses were on Sunday, because it was the day on which working men had more leisure, and withal with more money in their pockets. On the Monday morning the working man who had been indulging in drink on the previous day found himself in an unfit state to work, and Mr. Whitworth, M.P. had calculated that in one year he had lost £35,000 through his working men addicted to drink failing to pertorm their labours on the Monday. Dealing with the objection that the people of the country were not ripe for the passing of a Sunday Closing Act, he maintained that the country at large was in favour'of it, and gave statistics in support of his contention. The publicans of Runcorn were in favour of the measure, and in London over a thousand publicans were also in favour. Last time he was on that platform he spoke too long—(a laugh)—but he would not do so that night. Before sitting down, however, he would quote the opinion of a statesman who he could not agree with on some points, but he did on others—Mr. W. E. Gladstone. (Loud and continued applause.) It was "That the religious observance of the Lord's Day is the min prop of the re- ligious character of the country. From amoral, social, and physical point of view Sunday observance is a duty of absolute consequence." (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. WHITWELL (deputation) seconded the motion. He remarked that it seemed to him as if the Christian Church had been asleep to allow the day given to bless mankind body and soul, to become the day of their degradation and one which carried forward its pernicious influence through- out the whole country. They were called together that evening to see what could be done in the matter. He was glad to say that not only had Scotland spoken out, but Ireland and the various counties of England were now say- ing that if the rest of England was not prepared for Sunday Closing they would try to get it for their own county—to get their own neighbourhood delivered from this terrible infliction of Sunday immorality. He appealed to those in Runcorn and Cheshire to use their influence with their members to get them to vote on the right side. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Whitwell spoke of the hardship the opening of public-houses on Sunday was to the publicans and their servants. He thought Sunday schools gave one of the most remarkable evidence of the self-denying character of our holy religion; but the work of the Sunday school teacher was undone by the opening of public-houses on Sunday. There were more young people led wrong by the public- houses on the Sunday night than on all the other evenings of the week put together. (Hear, hear.) As an illustration of this fact, a friend of his was for some years a chaplain of the Salford Gaol, and out of 724 prisoners he found that 624 had been Sunday school teachers and con- nected with a church. An eminent public man had said that with education everything would be right, but here they feund our religious instructors going wrong. Mr. Whitwell quoted stitistics showing how greatly opinions in favour of Sunday closing preponderated over those against. He asked those present in favour of public-houses being open an hour at noon and at night to hold up their hands. [There was no response, and the audience loudly applauded. He then requested those in favour of closing public-houses the whole of Sunday, except in cases of lodgers and bona fide travellers, to hold up their hands. The response was apparently unanimous' and there was continued applause.] Public-houses had been closed in Scotland for the last 28 years with the most gratifying results. Before the passing of the Act Edinburgh gaol was crowded, but now, instead of having 578 cells full, they had only 329, awl 246 were empty. (Applause.) Fifty years ago Scotland 3 the best educated country in the world and the most unken. He found in a Blue 'Book, published this year, that the drunkenness of Scotland was one-eighth less than that of England. The drunkenness of Glasgow and Edinburgh together was not half what it was before Sunday closing. He was taking the whole week and every week in the year. The consumption of British spirits in Scotland was one- fourth less than ever it was before the measure was passed. In Ireland there were 120,000 a year fewer cases of drunkenness than they were before the houses were closed on Sunday. (Applause.) Mr. Whitwell urged upon those present to take a canvas of the householders of the town on the question, and to write to the two members of Parlia- ment for Mid-Cheshire, and earnestly beg of them to vote in favour of Sunday closing, and having done so, they would do a great service to the whole country. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT SHAW supported the resolution in a brief speech. He said in Widnes, which was, or had been, one of the most drunken towns in the country, and through the labours of the Salvation Army—(loud applause)—the Blue Ribbon Army, and various organisations in connection with the religious bodies, the takings in the public-houses had been reduced by some £4OO a week. (Applause.) If a change like that could take place in that dark, smoky town on the other side of the Mersey, what change would not take place in a town like Runcorn—(laughter)—where they had got such intelligent people—(laughter)—clean, decent working people,who knew the advantage of being temperate? (Applause.) The resolution was carried with acclamation.

The Rev. J. BILLINGTON moved the next resolution, which stated that the time for legislative action on Sunday clos- ing in regard to this country had fully come, and the meet- ing therefore requested the earnest support of the members for Mid-cheshire to a measure for stopping the sale of intoxicating liquor throughout Englaud during the whole of Sunday. Mr. Billington delivered a very humourous and energetic speech-, which was well received. The Rev. EVAN WILLIAMS seconded the motion, which was supported by the Rev. J. PICKWELL, who in the course of his observations said that he hoped the time would quickly an lye when the manufacturers in the town would see their way to closing their works on Sunday, a remark which was loudly cheered. Tbe resolution was passed with enthusiasm, and it was decided to forward it to the members for the division.

The Rev. GEo. HACK moved that the following gentle. men, with power to add their number, he the committee of officers of the Runcrn auxiliary of the Association :—Mr. J. D. Jones, convenor of the committee, the ministers of the town, Messrs. Jno. Simpson, T. Norman, J. R. Frith, R. Shaw, W. Handley, and W. H. Rogerson. He was extremely glad that they had selected Mr. Jones to be the convenor of the committee, as he was a thorough going and enthusiastic teetotaller, and as a bachelor he
" Had no wife to bother his life"
—(laughter)---and was thus able to devote a great deal of time to the movement. (Applause.) The Rev. J. D. THOMAS seconded the motion, which was carried.
Mr. J. D. JONES proposed a vote of thanks to the deputa- tion, Mr. Whitwell.
Mr. DIGGES seconded, and the motion was carried with acclamation. •, The LECTURER replied, and a vote of thanks having been accorded to the chairman for presiding, the proceedings terminated.

PRINCE 01 WALES THEATRE. " Recommended to Mercy," taken from one of Miss Braddon's works, is the title of a play which has been produced at the above theatre, this week. The chief character is that of "Joshua Haggard," which is very cleverly- sustained by Mr. E. H. Edlesten, an old Warring- tonian, who each night has been successful in drawing large audiences, and has on each occasion been greeted with continued rounds of applause. The piece is excellently staged, and the various parts are well impersonated by a powerful company. MANCHESTER CORN, THURSDAY. Messrs. W. Warburto and Co. report as follows :—The improvement reported last week has been maintained in the interval, and a considerable business has transpired at higher prices. American advices have also notified advanced rates. Imports into Liverpool have been heavy of wheat and flour, liberal of beans, but small of everything else. At to-day's market there was a good con- sumptive inquiry for most articles, though buyers were some- what checked by the advance demanded. English wheat was Id to ad, foreign red Id to 2d, and white Id per cental higher. Flour was held for an advance of Id to 2d per cental. Oats firm. Oatmeal rather lower. Beans slow at previous quota- tions. Canadian peas id dearer. with continued short shipments, commanded 2d to d per cents' over the currencies of last market day.

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES. STLLABUS:—Mondays : Practical Chemistry, 6-30 p.m. to 8-0 p.m. ; Alkali Manufacture, 8-0 p.m. to '9 0 p.m.; Electricity:(Ad- vanced) and Inorganic Chemistry (advanced) on alternate Mon- day nights. 9-0 to 100 p.m. Tuesdays: Art-Drawing, 7-0 p.m. to 8-0 p.m.; Machine Construction and Drawing, 8-0 p.m. to 9-0 p.m. Wednesdays: Art-Drawing, 7-0 p.m. to 8-0 p.m. ; Build- ing Construction and Drawing, 80 p.m. to 9-0 p.m. Thursdays: Inorganic Chemistry (Elerrentary Stage) 7-0 p.m. to 11.0 ; Electricity (Elersten'ary), 1-0 to 9-0 p.m. Fee, 3s. per Class for all Classes, except Practical Chemistry. Fee for Practical Chemistry Bs.. and a deposit of Is. for the use of apparatus. This deposit will bb returned at the end of the Session if breakages, &c., aze made good. The Laboratory is now being fitted up in the most complete manner. Each Student will have a separate bench with lock- up cupboard allotted to him, and he will have full control and charge of the apparatus and re-agents. At the end of each lesson each student must put away the apparatu i and re-agents In the lock-up cupboard. Should a Student lose his key he will be charged is. for a new one. As the rumber of benches is limited, it is desirable that intending students should make application at orce. If there are more applimnts than benches, the Committee reserve to themselves the right of deciding which students are to kave the preference. The Library will be open on Sundays from 6 until 9 p.m. The Laboratory will be complete and ready for Students on the 30th inst. There are still several benches vacant. J. MORRISON', Hon. Sec.

Joshua Povine Bend Eddy d'ed on the 26th ult. in the milet of filth and vermin, in an unsightly house at 561, South-street, in Philadelphia Edly was a negro, 84 years of age, and worth £20,000. Blaney was his god. Ha had nothing to do with his fellow- men. He fed scantily, clothed shabbily, and only thought of money. He owned 37 houses in different parts of the city, nine in Camden, two farms in New Jersey, some pro- perty in Frinkfort, and souse at Chester. He was born a slave to Virginia and learned the trade of a barber in Con- nallevitle, Pa. iubsequently he became a member of the ilnerancy of coloured preachers. He was ordained a deacon, and went to New York, where he was ordained an elder, and placed over eight churches, and travelled over the circuit from Elizabeth, N.J., to Mount Holly. Daring this time he married Bishop Allen's daughter, and settled down in Calumbia, Pa. This was in 1820. In addition to his duties as a preacher there, he carried on his trade as a barber. After a few years spent in Columbia, he came to Philadel- phia. Tnen came the turning point in his life. His wife proved unLithful, and the couple were divorced. Eddy then became a miser. He had loved his wife, the coloured ancients say, and her perfidy broke his heart. He took no interest La anything but money. Ile bent all his energies t its accumule*ien, and succeeded. Houses and lands were cheap then. 1e knew that in time their value would in- crease. He invested his money in this way, and his specu- ations were crowned with success. Geonne IV.
